exp.4:8:
Paul reminds the Corinthians that he had already written them an earlier letter, which has not been preserved, asking them not to mix with or keep close company with the sexually immoral, that is, with those who live in sexual sin. The phrase "company with" here means having close, personal association with them.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a serious case of immorality among its members. He speaks of Passover and leaven to show that tolerated sin spreads like yeast through the dough. He makes clear right away that he was not referring to people of the world, but to someone who calls himself a brother and lives in sin without repentance.

For today: the church must guard its purity with love and firmness, without judging harshly those who do not believe, but without approving sin among believers, always seeking their restoration.
exp.14:13:
Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, then what he and the other apostles proclaim has no meaning, and neither does the faith of the Corinthians. Here "vain" means empty, without value or result. The "preaching" is the message they were proclaiming.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul shows them the consequence: if the dead are not raised, then Christ was not raised either. And if Christ was not raised, the whole gospel falls apart. For him, the resurrection is not a detail but the center of the Christian message.

For today: our faith does not rest only on beautiful ideas or good advice, but on a fact: Christ lives. When you doubt or feel weary, return to this foundation and ask God to strengthen your trust in the risen Jesus.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that Paul and the other teachers are God's fellow workers, meaning collaborators or co-workers who serve alongside Him. It also calls believers a cultivated field and a building. Everything belongs to God: the workers labor, but the field and the house are His.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided because some lined up behind one leader and others behind another. To correct them, he reminds them that servants like himself and Apollos are not the most important. God is the one who gives the growth, and each worker will answer to Him for his work.

Today, if you serve in your church, do it with humility and without competing. Do not compare yourself to others or think you are indispensable. Work faithfully, knowing that the fruit comes from God and that His work is what counts.
exp.13:18:
Paul says that when the church is gathered, he would rather speak only five words with his understanding, so that he can instruct others, than speak ten thousand words in a tongue that no one understands. "Understanding" here means the mind. "Instruct" means to teach. The phrase "a tongue no one understands" refers to a language that those present do not comprehend.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who valued speaking in tongues very highly. He himself speaks in tongues more than they do, and he thanks God for it, but he corrects them: in the meeting, what matters is that everyone is built up. A message that no one understands does not help the congregation.

For today: before you speak, pray, or serve in the church, ask yourself whether what you say will help others understand and grow. Use clear and simple words, because loving others includes making sure they can follow you.
exp.1:1:
He says that when Paul was in Corinth, he decided to put forward no other subject as the most important, but Jesus Christ, and in particular Jesus Christ crucified. The phrase "I determined" means "I decided" or "I resolved."

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city that valued eloquence and human wisdom very highly. Some in the church were divided and boasted about their favorite leaders. Paul reminds them that when he visited them, he did not come with impressive speeches. He focused on the message of the cross, which seemed to many like weakness, but which God uses with power.

For today: before you speak about faith with someone, or teach others, ask yourself whether Christ and his work on the cross are the center, or whether you are trying to impress. Returning to Jesus keeps your faith simple and firm.
exp.9:7:
It says we must not fall into sexual immorality, as some of the Israelites did in the desert, and because of it twenty-three thousand died in a single day. The word "fornication" refers to any sexual relationship outside God's plan.

The apostle Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, a city known for its atmosphere of vice. He reminds them of what happened to Israel so that they might learn from their mistakes. That episode seems to refer to Numbers 25, where twenty-four thousand died; Paul mentions twenty-three thousand, and scholars explain the difference in several ways, with no definitive answer.

Today, the warning invites us to guard our purity without trusting in our own strength. We can avoid situations, images, or relationships that weaken us, and seek support from fellow believers, remembering that God cares for those who obey him.
exp.10:7:
It says that the first man, Adam, was not formed from a woman, but that the first woman, Eve, was formed from the man. Paul refers to the account in Genesis 2, where God forms the woman from Adam's rib.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a church with many disorders. In this passage he corrects practices in worship, such as covering the head. He uses the order of creation as an argument. Scholars disagree about what exact custom of the time was in view and how to apply it today. Paul himself balances this in verses 11 and 12: neither is independent of the other, and everything comes from God.

Today we can remember that men and women need each other. Let us honor others in the church with respect and humility, and seek the common good before our own comfort.
exp.14:56:
This verse says that we give thanks to God because He gives us the victory, and that this victory comes through Jesus Christ, our Lord. The word "but" here means "but", and "a" is simply "a". The victory is not something we win for ourselves; it is a gift.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, and he has been speaking about the resurrection. He has just said that death loses its power, and that sin is its "sting", that is, what does the harm, like the bite of an insect. He also mentions that the law showed sin without being able to remove it. So Paul ends with praise: Christ accomplished what we could not.

Today, when you feel defeated by your guilt or by the fear of death, begin by giving thanks. Rest in what Christ has already done, and from there keep going forward with courage.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that a person cannot take part in the Lord's supper and, at the same time, in feasts tied to demons. "Sharing" means that one takes part in, joins, or has fellowship with something. The "cup" and the "table" speak of fellowship and of loyalty.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city full of pagan temples. Some believers were eating at feasts where meat was offered to idols. Paul makes clear that the idol itself is nothing, but that behind that worship stand spiritual forces opposed to God. For this reason he asks them not to mix the two.

For today: examine whether there is anything in your life that competes with your loyalty to Christ, such as a habit, a friendship, or a practice that pulls you away from God. Ask him to give you a faithful and undivided heart.
exp.10:30:
It says that if each person examined themselves honestly before God, they would not have to be judged.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth because, when they celebrated the Lord's Supper, there were divisions, selfishness, and a lack of respect among them. Some ate and drank without thinking about others. Paul tells them that this attitude had consequences, and he invites them to examine themselves. The verses that follow explain that the Lord's correction aims to keep them from being condemned along with the world.

Before you pray, take part in the Lord's Supper, or spend time together as a church, take a moment to ask yourself honestly: is there something I should confess, or someone I should treat better? Correcting yourself in time is a sign of humility and of trust in God's grace.
exp.15:21:
It says that whoever does not love the Lord Jesus Christ is under a curse, or cut off from God. "Anathema" means something given over to judgment or set apart.

Paul writes this in his own hand, at the end of his letter to the Corinthians, a church marked by divisions, pride and disorder. Before saying goodbye, he reminds them of what is essential: love for Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our love for Jesus is real and not merely religious. That love shows itself in obeying him, in treating others well, and in living with hope, praying: "Come, Lord."
exp.9:32:
Paul says that in everything he tries to please everyone, that is, to be considerate of others. He does not seek what is good for himself, but what helps many, so that they may be saved.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were disagreements about eating meat that had been offered to idols. He teaches them that, even though they have freedom, they must not cause Jews, Gentiles, or the church to stumble. He presents himself as an example, since he gives up his rights for the good of others. In the next chapter, he invites them to imitate him as he imitates Christ.

Today, before you use your freedom in something debatable, ask yourself: "Does this help others draw near to God, or does it push them away?" Choose what builds up, even when it costs you something.
exp.8:21:
He says that Paul put himself on the level of the "weak," that is, those who were weak in faith or in conscience, in order to win them to Christ. Here "weak" means weak, not thin. Then he sums up his method: he became "all things to all men," adapting himself to each person, so that he might save some by every means possible.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth. He had been speaking about his freedom, and about how he gave up using his rights out of love for others. He adapted himself in customs and in dealings with people, without abandoning the law of Christ or betraying the gospel. He did all of it for the sake of the gospel, and right away he compares it to a race.

For today: before speaking about your faith, listen patiently and treat each person with respect, according to their situation and their struggles. You may yield in tastes and customs, but never in the truth of Christ.
exp.4:4:
It says that this person is to be "handed over to Satan," that is, removed from the fellowship of the church and left in the world where Satan holds sway. The phrase "destruction of the flesh" can mean the suffering or ruin of his sinful desires, or even physical harm; scholars understand it in different ways. The goal is that his spirit may be saved "in the day of the Lord Jesus," when Christ returns.

Paul writes to the Corinthians because a man was living in serious sexual sin, and the church was doing nothing about it, even taking pride in it. Paul asks them to act together, with the authority of Jesus. Then he reminds them that a little yeast leavens the whole batch.

Today we can learn that true love does not ignore sin. Correcting with humility, seeking the restoration of the person and not his punishment, protects the community and can lead to repentance.
exp.9:6:
It says we must not be worshipers of idols, as some of the Israelites were. The phrase "the people sat down to eat and drink" points to the sense of "worshipers": those who give honor to something as if it were God. Paul quotes Exodus 32:6: the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to "play," that is, to amuse themselves with feasting and excess, beside the golden calf.

The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, who lived surrounded by pagan temples and festivals. He reminds them of what happened in the desert as a warning: Israel was rescued by God, yet still fell into sin. Scholars understand that "play" also includes immoral behavior, although the text says it only briefly.

For today: examine what things have taken the place of God in your heart, even when they seem like simple pleasures. Enjoying a meal or a celebration is not wrong, but do not let pleasure, money, or fame rule you.
exp.0:2:
This verse is a greeting. Paul wishes the believers "grace," which is the undeserved favor of God, and "peace," which is the calm and harmony that come from being at rest with Him. Both come from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ. By naming them together as the source of these blessings, Paul places Jesus alongside the Father.

Paul writes, together with Sosthenes, to the church in Corinth. It was a community with many problems, such as divisions, which he will address in the letter. Even so, before correcting them, he greets them with affection and reminds them that they are sanctified in Christ. His wish for grace and peace shows that his dealings with them begin from love.

For today: before speaking with someone with whom you have a conflict, pray that they receive grace and peace from God, and try to offer both yourself in your words.
exp.7:2:
This verse says that if anyone loves God, God knows them. Loving God means having affection for him, and being "known by him" means that God recognizes that person as his own, in a close relationship. It does not only mean that God knows facts about that person, but that it is a relationship of affection.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was debating whether it was right to eat meat offered to idols. Some were boasting of having a great deal of knowledge. Paul reminds them that knowledge without love puffs up, and that what matters is loving God and loving others. Some scholars note that the text can also be understood as a warning against intellectual pride.

For today: instead of boasting about what you know of the Bible, seek to love God and to deal patiently with those who think differently. Knowledge helps, but love is what shows a real relationship with God.
exp.14:29:
Paul asks: "And why do we stand in danger every hour?" The word "stand in danger" here means "run into danger" or "put ourselves at risk." He is speaking of himself and the other apostles, who were under constant threat for preaching the gospel.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom denied the resurrection of the dead. He answers with a practical argument: if there is no resurrection, there is no point in risking one's life every day for Christ. His suffering makes sense only if the hope of the resurrection is true. Regarding the baptism "for the dead" mentioned in the previous verse, there are several interpretations, and it is not known with certainty what practice he had in mind.

For today: our hope in the resurrection gives value to what it costs to follow Jesus. Today you can forgive, serve, or be honest even when it costs you, trusting that nothing done for the Lord is lost.
exp.14:14:
It says that if the dead do not rise, the apostles would be found to be liars about God. They had declared that God raised Christ up from the tomb. But if resurrection were impossible, God would not have raised him up, and their witness would be false. The words "found" and "testified" in the source are explained here, so I have left those sentences out.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. He shows them the consequence: denying our resurrection also means denying Christ's. Paul and the other apostles had preached that Christ rose, and many witnesses had seen him alive (verses 3 to 8).

For today: our hope does not rest on a lovely idea, but on a fact in which God fulfilled what he promised. When you doubt or suffer, remember that Christ rose, and that gives firmness to your faith and your hope for the future.
exp.11:1:
They say that the Corinthians remembered their life before they knew Christ, when they were Gentiles, that is, not Jews. Then they were carried away toward idols, which were dumb: they did not speak, did not answer, and could do nothing. "Carried away" in the verse means being led along without choosing it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of temples and pagan religions. He is going to correct disorders about spiritual gifts. First he reminds them where they came from: the worship of idols that have no voice. This prepares the contrast with the Holy Spirit, who does speak and guide, and who leads people to confess Jesus as Lord.

For today: let us remember with gratitude where God brought us out from. It is also worth examining what things carry us along without our noticing, such as fashions, pressures, or desires, and asking the Spirit to guide us toward Christ.
exp.11:16:
It says that a body cannot be just one organ. If everything were an eye, there would be no hearing; if everything were hearing, there would be no sense of smell. The word translated as sense of smell is the sense of smelling. Paul uses questions to make us think: a body like that would not work.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and some considered themselves more important because of their spiritual gifts. He compares the church to a human body, where each member is different but necessary. The verses that follow say that God placed each member as he wanted.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or think that your service is worth little. Ask God how you can serve with what he has given you, and value those who have gifts different from yours. All of them are needed.
exp.6:7:
Paul tells the unmarried and the widows that it is good for them to remain single, as he is. The phrase "it is good" means that it is something advantageous and beneficial. The words "if they abide" mean "if they remain."

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. He makes clear that he is giving advice, not a command. He recognizes that each person has their own gift from God: some for singleness and others for marriage. He then adds that whoever cannot control themselves should marry. Many believe he also had in mind the difficulties of that time, although this is understood in different ways.

For today: do not see your marital status, whether married or single, as being of lesser value. Ask God how to serve him faithfully where you are, and do not let anyone pressure you in making your decision.
exp.0:11:
Paul says that in the church at Corinth the people were splitting into groups. Some said "I am of Paul," others "I am of Apollos," others "I am of Cephas" (that is, Peter), and others "I am of Christ." The phrase "Now this I say" means "I, for my part, belong to."

Paul writes this letter to a church that he himself helped to form. Some people from the household of Chloe told him that there were quarrels among the brothers. Before this verse he asks them to live in unity, and right after it he will remind them that Christ is not divided. Some think that the group "of Christ" also believed itself to be superior to the others.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we admire a particular leader, pastor, or style of church so much that we look down on other believers. We can be thankful for what God does through different people, but remember that we all belong to Christ.
exp.5:18:
He says that the body of each believer is a temple of the Holy Spirit, that is, a place where God himself lives. That Spirit is given by God; we do not earn him. That is why Paul concludes that you are not your own.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city with a great deal of sexual freedom, where some believers thought that what they did with their bodies did not matter. He reminds them that the body belongs to the Lord and is joined to him. The next verse adds that they were bought at a price, which Christian tradition understands as the sacrifice of Christ.

For today: before deciding how to use your body, whether in your relationships, your habits, or your rest, ask yourself whether that honors God, who lives in you and cares for you.
exp.7:3:
This verse speaks about meat that was offered to idols. Paul says that the idol is nothing: it has no real power and is not a true god. There is only one God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of pagan temples. The believers were debating whether they could eat meat that had passed through those temples. Paul starts from what many already knew, but first he warned that knowledge without love puffs up. Later he will ask them to take care of brothers and sisters with a weak conscience.

For today: being clear that only God deserves our trust frees us from fear of superstitions and false powers. But that certainty must be joined with love, taking care that what I do in freedom does not wound another person's faith.
exp.13:17:
Paul says that he thanks God because he speaks in tongues more than all the Corinthians. "Speaking in tongues" was a gift given by the Spirit to pray or praise in languages that the speaker had not learned.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some took pride in this gift and used it in gatherings without anyone understanding. He does not look down on tongues; he acknowledges that he also practices them, and a great deal. But he quickly makes clear that in the congregation what matters most is that everyone understands and is built up.

For today: give thanks for the gifts God has given you, but use them with humility and with others in mind. Before you speak or serve in your church, ask yourself: "Does this help others understand and grow in faith?"
exp.9:1:
It says that all the people of Israel, when they came out of Egypt, were "baptized unto Moses." That is, by following Moses under God's cloud and crossing the Red Sea, they were identified with him as their leader and united to him. The word "sea" in the verse is the same as "the sea" in ordinary speech.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church that felt secure because it had been baptized and took part in the Lord's Supper. He reminds them that Israel also received great blessings and miracles, but many later fell into sin. Paul sees in the crossing of the sea a picture of Christian baptism, although scholars explain in various ways how closely the two resemble each other.

For today: do not trust your past religious experiences as if they guaranteed your future. Follow Christ every day with humility and obedience.
exp.8:19:
Paul says that he adapted himself to the Jews, living as a Jew, in order to win them to Christ. He also adapted himself to those who were "under the law," that is, those who strove to keep the law of Moses, even though he himself was no longer under that law. "Win" here means leading them to believe in Jesus.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. He has just explained that he gave up his rights, such as receiving payment for preaching, so as not to hinder the gospel. He made himself a servant to all out of love for people. He did not change the message, but his manner of approaching people, showing respect for the customs of each group.

For today: before speaking about Jesus, try to understand and respect the culture and history of the other person. You can yield on tastes and customs, without compromising the truth of the gospel.
exp.14:40:
It says that the sun, the moon, and the stars do not shine alike. Each one has its own "glory," that is, its own splendor or beauty. Even among the stars there are differences: one does not shine like another. "Differeth" here means that it is distinct, that it has its own brightness.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. To explain it, he uses examples from creation: there are many kinds of bodies and of glory. So the risen body will be different from the present one, but it will still be real. Some think it also suggests differences among believers in the resurrection, but the text does not say so clearly.

Today, you can trust that God is the creator of variety and power. If He gives each star its brightness, He can also give you a new body. So do not compare yourself with others; live grateful for how God made you.
exp.2:3:
Here Paul says that some in Corinth were claiming, "I am of Paul," and others, "I am of Apollos." Paul asks them whether this is not being "carnal," that is, people who think and act according to their human nature and not according to the Spirit. Here "for sure" means "I am, without a doubt."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had split into groups around their favorite leaders. He had already rebuked them for jealousy and quarreling. His point is that these rivalries showed spiritual immaturity. Right away he reminds them that he and Apollos are only servants, and that God is the one who makes things grow.

For today: when we admire a pastor or teacher, let us remember that he is only a servant of God. Let us avoid boasting "my leader" in front of other believers, and seek unity around Christ.
exp.6:4:
This verse says that spouses should not refuse one another in the intimacy of marriage. They may step away only for a brief time, if both agree, in order to devote themselves to prayer. Afterward they should come together again. "Defraud" here means to deprive or withhold what is owed to the other. "Incontinency" is a lack of self-control, and "tempt" means to put to the test.

The apostle Paul is answering questions the Corinthians had written to him about marriage. In a city full of immorality, some thought the most spiritual choice was to abstain completely. Paul corrects that: in marriage, each belongs to the other with mutual respect.

For today: speak honestly and decide together about your intimacy and your spiritual life, caring for each other without imposing your will or using silence as punishment.
exp.9:30:
Paul says that everything we do, even the most ordinary things like eating or drinking, should be done to honor God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who were debating whether it was right to eat meat that had been offered to idols. He reminds them that they have freedom, but that this freedom must care for others. That is why, in the next verse, he asks them not to be a stumbling block to Jews, Gentiles, or the church, seeking the good of many so that they may be saved.

For today: before deciding what to watch, what to say, or how to spend your time, ask yourself whether it honors God and helps the people around you. Even everyday life can be a form of worship.
exp.11:0:
Paul begins a new topic: spiritual gifts. He says he does not want the brothers and sisters to be without knowledge about this. The phrase "I would not have you" points to his wish that they understand the matter clearly. Gifts are abilities or favors that the Spirit gives.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, a church with many strengths, but also with disorder and divisions. Before, they had lived in paganism, and so they could confuse what comes from the Spirit with other religious experiences. Paul wants to give them clarity and a good foundation, beginning by affirming that Jesus is Lord.

Today, we should not leave the subject of gifts to chance or to trends. We can study the Bible with humility, ask what it says about the Spirit, and use what God gives us to serve and strengthen the church, not to boast.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that each person should live according to the situation the Lord gave them and in which God called them. The word "but" stands at the start of the verse, "distributed" means that God assigned or gave each one their condition in life, and "walk" means to live or conduct oneself. Paul adds that he gives this same teaching in all the churches.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and Christian life. Earlier he spoke of marriages where one believes and the other does not. Then he mentions circumcision, that is, Jews and non-Jews. His idea is that being a Christian does not require changing one's social or family condition to please God.

Today, you do not have to wait to change your job, marital status, or circumstances in order to serve God. You can live your faith faithfully where you are, with love and peace, knowing that the Lord is with you.
exp.13:37:
It says that whoever refuses to acknowledge what Paul writes should remain in his ignorance. "Ignorant" means that he does not know or does not want to accept; the phrase "let him be" is a kind of "let him stay that way." Some ancient manuscripts instead read, "if anyone does not recognize it, he will not be recognized," and scholars debate which reading is original.

Paul corrects the Corinthians for the disorder in their meetings. He reminds them that they are not the source of God's word, nor the only ones who have received it. Whoever considers himself a prophet or spiritual must accept these instructions as commandments of the Lord. Paul does not argue further with the one who stubbornly refuses.

For today: if we boast of being spiritual, we should show it with humility, letting ourselves be corrected by Scripture and serving with order in the church, without imposing our experiences on others.
exp.0:15:
Paul says that he also baptized the household of Stephanas. Then he admits that he does not remember whether he baptized anyone else. The phrase "the household" refers to those of his house.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided because some followed one leader and others followed another. He makes clear that he did not want to form a group of his own. So, by correcting himself and acknowledging that he did not remember everything, he shows that baptizing was not the center of his calling. His priority was to preach the gospel of the cross of Christ.

Today, we can value the leaders God gives us without placing them in the place of Christ. May our unity be based on Jesus and his cross, not on people, styles or names.
exp.11:3:
It says that God distributes different gifts among believers, but that all of them come from one and the same Spirit. "Diversities" means "varieties" or "differences," and the verse speaks of different kinds of gifts that are given out. The gifts are spiritual abilities or gifts that God gives by grace, not as something earned.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with many problems of division and pride. Before this verse, he reminds them that they came from paganism and from mute idols, and that only the Spirit leads a person to confess Jesus as Lord. Now he wants them to understand that different gifts should not divide them, because they share a single origin. Then he links the Spirit with the Lord and with God, something many see as a reflection of the Trinity.

Today, instead of comparing yourself with others or envying their gifts, be thankful for the gift God gave you and use it to serve. And value the gifts of others as part of the same gift.
exp.8:16:
Paul says that if he preaches the gospel of his own free will, he will receive a reward. But if he does it under compulsion, he is still a steward who has been entrusted with a task. A "dispensation" means a responsibility or charge, like that of a steward who looks after what someone else has entrusted to him. The phrase "against my will" does not speak of mistreatment, but of a calling he cannot ignore.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He explains that, although he had the right to receive support for preaching, he did not use that right. He did not want anyone to think he preached for money, or that anything would hinder the gospel. His motive was to serve, not to collect payment.

For today: serve God gladly, not only out of duty. Even when a task costs you something, remember that God has entrusted you with something valuable, and do your part with a willing and grateful heart.
exp.11:9:
This verse continues the list of gifts that the Spirit gives. "The working of miracles" refers to supernatural acts of power; "prophecy" is speaking a message on behalf of God; "discerning of spirits" is the ability to tell what comes from God and what does not; "divers kinds of tongues" refers to different kinds of tongues or languages; and "the interpretation of tongues" is explaining what was said in them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride over spiritual gifts. He reminds them that all of them come from the same Spirit, who distributes them as he wills. The gifts are not prizes but gifts for the good of the whole body of Christ.

For today: instead of comparing yourself with others or boasting about what you know how to do, ask God how you can serve with what he has given you, and give thanks for what others contribute to your community.
exp.0:30:
It says that if anyone wants to feel proud or boast, let them do it for what God has done, not for what they themselves have accomplished. "To boast" means to show off or take pride in something. "Let him who glories" is the same as "let him who boasts." The phrase "as it is written" shows that Paul is quoting Scripture, probably an idea found in Jeremiah 9:23-24.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church full of divisions and of people proud of their wisdom and of their favorite leaders. He reminds them that their new life comes from God through Christ, who is for them wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption. No one has reason to boast before God.

Today we can practice humility: when something goes well for us, let us give thanks to God out loud. And when we see the success of others, let us rejoice without comparing ourselves, remembering that everything good is a gift from Him.
exp.13:4:
Paul says he would like everyone to speak in tongues, but he would prefer that they prophesy. In his view, the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets what was said. The reason is that in this way the whole church receives edification, that is, help to grow in faith.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church that valued spectacular gifts very much and had disorder in its meetings. He does not despise tongues, since he wants them to be spoken, but he corrects the focus. What matters is that everyone understands and is strengthened. Some scholars understand "prophesy" as speaking a message from God to encourage and guide; others see it in a somewhat different way.

For today: before you speak, sing, or serve in the church, ask yourself whether what you are doing helps others understand and grow, not only whether it makes you feel good.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that the "natural man", that is, the person who lives only by his human nature and without God's Spirit, does not accept the things of God. They seem like foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are only understood with the help of the Spirit. The word "natural" refers to the human nature, and it does not mean "brutish" or without reason.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who boasted of human wisdom and were divided into groups. He reminds them that the message of the cross is not discovered through cleverness or eloquence, but God reveals it by his Spirit. Those who have received it have the mind of Christ.

For today: before reading the Bible, ask God humbly that his Spirit open your understanding. And with those who do not believe, be patient: do not look down on them, and pray that God will open their eyes.
exp.14:18:
Paul says that if our hope in Christ were only for this life, we would be more to be pitied than all other people. The word "miserable" here does not speak of wickedness but of deserving pity, like someone who has staked everything on something that never comes true.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some were saying there is no resurrection of the dead. He answers that if Christ was not raised, the Christian faith is empty, forgiveness would not be real, and believers who have died would have no hope. The verses that follow affirm that Christ was in fact raised, and that his resurrection is the guarantee of ours.

For today: when faith costs you sacrifice or misunderstanding, remember that your hope does not end in this life. Live with patience, generosity, and faithfulness, trusting that Christ has risen and that your hope rests in him.
exp.1:3:
Paul says that when he announced the gospel to the Corinthians, he did not use fine speeches or arguments designed to impress. Instead, his message rested on a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that is, on clear evidence that God himself was at work.

Paul writes to a church in Corinth, a city that admired eloquence and human wisdom. Some there prided themselves on being good speakers or on following certain teachers. Paul reminds them that he arrived weak and fearful, so that their faith would rest on the power of God and not on human skill. Interpreters debate how that power was shown, but the text points to the work of the Spirit.

Today, do not trust that someone can be won over by good words alone, nor expect to win others that way. Share Christ with simplicity and pray that the Spirit will touch hearts.
exp.10:33:
He says that if anyone is very hungry, it is better for them to eat at home before going to the meeting. In this way the church's meal does not become a cause for judgment, that is, for correction from God. "Set in order" means that Paul will arrange the other pending matters. "When I come" means when he comes to visit them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. They celebrated the Lord's Supper within a common meal, and some ate and drank without waiting for the others, while others were left hungry. This shamed the poor and showed a lack of love. Paul corrects them so that the Supper becomes a time of unity.

For today: when we gather together as a church, let us think of others before ourselves. We can arrive with patience, share what we have, and make sure that no one feels left out.
exp.14:39:
Paul says there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, and that each kind has its own glory, that is, its own splendor or beauty. They are not the same, but both have value.

The apostle Paul responds to those in Corinth who were asking how the dead can be raised and with what kind of body they will come. He uses examples from creation: seeds, animals, birds, and heavenly bodies. His point is that God makes bodies that are very different according to his purpose. If the Creator makes so much variety, he can give the believer a risen body suited to the new life. Scholars discuss exactly what the heavenly bodies are, but the central argument is clear.

For today: do not be afraid of what you do not understand about the resurrection. Trust the God who made a world so varied. And if today you suffer because of your weak or sick body, remember that God has a glory prepared for you.
exp.12:10:
Paul says that as a child he spoke, thought, and reasoned like a child, but when he became an adult he set aside those childish ways. A mature person is what the verse means by becoming a man. The verb is simply "was" in ordinary modern usage.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church that greatly valued spiritual gifts such as prophecy and tongues, yet lived divided and proud. In this chapter he explains that love is more important than any gift. He uses the picture of the child and the adult to say that the gifts we have now are partial, and that what is "perfect" will bring complete knowledge. Believers have understood what "that which is perfect" refers to in different ways, and it is often thought to mean the return of Christ.

Today we can ask whether, in some area of our lives, we still react with immaturity: pride, arguments, or selfishness. Growing in faith shows less in how much we know and more in how we love others with patience and humility.
exp.7:9:
Paul says that if someone with knowledge, that is, with understanding and maturity in the faith, is seen eating in the temple of an idol, a weaker brother (one whose conscience is fragile and unsure) might be emboldened to eat what has been sacrificed to idols. "Emboldened" here means encouraged or pushed to do it, even though his conscience tells him it is wrong.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who lived surrounded by pagan temples. Some believed that idols are nothing and ate that meat without any problem. Paul agrees with the principle, but warns them that their freedom can cause other believers who do not see it that way to stumble.

Today, before using a freedom that God permits, ask yourself how it will affect someone whose faith is more fragile. Sometimes loving a brother is worth more than exercising my right.
exp.15:15:
This verse says that the believers of Corinth should "submit themselves," that is, respect and follow the good example of people such as the household of Stephanas, and of everyone who helps and labors in God's work. Such people are those who serve with devotion.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. He has just mentioned that the household of Stephanas was among the first converts in Achaia (a region of Greece) and that they devoted themselves to serving the believers. Paul asks that they be valued, because their service had supplied what was lacking. Submitting here does not seem to mean blind obedience, but recognizing and supporting those who serve with love.

Today we can look to those who serve quietly in the church, thank them, support them, and, when possible, help alongside them.
exp.8:17:
Paul asks what his reward is, and answers: that when he preaches the gospel, he offers it free of charge, so that he does not make full use of the right he has as a preacher.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends the way he serves. Earlier he explained that those who work for the gospel have the right to be supported by the church. But he chose not to charge, so that nothing would get in the way of the message. His joy was in preaching without placing obstacles in anyone's path. Then he says that he became a servant to all in order to win more people.

Today, we might ask ourselves whether there is something we have the right to do or demand, but which could hinder others from drawing near to Christ. Sometimes love means letting go of a right for someone else's good. Serve generously and expect nothing in return.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that those who work in the sanctuary, that is, in the temple, receive their food from what is offered there. And those who serve at the altar, where the sacrifices were presented, receive a share of what is offered. Having a share is what the verse describes when it speaks of those who "live of the things of the temple" and "are partakers with the altar."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and defends his right to receive support from them for preaching the gospel. He relies on the example of the Jewish priests, who lived from the offerings of the temple. However, he makes clear that he did not use that right, so that no one would think he preached for money and the gospel would not meet any obstacles.

For today: let us support generously those who serve full time in the church, and, if we serve, let us do so with a heart free from financial ambition.
exp.6:33:
This verse says that the unmarried woman can devote herself fully to the things of the Lord, so as to be holy in body and in spirit. By contrast, the married woman is concerned with the things of the world, that is, with everyday life and the home, and with how to please her husband. The word "care" in the verse means concern or attention.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage. He wants them to live without anxiety. He clarifies that he does not intend to put a burden on them or restrict them; he only seeks that they serve the Lord without hindrance. Paul does not say that getting married is a sin.

For today: whatever your situation, single or married, ask yourself how you can serve the Lord with your time. If you are married, caring for your family is also serving God; do it with love and without losing your devotion.
exp.8:4:
Paul asks whether he and Barnabas do not have the right to bring along a believing wife, as the other apostles, the Lord's brothers, and Cephas (Peter) do.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to defend his apostleship, since some were questioning it. He shows that he has the same rights as other leaders, including the right to be supported by the church. This text suggests that Peter and others were married, although we do not know in detail how their wives traveled. Paul does not insist on these rights; he mentions them to explain why he gives them up for the sake of the gospel.

Today we can learn to use our freedom with humility. Having a right does not always mean we must demand it. Before doing so, it is good to ask ourselves what will help others come to know Christ most.
exp.11:2:
He says that the Spirit of God never leads anyone to curse Jesus, and that no one can sincerely confess Jesus as Lord without the work of the Holy Spirit. "Accursed" means cursed, given over to condemnation. The phrase "I give you to understand" simply means "I want you to know."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, made up largely of people who once worshiped silent idols. They had doubts about the spiritual gifts and how to recognize what comes from God. Paul first gives them a basic test: the true Spirit always exalts Jesus. Later he will speak about the variety of gifts and about unity.

For today: before we are impressed by an experience or a gift, let us ask whether it honors Jesus as Lord. And if today you can sincerely say that Jesus is your Lord, give thanks that the Spirit is at work in you.
exp.11:11:
The verse says the human body is one, yet it has many parts. Although the parts are many, all of them form one body. Paul says that Christ is the same way, meaning Christ and his church, which he calls his body.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and argued about who had the most important spiritual gifts. Earlier he listed gifts such as miracles, prophecy, and tongues, and he said that all of them come from the same Spirit. With the picture of the body, he teaches them that diversity does not break unity.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or look down on them for being different. Ask God how you can serve with what he has given you, and value what others contribute in your church.
exp.6:23:
He says that each person, brothers and sisters, should remain before God in the condition they were in when God called them. "Called" refers to when someone receives faith in Christ. "Remain" means to stay. The phrase "before God" indicates that they live that situation in God's presence.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. Earlier he speaks of slaves and free people: before Christ, all belong to Him. Paul does not say that one can never change one's situation, but that faith does not depend on it. Some interpret that he also advises calm because of the pressing circumstances.

Today, your work, your family, or your situation can be places where you serve God faithfully. Live each day aware that He is present with you.
exp.4:1:
They say the Corinthians were "puffed up," that is, proud or full of arrogance, instead of mourning over the serious sin that was among them. Paul expected them to take away from among them the one who had done this deed. "Ye" means "you."

Paul, the apostle, writes to the church in Corinth. He had learned that a man was living with his father's wife, something that not even the pagans accepted. What concerns him most is the church's attitude, which was not reacting. It is not known for certain why they were proud; some think they boasted of their freedom or their wisdom.

For today: when we see serious sin in our community, let us not ignore it or present it as tolerance. We must respond with sorrow, humility, and a desire to restore, seeking the good of the person and of the church.
exp.12:9:
It says that "the complete" will bring an end to what is now incomplete. "That which is in part" refers to gifts such as prophecy, tongues, and knowledge, which today give us only a limited view. "Will be taken away" means they will no longer be needed when the complete arrives.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were boasting about their spiritual gifts. He reminds them that love is more important and lasts forever. Christians have understood "the complete" in different ways: the return of Christ, heaven, or the maturity of the church. The context, with "face to face," strongly points to the meeting with God at the end.

For today: be humble about what you know, because your knowledge is partial. Seek to love more than to show off, and trust that one day you will see everything clearly.
exp.8:24:
This verse says that whoever competes in a contest or race gives up many things to prepare. Saying "is temperate in all things" means they control themselves and set aside whatever gets in the way. Athletes do this for a crown that fades, a prize of leaves or branches that wilts. We fight for a crown that does not fade, one that never comes to an end. The word "verily" means "certainly."

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a city known for its athletic games. He uses that picture to encourage them to live with discipline and not to take their faith lightly. He himself says he pushes hard, because he serves the gospel and wants to finish well.

For today: think of one thing that distracts you or holds you back in your life with God, such as your phone, a bad temper, or laziness. Give it up this week and use that time to pray or read the Bible.
exp.11:10:
This verse says that all the gifts mentioned earlier (faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, tongues, and others) come from one and the same Spirit. He distributes them personally and individually to each believer, according to his will. Where the verse says "dividing to every man severally," that means he gives to each person one by one, as he chooses. The small word-level notes about the original wording do not appear in this verse, so there is nothing further to explain there.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over spiritual gifts. Some felt superior to others. Paul reminds them that every gift has the same source, the Spirit, and that the church is like a body with many members, each one necessary.

For today: instead of comparing yourself with others or envying their gifts, be thankful for the gift God has given you and use it to serve others, knowing that your place in the church is important.
exp.2:15:
It says that believers are God's temple, that is, the place where God dwells. The source's quoted words for "know" and "you" are not used in the reader's verse, so I'll simply translate the meaning here: the question is whether you do not know that you are God's temple. Here "you" is plural: it speaks of the whole community, and God's Spirit dwells in the midst of it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which is divided by rivalries between leaders. Earlier he spoke of workers who build on the foundation, which is Christ, and of how God will test each work. Now he reminds them that the church itself is God's holy building. For this reason he warns against anyone who would harm it with divisions or pride. Some also apply the principle to each individual body, but in this passage the emphasis is on the community.

For today: take care of the unity of your church. Before you criticize or divide, ask yourself whether your words build up or damage the place where God lives.
exp.10:1:
Paul commends the believers in Corinth because they remember him in everything and keep the teachings he passed on to them. The word "praise" means to commend or recognize something good. "Teachings" translates a word that can also be understood as "traditions" or instruction handed down, that is, what he taught them by word and by his example.

Paul writes this letter to a church with many problems and disagreements. Even so, he begins here with a sincere acknowledgment before correcting them. The verse just before this one says to imitate his example as he imitates Christ. Then, starting in verse 3, he addresses matters of order in worship. Some details of those topics are interpreted in different ways.

Today we can learn to encourage first and correct afterward. Before pointing out a fault, honestly recognize the good you see in someone.
exp.6:35:
It says that if a father thinks it would be unseemly or shameful for his unmarried daughter to pass the age of marriage, and that the proper thing is to marry her off, he may do so without sinning. The phrase "unseemly" means something improper; "passes the flower of her age" refers to having gone beyond the usual age for marriage; "let them marry" is a permission, not a command. Some understand it as speaking of a father and his daughter, and others of a man and his betrothed; the text allows both readings.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. He advises them to live without distractions for the Lord, but makes clear that he does not want to impose a burden on them: marrying is not a sin.

For today: let us not turn our own preferences into a law for others. We can decide with prayer and freedom, without guilt or pressure, seeking to serve the Lord wholeheartedly at every stage of life.
exp.8:3:
Paul asks a rhetorical question: don't we have the right to eat and drink? The word "power" in the verse means right or authority. He means that, as an apostle, he has the right to receive food and drink, that is, support, from the churches he serves.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his apostleship, since some were questioning it. He reminds them that they themselves are the proof of his calling. Then he shows that other apostles receive support, but he and Barnabas have worked with their own hands. He does not demand his rights, although he has them.

Today we can learn to generously support those who serve in the church. We can also ask ourselves whether we are willing to set aside a legitimate right out of love for others and for the good of the gospel.
exp.3:7:
He says the Corinthians feel completely satisfied and rich, as if they were already kings, and they believe this without needing the apostles. "Full" means filled, satisfied. "I would to God" expresses a wish: Paul would want them truly to reign, so that he could reign with them. It is irony, not sincere praise.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was pride and division, with groups boasting of their favorite teachers. The Corinthians acted as if they already lived in the fullness of God's kingdom, without going through suffering. Paul uses this ironic tone to shake them, and in the verses that follow he contrasts their pride with the humble, suffering life of the apostles.

For today: when you feel you have already arrived or that you have more than enough spiritually, remember that everything you have received comes from God. Ask for humility and value those who serve with simplicity.
exp.15:16:
Paul says he is glad ("I am glad of the coming of") because three brothers from Corinth have arrived: Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus. Their presence filled the gap left by the distance between Paul and the Corinthians. What was lacking on the Corinthians' part, they supplied: they did what the church could not do, which was to be with him and encourage him.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus, at the end of a letter to a church with many problems. Earlier he asked that the church respect Stephanas and his household, who had devoted themselves to serving the believers. We do not know in detail what help these three gave, but the next verse says they refreshed his spirit.

For today: notice the people who serve quietly, like those who visit, help, or encourage others. Thank them with specific words, and look for a simple way to serve this week yourself.
exp.6:31:
He says that Paul wants believers to live without worry or anxiety. The word that was rendered as "anguish" points to distress or restlessness, and Paul notes that the unmarried person can give their attention to the things of the Lord, seeking how to please him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. He has just said that the present form of this world is passing away, meaning that everything present is temporary. He does not condemn marriage; he gives practical advice, since the married person naturally also seeks to please their spouse. Some scholars think that a difficult situation of that time also influenced his counsel.

Whatever your situation, ask yourself: "Do my concerns draw me closer to the Lord or pull me away from him?" Give him your cares today, and seek to serve him where you are.
exp.14:48:
It says that we have all borne the likeness of Adam, the first man, made from the dust of the earth. But one day we will also bear the likeness of Christ, who is from heaven. "To bear the image" means to carry the resemblance or likeness. "Earthy" means made of earth; "heavenly" means from heaven.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to correct doubts about the resurrection. He compares Adam, who left us a weak and mortal body, with the risen Christ, who will give us a transformed body. The verses that follow explain that our present body cannot enter the kingdom of God as it is, and that we will be transformed. Christians understand the details of that change in different ways, but they all share the same hope.

Today, this promise gives us encouragement in the face of sickness, weariness, and death. It also invites us to resemble Christ now: choose one of his attitudes, such as forgiveness or patience, and practice it today.
exp.6:6:
Paul says he would like everyone to be as he is, that is, single and free to serve the Lord. But he recognizes that each person receives from God their own gift, their particular ability or calling: some for marriage and others for singleness.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and sexual life. He has just spoken about life as a couple and makes clear that he gives advice, not a command. Many think that when he says "even as I myself" he is referring to being unmarried, though some believe he is also speaking of his self-control.

For today: do not compare your path with that of others, and do not feel lesser for being married or single. Ask God how he wants you to serve him in your present situation, and live it with gratitude.
exp.3:11:
They say that Paul and his companions worked with their own hands to support themselves. When people insulted them, they answered with a blessing. When they were persecuted, they endured it with patience. "Working" means laboring, and "suffer it" means they bore it without striking back.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some felt superior and boasted of their wisdom. With an ironic tone, he contrasts his humble life as an apostle with that pride. He does not aim to shame them but to correct them, like a father who loves his children. His way of living reflects the example of Christ.

Today, when someone speaks badly of you or treats you unfairly, you can choose to respond with a kind word or a prayer for that person, instead of returning the same treatment. It is hard, but it is a real way of becoming more like Jesus.
exp.0:17:
It says that the message of the cross, that is, the news that Jesus died and rose again for us, seems like foolishness to those who are walking the road to destruction. But for those who are being saved, it is the power of God. The word "foolishness" means lack of sense, and "power" means strength or might.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who were divided and took pride in following different teachers and in their human wisdom. He reminds them that their task was to preach the gospel with simplicity, so that nothing would take away the strength of Christ's cross. He will later show that God works differently from how the world thinks.

For today: do not be ashamed of a simple message. If someone mocks your faith, remember that the cross does not need human decorations to transform lives. Trust in the power of God and share your faith with humility and love.
exp.6:28:
Paul tells the brothers that the time is short. For this reason, even those who are married should live as though they had none. He does not command leaving marriage, but not making marriage the center of life.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and being single. He speaks of a present distress (v. 26), though the text does not fully make clear what it was; some think of persecution or scarcity. "The time is short" may also point to the imminent return of Christ. His intention is pastoral: to guard their devotion to the Lord.

For today: love your family and your work, but remember that nothing in this life is the last word. Today, put God first and let Him order your other loves.
exp.3:13:
Paul says that he is not writing these things to make you feel bad or to leave you in shame. His purpose is to correct you and advise you with affection, the way a father does with children he loves.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, a church he himself founded. They were dealing with problems of pride and division. Earlier, Paul had described with irony how the apostles suffer and are looked down on, while some Corinthians felt very important. Now he makes clear that his hard words come from love, not from a wish to humiliate them.

For today: when you need to correct someone, do it with love and with the desire to help them grow, not to put them down. And when someone corrects you, remember that honest correction can be a sign of care.
exp.9:9:
It says we should not complain bitterly against God, as some of the Israelites in the desert did. They suffered for it: they died by "the destroyer", that is, an angel or agent of destruction sent by God. The words "murmur" and "murmured" mean to complain under one's breath, with rebelliousness and distrust.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who were tempted by idolatry and immoral living. He reminds them of examples from Israel after they left Egypt. He probably has in mind episodes such as the one in Numbers 16, where the people complained against Moses and Aaron, though the text does not say which one exactly. He uses it as a warning.

Today we can examine our own complaints. There are moments of pain when we can cry out to God with sincerity, as the Psalms do. But rebellious complaining arises from not trusting his care. When it arises, it is good to stop and give thanks for something concrete.
exp.10:18:
Paul says that divisions among them are unavoidable, and that they serve to show who has genuine faith. The word "heresies" here comes from a Greek word meaning groups or factions that separate, rather than false doctrines. And "there must be" means the divisions are unavoidable, not that God desires them.

Paul is writing to the church at Corinth, correcting their behavior at their gatherings. He has already mentioned the divisions, and he will soon rebuke how the wealthy ate without waiting for the poor at the Lord's Supper. Commentators explain this verse in different ways, but they all agree that divisions expose the character of the people involved.

Today: when tensions arise in your church or family, do not be scandalized. Use them to examine your own heart, and seek to act with humility and love toward those who are weaker.
exp.2:20:
It says that no one should boast or take pride in following certain human leaders. The reason is that "all things are yours": believers do not belong to a leader, but the leaders and God's gifts are at the service of believers. The word "glory" in "let no man glory in men" means to boast or to put one's trust in something.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided: some said they followed Paul, others Apollos, others Cephas (Peter). Earlier he had reminded them that human wisdom has no value before God. So he corrects them: the teachers are servants, not masters or rival teams. The verses that follow explain that all things belong to the believers, but they belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

Today we can thank the pastors and teachers who help us, without competing or boasting about whom we follow. If something in the church divides us over preferences for leaders, let us remember that our identity is in Christ.
exp.6:21:
Here the verse says that whoever was called by the Lord while a slave is, in truth, a freedman, that is, someone whom his master has given freedom; now he belongs to the Lord as a free person. And whoever was called while free is a servant of Christ, since he belongs to Him. Being called refers to being invited by God to believe.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about how to live the faith in concrete situations. He teaches them that their social condition does not limit their worth before God. Even so, in the preceding verse he advises taking the opportunity to become free if it presents itself. Paul does not approve of slavery; he speaks to people who were living within it.

For today: your work or your social position does not define who you are. If Christ has called you, you are free and valuable; live with that dignity and treat everyone with that same respect.
exp.0:28:
He says that God acted this way so that no one would feel proud in front of him. The word "flesh" in the verse is an old way of saying "human being," with all their weakness. "Glory" means to boast or to feel superior because of what one is or does. "His presence" refers to God himself.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a divided community where some boasted of their wisdom, their favorite leaders, or their social standing. He reminds them that God called ordinary people, without influence, to show that salvation does not come from human merit. Everything they have they receive by being united with Christ, who is their wisdom, righteousness, and redemption.

For today: when you feel pride in your achievements, studies, or successes, remember that everything is a gift. Give thanks to God and treat with humility and respect those who seem to have less.
exp.10:16:
Paul says that what he is about to mention now is not a reason for praise. The idea is that when the Corinthians come together, those gatherings do not make them better, but worse.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and disorder. Earlier he had spoken about customs in worship, and in verse 2 he had commended them. Now he changes his tone, because he is going to correct what was happening at the Lord's Supper: the divisions and the unfair treatment among brothers and sisters (verses 18 to 22).

For today: gathering together as a church is not enough; how we treat one another matters. Before going to a service, we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking unity, humility, and respect for others, and not just fulfilling the duty of attending.
exp.3:10:
It says that Paul and the other apostles, up to that very moment, went hungry and thirsty, did not have enough clothing, were struck, and had no fixed home. The words for going hungry, being poorly clothed, and wandering are explained in the verse itself: "we both hunger" describes going without food, "naked" here probably means poorly clothed, and "no certain dwellingplace" refers to people without a stable home.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who felt proud, rich, and superior to others. With an almost ironic tone, he shows them the contrast: while they boasted of their position, the apostles lived suffering for serving Christ. He wants to correct their pride and remind them that the way of Jesus includes humility and self-giving.

For today: let us not measure the value of a Christian life by comfort or success. Let us honor those who serve with sacrifice and, if we are called to suffer for doing good, let us keep trusting God with humility.
exp.14:1:
This verse says that the gospel Paul preached to them is the same gospel through which they are saved, with one condition: that they hold firmly to that message. To "hold fast" means to keep, to hold tightly onto. To believe "in vain" means without foundation or without result, that is, that their faith was never real from the beginning.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. For that reason he reminds them of the basic message they received: Christ died, was buried, and rose again. Christians have understood the phrase "if ye keep in memory" in several ways: as a call to persevere, or as a sign that the faith is genuine.

Today we can often return to the essentials of the gospel, by reading the Bible and remembering what Christ has done for us, so that our faith does not grow weak with doubts or with passing trends.
exp.14:5:
It says that the risen Jesus appeared to more than five hundred believers at the same time. Paul adds that, when he writes, many of them are still alive, and others have already died. The word "appeared" means that he was truly seen. The "brethren" are the followers of Jesus.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. To answer them, he lists those who saw Christ alive. By mentioning that many witnesses were still living, he invites his readers to ask them directly. This event is not told in the Gospels, so we know of it only from this text.

For today: our faith rests on a fact that was proclaimed publicly, and not on a private idea. When you have doubts, do not be ashamed to ask and to study. Read the accounts of the resurrection calmly, and ask God to strengthen your trust in Christ.
exp.10:25:
It says that each time believers eat the bread and drink the cup of the Lord's Supper, they are announcing or proclaiming that Jesus died. They will do this until He returns. The sentences quoting the old forms and the word for "announce" are removed here, since your reader sees the King James wording of the verse.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church with divisions. Some turned the supper into a time of disorder, and even of selfishness toward the poorest. Paul reminds them of what he himself received: Jesus instituted this supper in memory of His sacrifice. For that reason it should be observed with respect and unity.

For today: the next time you take part in the Supper, do not do it out of routine. Think about what Christ did for you, give thanks, and be reconciled with anyone you have something unresolved with. In this way your participation will be a sincere proclamation of His death and of His return.
exp.13:34:
It says that if women want to learn something, they should ask their husbands at home.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to correct the disorder in their meetings (14:26-40). Before this, he speaks of weighing prophecies calmly. Many believe that here he is correcting questions or interruptions that were disrupting that moment. Others understand it as a general rule for worship. In 11:5 he mentions women who pray and prophesy, and for this reason Christians interpret this passage in different ways.

For today: seek to have everything in your church done with order, respect, and a desire to learn. Ask questions with humility, listen well, and create spaces where everyone can learn without disrupting others.
exp.13:5:
Paul tells the brothers in Corinth: if I came to you speaking in tongues, what good would that do you? It would only benefit you if I spoke to you with something you can understand. He mentions four forms: revelation (something God makes known), knowledge (understanding), prophesying (a word from God), and doctrine (teaching).

Paul writes to a church that was very divided and enthusiastic about spiritual gifts. Some valued speaking in tongues in the meetings a great deal, even though no one understood it. Paul does not despise that gift, but he insists that what matters is that the church be built up. He sets himself up as an example.

For today: before speaking, singing, or serving in the church, ask yourself whether what you are doing helps others understand and grow in faith, not just whether it makes you look good.
exp.11:13:
This verse says that the body is not made of just one part, but of many. It is very obvious: no one would say that a single hand is a complete body. The word "member" refers to a part of the body, such as the hand, the foot, or the eye.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, a church with divisions and with people who thought they were more important because of their spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the body to explain that, although they are different, all of them belong to Christ through one and the same Spirit. The verses that follow continue with examples of the foot and the ear.

For today: do not compare yourself with others in your church. If your gift seems small, it is still necessary. And value those who serve differently from you, because God placed them there on purpose.
exp.13:38:
This verse says that believers should earnestly desire and pursue the gift of prophesying, that is, speaking words from God that build up, encourage, and comfort. It also says that speaking in tongues should not be forbidden. The word "covet" means to strive for something, to desire it eagerly.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was disorder in the meetings, because many wanted to speak at the same time and boasted about their gifts. In this chapter he teaches them that what matters most is that everything builds up the church. For this reason he values prophecy more, but he does not look down on tongues. Right after this, he asks that everything be done with decency and order.

For today: value the gifts of others even when they are different from yours. Seek to serve in a way that builds up everyone, and make sure that in your church everything is done with respect and love.
exp.9:29:
Paul asks: if I eat and give thanks to God for the food, why would someone speak badly of me or condemn me for something I receive with gratitude? "Partake" here means I eat or take part in the meal. "Spoken of" here means criticized or spoken ill of, not necessarily insults against God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians about meat that had been offered to idols. He teaches that, in itself, the food is good, because the earth belongs to the Lord. But he also asks us to care for the conscience of others. This question defends his freedom, although some believe it is a rhetorical question that he himself answers later: everything must be done for the glory of God.

For today: before using your freedom, ask yourself whether it gives thanks to God and whether it helps or confuses the one who watches you. Sometimes love means giving way.
exp.14:41:
Paul says that the resurrection is like a sowing. A body is "sown" when it is buried, and it is subject to decay, that is, to breakdown and death. But it "is raised in incorruption," that is, it will rise without any power to be harmed or to die ever again.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. Before this verse he spoke of the variety of bodies and glories, such as the sun, the moon, and the stars, to show that God can give bodies of different kinds. With the image of the seed, which seems to die and then gives life, he explains that the risen body will be different and better.

For today: if God promises a life that never ends, we can face pain, sickness, and grief with hope, and live serving him without fear of losing everything.
exp.13:23:
This verse says that if, during the gathering, everyone prophesies (that is, speaks words from God that teach and encourage) and someone comes in who does not believe or who does not understand these things, that person feels convinced and examined by what they hear.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to bring order to their gatherings. They valued speaking in tongues very highly, even without interpretation. Paul explains that if no one understands, a visitor will think they are out of their minds. By contrast, a clear message reaches the heart and uncovers it.

For today: when the church gathers, let us make sure that everything is said clearly and with love, so that any visitor can understand and meet with God.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that the message about Christ, that is, what Paul proclaimed to them, was established and made firm in the lives of the Corinthians. "Testimony" is the proclamation or truth about Jesus, and "confirmed" means made sure, proven. It refers to what God did among them, giving evidence that the gospel was real.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with many problems and divisions, as the letter will show. Even so, he begins by giving thanks for what God has already done in them. He reminds them that their spiritual gifts and riches do not come from themselves, but from God's grace in Christ.

For today: before correcting or criticizing others, let us learn to recognize and be thankful for what God is doing in your life. And let us examine whether the truth of Christ is taking firm root in ours.
exp.11:18:
If all were one part of the body, such as only an eye or only a hand, there would be no complete body. The word "member" here means a part of the body. In the King James wording the verse asks, "where were the body?"

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride over spiritual gifts. Some felt superior to others. Paul uses the image of the body to show that God placed each believer in the church with a place and a function, as he willed. Variety is not a problem; it is part of God's plan.

Today we can stop comparing ourselves with others in the church. If your gift seems small or less visible, it is still necessary. And if another person's gift is different from yours, thank God for that difference and seek to serve alongside that person.
exp.2:0:
Paul tells the believers in Corinth that he could not treat them as spiritual people, meaning mature in the faith, but had to treat them as people who are still ruled by their desires and human attitudes. He calls them infants in Christ: they are believers, but still immature.

Paul, who founded the church in Corinth, writes to them because there was jealousy, quarreling, and division among them. Some lined up behind different leaders. He uses the image of milk and solid food to show that their behavior revealed little spiritual growth.

Today we can ask ourselves: do my attitudes reflect growth? Jealousy and arguments show that we need to mature. One practical step is to read the Bible regularly, pray, and seek peace with anyone we are at odds with.
exp.14:50:
Paul says he is going to reveal a "mystery," that is, something that was not well understood before. "Sleep" means death. So he explains that not all believers will die before Christ returns, but all will be "changed," transformed to receive a new body.
