Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, who had doubts about the resurrection. He has just explained that our present body, weak and mortal, cannot enter the kingdom of God as it is. That is why we need to be changed, whether we have died or are still alive at that moment.

Today, this promise gives us hope in the face of sickness, aging, and death. We can live with peace and confidence, knowing that God has prepared a new body for those who trust in Christ.
exp.10:12:
Paul asks the Corinthians to judge for themselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered? The word "fitting" here does not mean sincere; it means what is proper, worthy, and suitable. The "covering" refers to some kind of veil or covering on the head.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth to correct disorders in their gatherings. He has just said that man and woman depend on one another in the Lord, and that everything comes from God. Scholars discuss what the custom of that city exactly was and how it should be applied today, so it is wise to be humble when interpreting it.

For today: when we worship, let us seek to have our conduct honor God and not cause stumbling to others, taking care with order, respect, and cultural sensitivity, without losing unity among brothers and sisters.
exp.13:27:
It says that if someone has the gift of speaking in tongues and there is no one to interpret what he says, he should keep quiet during the church meeting. He may speak in private, alone, between himself and God.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly and each person wanted to show off his gifts. Paul asks them for order and that everything serve for building up, that is, for strengthening everyone. A message that no one understands does not help the congregation.

For today: before you speak or take part in church, ask yourself whether what you are about to do will help others grow. Your love for God can also be expressed in silence and in personal prayer.
exp.3:15:
Paul asks the Corinthians to follow his example. The word "be followers" means copying his way of living and serving Christ. "I beseech you" is a loving appeal, not a cold command.

Paul writes to them as a spiritual father, because it was through his preaching of the gospel that they came to believe. The guardians who looked after children were the ones who guided them. The church in Corinth was divided and proud, and Paul corrects them tenderly, without wanting to shame them. Soon he will send Timothy to remind them of how he lives in Christ.

Today we can be thankful for the people who have given us a good example of faith and look closely at how they live. Our own conduct also teaches others, so it is wise to live with humility, love and perseverance, and not only to talk about it.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that the world, with all its human wisdom, did not come to know God. Although God had revealed himself in his creation and his work, people did not recognize him through their own reasoning. So God chose to save those who believe through the preaching of the message, which to the eyes of the world seems foolish. The word "pleased" means that it was his good will. "Foolishness" means something that makes no sense.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city that admired eloquence and learning. There were divisions among the believers, and some boasted of being wise. Paul reminds them that salvation does not depend on human cleverness, but on the message of Christ crucified.

For today: you do not need to be brilliant or to have all the answers to draw near to God. Trust the simple gospel, and share it with humility, without being ashamed that some see it as foolish.
exp.12:12:
This verse says that three things remain: faith, hope, and love. "Charity" is an old word that here means generous, selfless love (in Greek, agape). Of the three, the greatest is love.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and boasted about spiritual gifts. Earlier he spoke of things that will come to an end, such as tongues and prophecy, and he compared our present knowledge to seeing in a blurry mirror. Interpreters debate when the partial will come to an end, but many see it in the return of Christ, when we will see face to face.

For today: before seeking to be right or to shine in something, ask yourself how you can love a specific person this week. Listen to them with patience, help them, or forgive them. That remains.
exp.8:0:
Paul asks four questions, and all of them expect a "yes" as the answer. He says that he is an apostle, that he is free, that he has seen Jesus, our Lord, and that the Corinthians are the fruit of his work in the Lord.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some doubted his authority as an apostle. Earlier he had spoken of giving up his freedom out of love for others, and now he defends his calling. His proof is the very existence of the church he helped to found. Scholars understand in different ways what he means by "I have seen Jesus," but many think of his encounter with the risen Christ on the road to Damascus.

Today, the fruit of a life given to God speaks louder than words. Serve faithfully, and let God show the results in people.
exp.11:8:
It says that the Holy Spirit gives to some "faith" and to others "gifts of healing." "Gifts of healing" means the ability to help the sick be healed, and it is in the plural, perhaps because there are different kinds of healing. This "faith" is not the basic faith for salvation, but a special trust in God for difficult situations.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and proud of its spiritual gifts. He reminds them that all the gifts come from the same Spirit, are given for the good of everyone, and are not meant for showing off.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or look down on your gift or your brother's. Ask God how you can serve with what he has given you, and give thanks for what others bring to the church.
exp.5:0:
Paul asks a question that sounds like a rebuke: how does a believer who has a problem with another believer dare to take it before judges who do not know God, instead of settling it among the brothers?

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which had many divisions and disorders. Some brothers were suing each other in civil courts, and this damaged the church's witness before the city. The following verses explain that believers will take part in God's judgment, so they should be able to settle small matters. Some debate how far this applies today, especially in serious cases or crimes.

For today: if you have a conflict with another believer, first seek to talk it through with humility and ask wise leaders in your church for help, before making it public.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that believers have not received the spirit of the world, meaning that way of thinking and valuing things that turns away from God. We have received the Spirit of God, so that we may understand what God has freely given us through grace. Here, the word "know" means to understand and recognize.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, a church that boasted of human wisdom and was divided into groups. Paul reminds them that the gospel is not understood through talent or philosophy, but because God himself reveals it through his Spirit. The verses that follow show that someone without the Spirit sees these things as foolishness.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God for his Spirit to understand and give thanks for what he has already given you, rather than relying only on your own intelligence or on what people think.
exp.14:42:
It says that the human body, when it dies and is buried, is like a seed that is sown. It is laid in dishonour (dishonour, weakness before death) and in weakness (lack of strength). But God will raise it in glory (honour and splendour) and in power (strength and vigour). Our raised body will be very different from the present one.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. To explain it he uses the image of the seed: what is buried does not look the same as what sprouts. Earlier he spoke of corruption and incorruption, and later he will speak of the spiritual body. Exactly what that body will be like, the Bible does not fully describe.

For today: if you are tired, sick, or in mourning, remember that weakness is not the last word. You can entrust to God your frailty and your loved ones who died in faith, with a firm hope.
exp.14:9:
Paul says that what he is today, an apostle, is due to the grace of God, that is, to his undeserved favor. That grace was not without result: Paul worked harder than the other apostles. But he immediately clarifies that it was not by his own strength, but by the grace of God working with him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who doubted the resurrection. Earlier he reminded them that the risen Christ appeared to him, even though he had persecuted the church. He calls himself the least by humility and because of that past. Here he defends his calling, and then he will remind them that all the apostles preached the same message.

For today: do not live crushed by your past or proud of your achievements. Put your effort into what God has given you, and give thanks, because even the strength to serve comes from Him.
exp.5:14:
Paul asks whether they do not know that their bodies are members of Christ. So, would anyone take what belongs to Christ and join it to a prostitute? "Harlot" means a prostitute, and "God forbid" is a strong way of saying: "Never!" or "By no means!"

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city with a great deal of sexual immorality. Some thought the body did not matter, because God will undo it, like food. Paul answers that the body does matter: it is for the Lord, and God will raise it, as he raised Jesus.

For today: our body is not only our own, it belongs to Christ. Before deciding what to do with your body, your time, or your relationships, ask yourself: "Does this honor Christ, to whom I belong?"
exp.8:25:
Paul says that he runs with a clear course, knowing where he is going, and not like someone who runs without a goal. He also says that he fights with purpose, and not like someone who swings blows at the air without hitting anyone. Phrases from the original wording have been left out here, so the verse now uses only words found in the verse above: "running without a goal" means running with no direction or defined aim, and "beating the air" means throwing blows that do not hit any target.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city that knew the athletic games well. He uses the image of the athlete to speak of discipline and of his commitment to the gospel. Shortly before, he explained that he gives up certain rights in order to win others. Then he adds that he keeps his body under control so that he does not disqualify himself after preaching to others.

For today: define what matters most in your life with God, such as prayer, serving, or growing in his Word, and practice it with consistency, not only when you feel like it.
exp.12:2:
Paul says that even if I give away everything I have to feed the poor, and even if I give my body to be burned, if I do not have love, I gain nothing. The word "charity" here means love, the kind of love that seeks the good of the other. "Goods" means possessions or belongings.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions, pride, and rivalry over spiritual gifts. This verse follows a list of impressive things: speaking in tongues, prophesying, having great faith. Paul shows that even the greatest sacrifices are empty without love. Some scholars debate the exact meaning of the phrase about being burned, since the ancient manuscripts vary, but the central idea is clear.

Today, before you serve or help others, ask yourself: am I doing it out of love for the other person, or so that people will see me? Ask God to purify your motives.
exp.14:31:
Paul says that if the dead do not rise, all his suffering is worth nothing. The phrase about fighting with beasts at Ephesus means that he faced an extremely hard struggle. The words "as a man" mean "in a human way," or "with merely human strength." The saying "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" expresses living only for the pleasure of the moment.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, some of whom denied the resurrection. We do not know whether the "beasts" were real animals or hostile people; many believe it is a figure of speech. The final saying sounds like a popular proverb that also appears in Isaiah 22:13. Paul shows that, without the resurrection, faith and sacrifice lose their meaning.

For today: the hope of the resurrection gives us strength to persevere and to live with purpose, not only for today's pleasure. Ask yourself what decision you could make this week with eternity in mind.
exp.5:2:
Paul reminds the believers in Corinth that they will judge angels.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had many problems. Some brothers and sisters were taking one another to court before unbelieving judges. Paul is ashamed of this and wants them to settle their disputes within the church. It is not known in detail how or when they will judge angels; interpreters understand this in different ways.

Today, when you have a conflict with another believer, seek first to resolve it with humility, prayer, and the help of mature brothers and sisters, before turning to lawsuits that harm the church's witness.
exp.1:12:
Paul says that he and his companions speak about what God has given them, but they do not use elegant words or the wisdom that the world teaches. They speak with the words that the Holy Spirit teaches. The phrase "comparing spiritual things with spiritual" can be understood in several ways: joining spiritual truths with spiritual words, or explaining spiritual things to people who have the Spirit.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who greatly admired eloquent speech and human wisdom, and for that reason they were divided. He reminds them that his message does not depend on brilliant speeches, but on what the Holy Spirit reveals about Christ.

For today: when speaking about God with others, do not try to impress. Pray, ask for the Spirit's guidance, and explain the Bible with simple and sincere words.
exp.5:12:
It says that food and the stomach were made for each other, but both are temporary: God will bring them to an end. The body, however, was not made for sexual immorality (sexual relations outside of marriage), but for the Lord, and the Lord cares for and takes an interest in the body. "Meats" refers to food, and "destroy" means that God will bring them to an end or leave them without use.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of immorality. Some used the saying "All things are lawful for me" to justify their behavior. Paul answers that being free does not mean doing anything at all. What seems natural, such as eating, cannot be compared with the use of the body in sexual matters, which belongs to the Lord. He also announces that God will raise up the bodies.

Today we can ask ourselves: "Am I using my body to honor Christ?" Before deciding anything, let us think about whether it is good for us and whether it enslaves us, and ask the Lord for help to live in purity.
exp.12:4:
This verse continues describing what love is like, which here is called "charity." "Doth not behave itself unseemly" means that it does not act rudely or offend others. "Seeketh not her own" means that it does not demand its own benefit first. "Is not easily provoked" means that it does not get angry quickly. "Thinketh no evil" can be understood as not keeping track of offenses or assuming bad intentions in others.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, pride, and disorder, even in the use of spiritual gifts. Before this passage, he says that even the most impressive gifts or the greatest sacrifices have no value without love. That is why he describes what this love looks like in daily life.

Today, when someone bothers you, before responding in anger, pause and pray. Try to think the best of that person and respond with calm, also seeking their good.
exp.2:12:
It says that the work of each person in God's service will be brought out into the open. "The day" refers to the day of Christ's judgment, and the fire is an image of testing: it shows what quality each work has. The words "made manifest" and "shall declare it" are rendered in the verse above as "made manifest" and "the day shall declare it," so the comment is simply that "made manifest" means brought out into the open, and "shall declare it" means it will make things clear.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided over following different leaders. He reminds them that teachers are God's co-workers, and that Jesus Christ is the only foundation. Each person must take care how they build on him. Christians do not agree on the details of this judgment, but Paul affirms that the believer's salvation is not at stake, but rather their reward.

Today, before we serve, let us ask ourselves with what motives and with what faithfulness we do it. Let us seek what endures: love, truth, and obedience to Christ, rather than applause or fame.
exp.13:9:
This verse says that there are many kinds of languages in the world, and that none of them is without meaning. The phrase "kinds of voices" refers to different languages or tongues. The word "without signification" here means without sense, unable to communicate. In other words, each language exists so that someone can make themselves understood to others.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where many spoke in tongues during the gatherings without anyone understanding them. He uses the example of the trumpet and of languages to show that a sound that is not understood helps no one. His goal is that the congregation be built up.

For today: before you speak or share something at church, at home, or at work, ask yourself whether the people around you are really understanding you. Use clear and simple words, because loving your neighbor also means making yourself understood.
exp.4:2:
Paul says that although he was not physically in Corinth, he felt present "in spirit." Because of this, he had already passed judgment, as if he were there, on the man who committed that sin. Here, "judged" means that he had already made a decision about the case.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a serious case of sexual immorality: a man was living with his father's wife. Instead of grieving, the Corinthians were proud. Paul asks them to act with firmness. Interpreters explain the phrase "handed over to Satan" in different ways, but many understand it as removing the man from the community, in the hope that he would repent.

Today, the church and every believer must take sin seriously, without pride or indifference. Correcting with humility, prayer, and a desire to restore is a demonstration of love.
exp.12:3:
This verse says that love (in the old translation, "charity") is shown in how we treat other people. Being "long-suffering" means patient, enduring without giving up or taking revenge. "Kind" means gentle and good. Love does not envy, that is, it does not become bitter over what others have. Love does not act improperly or foolishly. Love does not swell with pride or boast.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, rivalries, and pride over spiritual gifts. Just before this verse, he says that even the most impressive gifts are worth nothing without love. Here he describes what love looks like in practice.

For today: when someone irritates you or things go better for them than for you, respond with patience and a kind word instead of envy or self-importance. Ask God to help you love in this way.
exp.0:18:
Paul quotes a line from Scripture to say that God will overturn the plans of those who trust only in their own wisdom. The word that the verse uses here means to reject or set aside as worthless. The word translated as "prudent" refers to people who are very intelligent or well educated. God does not say that knowledge is bad, but that human wisdom cannot save.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was divided and admired certain teachers for their eloquence. He reminds them that the message of the cross seems like foolishness to the world, but it is the power of God. This quotation comes from Isaiah 29:14, where God was speaking to a people who prided themselves on being wise.

Today we can study and learn with gratitude, but without thinking we are self-sufficient. Before trusting only in our own ideas, we can pray with humility and ask God to teach us to depend on Christ.
exp.8:6:
He says that no one goes to war paying his own wages, that whoever plants a vineyard has the right to eat its grapes, and that whoever tends a flock may drink of its milk. The phrase "at his own charges" means "at his own expense." These are three examples from everyday life: the soldier, the farmer, and the shepherd.

Paul is speaking to the Corinthians to defend his right as an apostle to receive support from the church. Although he chose not to charge and to work with his own hands, he wants to make it clear that those who serve in the gospel have the right to live from that service. He will then back this up with the law of Moses.

For today: let us give fair and generous support to those who teach and care for us spiritually, such as pastors and missionaries, and not assume that their work should be free.
exp.10:3:
This verse says that a man who prays or prophesies with his head covered "dishonors his head," that is, he brings shame or disgrace on it. To pray is to speak to God in public; to prophesy is to speak on God's behalf to encourage or teach. The word "dishonors" means to bring shame or disgrace upon something. The word "head" can refer to the physical head and also to Christ, who was mentioned earlier. Scholars debate this.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its gatherings. He responds to customs about how people should present themselves when worshiping. It is not known with certainty what covering was meant (a veil, a shawl, or a hairstyle), nor what exact custom in Corinth he had in mind. That is why interpreters differ. What is clear is that Paul seeks order and honor to God.

For today: when you worship, take care that the way you present yourself and behave honors God and does not distract or offend others, according to your culture and with a humble heart.
exp.7:7:
This verse says that food does not change our relationship with God. The word for "food" in the source has no direct equivalent in the verse, so no comment is needed on it. The idea of "accepted" or "well regarded" is stated in the verse as "commend us," so I can express it that way. If we eat, we gain nothing before God; and if we do not eat, we lose nothing either. The food itself does not bring us closer to Him or push us away from Him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were doubts about eating meat that had been offered to idols. Some believers, with a sensitive conscience, still felt troubled when they ate it. Paul acknowledges that there is one God and that idols are nothing, but he teaches that knowledge must be accompanied by love toward those who are weaker in the faith.

For today: there are things that, in themselves, do not make us better or worse before God. Before using my freedom, I can ask whether it helps or causes a brother to stumble. Love sometimes means giving up something that is permitted.
exp.14:45:
It says that God's order is first the natural and then the spiritual. The word "natural" here does not speak of beasts, but of what has ordinary life, with a soul, as every human being has in this world. "Spiritual" refers to the risen body, renewed by God's Spirit.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection of the body. He explains that just as we all receive from Adam a frail and earthly life, those who believe receive from Christ, the last Adam, a risen and heavenly life. First comes what we are now; then, what God promises.

For today: if your body or your strength grows weak, do not lose hope. This life is the beginning, not the end. Live with patience and confidence in the promise of Christ.
exp.4:0:
Paul says that there is a sexual sin reported with certainty among the church in Corinth, so serious that even the pagans did not tolerate it. A man was living with his father's wife, that is, his stepmother. "Fornication" here means sexual immorality in general. "Gentiles" are the non-Jews, that is, the pagans.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he founded. Word of this case had reached him, and what troubles him most is that the church was not responding. The verses that follow say they were puffed up, that is, proud, instead of grieving. Paul asks them to act with seriousness. The Bible does not clarify the details of the relationship, and that does not change the gravity of the matter.

For today: let us not take sin lightly or tolerate it out of pride or out of unwillingness to cause discomfort. If a brother is in serious error, let us act with humility, prayer, and love, seeking his restoration.
exp.13:30:
Paul says that all who have the gift of prophecy may speak, but "one by one," that is, in turns and without interrupting one another. The goal is twofold: that all may learn, and that all may be comforted, that is, encouraged and strengthened. Here, to prophesy means to speak a message from God in order to build up others.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly, with many speaking at the same time. That is why he gives rules: only a few prophets speak, the others weigh what is said, and if someone receives a revelation, the one speaking gives way. The following verse clarifies that God is a God of peace, not of confusion.

For today: when you take part in your church or group, listen with patience, wait your turn, and seek for what you share to help others grow, not to draw attention to yourself.
exp.13:2:
This verse says that the one who prophesies speaks to people for three purposes: building up, which means helping them grow and become stronger in faith; exhortation, which means encouraging them and urging them to obey God; and comfort, which means giving them consolation in their sorrows.

The phrase "speaks to men" simply means "speaks to people."

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued speaking in tongues very highly. He does not despise that gift, but he reminds them that if no one understands, the church receives no help. So he emphasizes prophecy, which is understood and serves everyone. Christians have understood prophecy in different ways, but here it is described by its practical fruit.

For today: before speaking with someone in the church, ask yourself whether your words will help them grow, encourage them, or comfort them. May your service be clear and useful to others.
exp.8:11:
Paul asks: if other preachers have the right to receive support from the Corinthians, would he not have it even more, since he founded that church? "Power" here means the right or authority. But Paul did not use that right. "We suffer all things" means he endured lack and hardship. He did this so as not to put a hindrance, a stumbling block, in the way of the gospel of Christ.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he himself started. He defends his apostleship and explains that workers of the gospel deserve support, just as the one who plows or threshes expects a share of the harvest. Even so, he gave up that right so that no one would think he preached out of self-interest or for money.

For today: sometimes exercising a right is not the wisest course. Ask yourself whether something that is lawful for you might hinder others in their faith, and whether it is worth yielding for the sake of the gospel.
exp.8:8:
Paul quotes a command from the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 25:4): the ox that treads out the grain must not have its mouth muzzled, that is, a strap put over it to keep it from eating. In this way the animal could eat while it worked. Then Paul asks, "Doth God take care for oxen?", a question that invites us to look beyond the animal.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and defends his right, as an apostle, to receive support from the church. Earlier he gave examples from the soldier, the vinedresser, and the shepherd. Here he supports his argument with Scripture. Although God does care for animals, Paul explains right away that the principle also applies to those who serve in spiritual work.

For today: value and support with generosity those who teach you the Word and serve your church. Whoever works for the good of others deserves to be cared for.
exp.14:55:
It says that what makes death so painful is sin, like the sting of a scorpion that pierces and wounds. And sin has strength because the law, by showing what God requires, exposes our guilt. The word "strength" means power or force.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to affirm the resurrection. He has just quoted the question: "Where, O death, is your sting?" Here he explains why death seemed so fearsome: it confronted us with sin and the law. Right after this, he thanks God because Jesus Christ gives us the victory.

For today: if guilt weighs on you or you fear death, bring that to Christ. He bore your sin, so you can live with peace, forgiven and steadfast in serving God.
exp.14:43:
It says that our present body is like a seed that is buried, and that God will raise it up as a new body. "Natural" here does not mean wild animal, but a body made for life in this world, with hunger, sleep, and weakness. "Spiritual" does not mean invisible, but a renewed body guided by the Spirit of God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. He uses the image of sowing to show that what dies does not disappear, but that God transforms it. It is believed that he describes a real body, yet glorious, although exactly what it will be like is a mystery.

For today: if your body is tired, sick, or limited, do not lose hope. Care for it with gratitude and serve God with it, knowing that God is preparing something much better.
exp.6:37:
He says that the one who gives his virgin daughter in marriage does well, but the one who decides not to give her in marriage does better. "Gives her in marriage" means allowing or arranging for her to marry. "Does better" does not mean that marrying is a sin, but that the other option is more fitting in that situation.

Paul is speaking here, answering questions from the Corinthians about marriage and remaining single. He gives his advice with "the present distress" (v. 26) in mind, and makes clear that marrying is not a sin. Some scholars think the verse is about a father and his daughter; others think it is about a man and his fiancée. The text allows for both readings.

For today: when faced with decisions such as marrying or remaining single, avoid judging others. Seek what God shows you, decide with freedom and conviction, and serve the Lord wholeheartedly in either case.
exp.8:10:
Paul asks: if we have sown spiritual things among you, meaning the teaching of the gospel, would it be too much to ask that we receive material things from you? "Reap" means to gather a harvest, and "carnal" here refers to material things, such as food or help for living.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his right as an apostle to receive support from the church. He uses examples like the ox that treads out the grain and the one who plows in hope of a harvest. However, he soon makes clear that he did not use that right, so as not to hinder the gospel.

For today: if we receive spiritual teaching from someone, it is right to support those who serve in the church with generosity. And those who serve can do so with humility, without demanding, thinking first of the good of the gospel.
exp.10:29:
According to the verse, because of the wrong way the Lord's Supper was being shared, many in Corinth were sick and weak, and some were dying, which is a gentler way of saying they had died. The word "irreverently" describes a disrespectful manner, not the idea that someone is not perfect.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where at their shared meals some ate too much while others went hungry, looking down on the poor. Paul sees this as failing to recognize the body of the Lord, that is, not valuing what the Supper means or the community. He understands it as a correction from the Lord, so that they would not be condemned with the world. He does not say that every illness is a punishment.

Today, before taking part in the Lord's Supper, examine your heart: ask for forgiveness, be reconciled with anyone you have offended, and treat your brothers and sisters with respect and love.
exp.0:1:
Paul writes to the church of God at Corinth. He tells them they are "sanctified in Christ Jesus," that is, set apart for God through Christ. They are also "called to be saints," meaning invited by God to live as his people. The greeting includes all who call upon the name of Jesus in every place, because Jesus is Lord of them and of Paul.

Paul and Sosthenes write to a church with many problems: divisions, pride, and disorder. Even so, Paul begins by reminding them of their identity in Christ before correcting them. Who Sosthenes was is not known for certain; some connect him with a man mentioned in Acts 18, but this is not certain.

Today, your worth before God does not depend on your perfection, but on the fact that Christ made you his. Remembering this helps you live with humility and feel united with other believers, even when they are far away or very different from you.
exp.0:7:
He says that God himself will keep on strengthening and sustaining the believers in Corinth until the end of their lives or until Christ returns. The purpose is that they will be blameless, meaning without any valid charge against them, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, the day of his return and of judgment.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, a community rich in spiritual gifts but also marked by divisions and serious failings. Before correcting them, he reminds them of what God has done in them. His confidence rests not in their own strength but in the faithfulness of God, as the next verse says.

For today: if you feel weak or fall short, remember that your steadiness rests on God, not on your own perfection. Trust that he holds you up, and respond with a life of obedience and unity with other believers.
exp.10:32:
When the believers come together for the church meal and the Lord's Supper, the verse says, they should wait for one another. The phrase "you gather to eat" means "they come together to eat," and the phrase "wait" means "wait for one another." It is an invitation not to begin alone or in a hurry, but to share together.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions. According to the verses before it, some were eating and drinking without considering the others, so while some went hungry, others had too much. For this reason Paul corrects that unequal treatment and calls for personal self-examination. Some think the waiting also included the poor who arrived late, although the text does not spell this out.

Today, before we serve ourselves, eat, or take part in the church, we can look at who is missing, who is alone, or who needs a place. Waiting and making room is a concrete way of showing love.
exp.6:32:
It says that the married person is concerned with the matters of everyday life, such as the home, work, and providing for the family, and looks for how to please his wife. "But" means "but," and "careth" means "is concerned" or "takes thought for." "The world" here is not something bad, but the normal affairs of this life.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage. He believes that the times are difficult and short, and he wants them to live without anxiety. He does not say that marriage is sinful, but that the married person has more responsibilities to attend to. He himself makes clear that he does not want to put a snare on them, but to help them serve the Lord without distractions.

For today: whatever your situation, review how you divide your time and your attention. Care for your family with love, but set aside space each day to be with God.
exp.15:22:
Paul says he wishes the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ to be with the believers in Corinth. "Grace" means the undeserved favor of God, his kindness that we cannot earn. It is a closing blessing, like a farewell full of affection.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, disorder, and difficult questions. Just before this verse, he takes the pen himself to sign with his own hand, and he gives a serious warning about loving Christ. Having corrected so much, Paul ends with grace and with love.

Today, before speaking with someone with whom you have tension, ask God that his grace accompany both of you. Correct with truth, but say goodbye with kindness.
exp.6:9:
Paul now turns to those who are already married. He gives a clear command: the wife must not separate from her husband. Paul's own words are not his personal opinion alone, since Jesus had already taught about marriage.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. Earlier he spoke about the unmarried and the widows; now he moves on to married couples. The verses that follow explain that if a separation does happen, reconciliation should be sought. Many scholars think this reflects what Jesus taught in the Gospels.

For today: if your marriage is going through difficulties, do not give up quickly. Seek honest conversation, forgiveness, and help from the church or a wise counselor, and ask God to heal the relationship.
exp.9:15:
Paul asks the Corinthians whether the cup we bless at the Lord's Supper is not a sharing in the blood of Christ, and whether the bread we break is not a sharing in his body. "Sharing" here means holding something together with others, having a part in it. The "cup of blessing" was the cup taken while giving thanks to God.

Paul writes to a church surrounded by pagan temples. Some Christians were eating at feasts connected with idols. He reminds them that the Supper unites believers with Christ and with one another, so they cannot also share the table of idolatry. How Christ is present in the Supper is understood differently among the various Christian traditions.

For today: when you take the Supper, do so with gratitude and reverence, remembering that you belong to Christ and to his people. Check whether there is anything in your life that competes with your loyalty to him, and let it go.
exp.2:14:
It says that if a person's work is burned by the fire of testing, that work is lost and the person receives no reward. But that person will still be saved, though only just, like someone who escapes a fire.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided by followers of different leaders. He reminds them that the foundation is Jesus Christ, and that teachers and workers only build on him. God will test the quality of each work with fire. Interpreters debate exactly what that fire is, but the clear point is that God judges the service, not the salvation.

For today: serve God with pure motives and with faithfulness, not seeking fame or applause. What you do out of love for Christ and to build up others is what remains.
exp.8:26:
He says Paul deals firmly with his own body: the word for "strike" means to beat or discipline, and the phrase about bringing it under control means he subjects it like a servant, so that it does not rule over him. The word for "castaway" means disqualified, rejected after the test. His fear is that after preaching to others, he himself would be left outside the prize.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth, and he uses the image of athletes in the Greek games, which they knew well. He has just been speaking about giving up rights for the sake of the gospel. Interpreters debate what exactly "castaway" means: some think of losing salvation, others of losing approval or reward in service. The text does not fully settle it.

For today: choose one concrete habit, such as rest, phone use, or daily prayer, and set limits on it consistently, so that your desires do not direct your life and your witness is consistent.
exp.9:25:
He says that the whole earth belongs to God, and also everything in it. The word "fulness" is an old form of "full": the earth and everything that fills it belong to the Lord.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city where a lot of meat sold in the market had first been offered to idols. Some wondered whether eating it was a sin. Paul quotes Psalm 24:1 to say that food does not belong to idols but to God. So in the market one may eat freely, without anxiety. Later he adds that one should look after the conscience of a brother who may be offended.

For today: receive with gratitude what God gives you, without fear or unnecessary guilt, but use your freedom with love, thinking about how your decisions affect those around you.
exp.6:20:
Paul tells the one who was called by God while a servant (a slave): don't be troubled by it. But if you have the chance to be free, take hold of it. "Servant" here means slave; the verse's final phrase means "take hold of it with all the more reason" (rewritten from the source's gloss).

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about the Christian life. He teaches that social status does not determine a person's worth before God: the slave is the Lord's freedman, and the free person is a servant of Christ. Some scholars debate whether the final phrase means "use it" (take hold of your freedom) or "remain in your condition as it is"; most prefer the first reading.

For today: your work or difficult situation does not define your worth before God. Live with peace and faithfulness where you are, but if an honest door opens to improve your situation, dare to take it.
exp.11:22:
Paul says that the parts of the body that seem less valuable or less presentable are the ones we cover with the most care and respect. "Of little value" is the meaning of the first term; the second refers to the parts that are less becoming, or that we prefer not to show; and the third is the arrangement or care given to them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided, and where some boasted of their spiritual gifts and looked down on others. He uses the image of the human body to show that all believers are necessary, and that God himself chose to give more honour to those who seemed to have less.

Today we can notice the people who go unnoticed in the church, such as those who clean, care for children, or help quietly. Let us do something concrete this week: thank them personally and treat them with special respect.
exp.14:12:
This verse says that the resurrection of Christ and the resurrection of the dead are bound together. If it were impossible for the dead to rise, then Christ would not have risen either. "Resurrection of the dead" means that the dead come back to life with a body raised up by God.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul answers them with logic: they believed that Christ rose, because that is what they were taught. But denying all resurrection would leave that message without any basis. For Paul, the resurrection of Jesus is the center of the gospel.

For today: our hope is not just a pleasant idea, but rests on a fact. Because Christ rose, we can face the loss of loved ones and our own death with a firm hope, and not with despair.
exp.15:4:
Paul tells the Corinthians that he will come to visit them after passing through Macedonia. That region lay to the north of Greece, and his travel route went through there.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth from Ephesus, near the end of the letter. He has already spoken to them about the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, and now he explains his travel plans. He wants them to know that he will not visit in a hurry, but desires to stay with them for a while, if the Lord permits.

For today: Make your plans with order and sincerity, but with humility, leaving room for God's will. Planning well is not a lack of faith; just remember that He has the final word.
exp.10:6:
Paul says that a man should not cover his head when praying or prophesying, because he is the "image and glory of God." By contrast, the woman is the "glory of the man." "Man" here means male, and "created" means made by God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to correct the order in their gatherings. He refers to the customs of covering the head in that culture, and it is not entirely clear what exact practice he had in mind. His argument recalls Genesis, but scholars disagree about what it means for the woman to be the "glory of the man": some see order, and others see mutual honor. Later in this same chapter, Paul clarifies that both depend on one another in the Lord.

For today: seek to worship in a way that honors God and does not cause others to stumble. Treat people with respect, recognizing that all of us reflect the glory of God.
exp.5:13:
It says that the same God who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us up by his own power. The word "á" is an old way of spelling "a", and "levantó" means "raised up" in the sense of "resurrected."

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a city where sexual immorality was common. Some people thought the body did not matter, because God would one day bring it to nothing, like food. Paul answers that the body is not disposable: it belongs to the Lord, and God will raise it. That is why what we do with our bodies truly matters.

Your body has eternal value to God. Today you can honor it by taking care with what you do, what you look at, and who you join yourself to, remembering that you belong to Christ and that your hope is the resurrection.
exp.13:10:
It says that if someone does not understand the meaning of a language or a sound, then the speaker will be like a foreigner to the one who hears him, and the one who hears will be like a foreigner to him. The word "barbarian" here does not mean a savage, but someone who speaks a language that another person cannot understand. The phrase "the meaning of the voice" refers to what is being said.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some took pride in speaking in tongues during the gatherings. He uses everyday examples to show that speaking in a way others cannot understand helps no one. His goal is that the congregation be built up, that is, strengthened in faith.

For today: when you teach, pray aloud, or share your faith, use simple words that others can understand. Avoid technical or religious language that leaves others out, because love seeks for the other person to understand.
exp.9:13:
It says we should stay completely away from idolatry. The word "flee" means running far away, not merely avoiding something or looking at it carefully. The phrase "my dearly beloved" shows Paul's affection as he gives them this command. The word "therefore" shows that this follows from what came before: if God provides a way out in temptation, they should take it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a city full of temples and meals tied to idols. Earlier he reminded them how Israel fell in the wilderness. Then he speaks of the Lord's Supper, to show that a person cannot be united to Christ and also to idols.

For today: idolatry is not always statues. It is anything that takes the place of God in the heart, such as money, fame, or success. Ask yourself what is pulling you away from Him, and today make one concrete decision to turn away from it.
exp.2:18:
What it says: Paul states that what the world calls wisdom is, in God's eyes, foolishness, meaning something of no true value. He quotes Scripture (Job 5:13) to show that God catches the wise in their own cleverness, that is, in their own clever schemes.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided over following different leaders and boasting in human wisdom. He reminds them that they are God's temple and that they must set aside intellectual pride. Being simple-hearted here does not mean being ignorant, but depending humbly on God.

For today: Before making an important decision, pray and ask God for guidance, even when you have good arguments. Be humble in listening to the Bible and to other believers, and do not boast in what you know.
exp.2:7:
This verse says that the one who plants and the one who waters work together, with one shared purpose, and do not compete. Even so, God does not overlook anyone's effort: each one will receive his reward according to his labour. The phrase "according to his own labour" means "in keeping with the work he has done." A "reward" is the payment or prize that God gives.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were divided and gathered around leaders, some saying "I am of Paul" and others "I am of Apollos." Paul reminds them that he planted, Apollos watered, but only God makes things grow. Both are servants, not stars.

Today, serve in your church with humility, without comparing yourself or competing. Rejoice in what others contribute, and do your part faithfully, trusting that God sees your work and is the one who gives the fruit.
exp.10:17:
He says that Paul hears that when the Corinthians gather as a church, there are divisions among them, that is, splits or factions between them. He says that he partly believes it: he does not accept every rumor outright, but he recognizes that there is some truth to it. The word "hear" indicates that reports reached him from other people.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and begins to correct problems in their meetings. Earlier he has said that their gatherings harm them instead of helping them. Later he shows that the divisions even affected the Lord's Supper, since some ate without waiting for or sharing with others. Scholars debate the exact details of these groups, but the text makes the conflict clear.

For today: before we gather to worship, it is good to examine our hearts. If there is pride, resentment, or contempt toward someone, let us seek reconciliation so that our unity is real.
exp.5:11:
It says that, although many things are permitted to me, not all of them are good or helpful, either for me or for others. "Lawful" means allowed, and "beneficial" means that they do good. It also says that it will not be dominated by anything: "brought under the power of any" means becoming a slave or falling under the control of something.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth, a city with a great deal of moral freedom. Some believed that, since they had been forgiven, everything was allowed to them. Many interpret that Paul is quoting one of their slogans and correcting it. He reminds them that they were washed and made holy, and that their body belongs to the Lord.

For today: before doing something that is not sinful in itself, ask yourself whether it helps you grow or whether, little by little, it dominates you, like a phone, food, work or a habit. Use your freedom to serve God.
exp.0:13:
Paul says he thanks God that he baptized very few people in Corinth: only Crispus and Gaius.

Paul is writing to a church divided into groups that identified with different leaders: Paul, Apollos, Cephas (Peter), or Christ. He reminds them that Christ alone was crucified for them. He gives thanks that, since he baptized so few, no one can say they were baptized in his name. He is not downplaying baptism; he is correcting pride and factionalism.

For today: value the leaders God has given you, but do not place your identity in them. Let your main loyalty be to Christ, and seek unity with other believers.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that not all believers have the same knowledge. Some, even until now, still think of the idol when they eat meat that was offered to idols. The explanatory notes on the wording have been left out because they refer to words that do not appear in the verse you are reading.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, who lived surrounded by pagan temples. He had just said that idols are nothing and that there is only one God. But here he clarifies that not everyone has taken this in equally, and for that reason he asks for love and care toward those who are still struggling with their conscience.

Today, even if something is not sin for you, another brother or sister may feel hurt or confused by it. Before using your freedom, ask yourself whether it helps or causes someone else to stumble. Love with patience those who are growing in faith.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that what happened to the Israelites in the desert serves as an example for us. The sentence that explains the old wording (what the source's quoted words mean) is removed here, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees. The purpose stated is that we should not desire evil things, as they did.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a city full of immorality and idolatry. He reminds them that Israel was freed and cared for by God, and yet many fell in the desert. Paul uses that story to warn the Corinthians that having spiritual privileges does not protect them if they become careless.

For today: do not assume you are secure just because you know God. Examine which desires are gaining ground in your heart, and learn from the biblical mistakes so that you turn quickly away from whatever pulls you away from God.
exp.3:9:
Paul contrasts the apostles with the Corinthians. He says that they are regarded as fools and weak for Christ's sake, while the Corinthians consider themselves wise and strong. "Honourable" means respected or of good standing; "despised" means looked down on, without value in the eyes of the world. It is ironic language.

Paul writes to a proud church, divided by following different leaders and boasting of wisdom. With irony, he shows them that they feel like kings, while the apostles suffer hunger, blows, and contempt for serving Christ. He does not seek to humiliate them for its own sake, but to correct them as a father would, so that they will give up their arrogance.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek applause and a good image, or faithfulness to Christ. Serving Jesus sometimes means being looked down on or being thought foolish. Let us ask him for humility, so that we measure our faith not by success, but by love and obedience.
exp.14:37:
It says that God is the one who gives form to the body of the plant that grows from the seed, just as he chose to. Each kind of seed receives the body that belongs to it.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some there doubted the resurrection of the dead. Paul uses the example of the planted seed: what dies in the ground comes up different, with a new body. In this way he helps us understand that the risen body will have continuity with the present one, but will also be transformed by God. The exact details of what it will be like, the Bible does not fully explain.

Today we can trust that God takes care of what we do not understand. If you are going through a loss or a season that seems like an ending, you can entrust it to God, for he knows how to make new life grow.
exp.14:38:
This verse says that not every physical body is the same. Here "flesh" means the kind of body or living matter. Human beings have one kind of body, animals another, fish another, and birds another. Each creature has the body that belongs to its kind.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. He answers the question of how the dead rise and with what kind of body. He uses the example of the seed and the variety of creation to show that God can give each thing the body he chooses. So a risen body does not have to be identical to the present one.

For today: when it is hard to believe God's promises, look at creation. If he made bodies so different from one another, you can trust that he will also keep his promise of new life in Christ.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that we should not pass final judgment on others before the appointed time, that is, before the Lord returns. When He comes, He will bring into the light what is now hidden in darkness and will reveal the true motives of the heart. The word the verse uses for "counsels" refers to motives or purposes. Then each person will receive praise from God, that is, his approval.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were criticizing their leaders and dividing into camps, one favoring Apollos and another favoring Paul himself. Paul says that he does not even judge himself, because only the Lord knows each life and each motive thoroughly.

Today, before you criticize someone for what they did, remember that you see only a part. Leave the final verdict in God's hands and treat others with humility.
exp.14:52:
It says that our present body, which wears out, gets sick, and dies, will be changed into one that is not damaged and does not die. The word "must" simply means "need to," so the sentence says this change is necessary. "Corruptible" refers to what spoils or decays, and the words "incorruption" and "immortality" are their opposites: what cannot be destroyed or die. The picture of "put on" suggests that we will receive something new, like someone putting on different clothing.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. In this chapter he reminds them that Christ rose and that believers will also be raised and transformed when He returns. This verse explains why that change is needed.

For today: if your body gets tired or sick, do not lose hope. Serve God with what you have today, trusting that He is preparing something better.
exp.9:27:
He says that if someone tells you, "This was offered to idols," do not eat it. You do this out of consideration for the person who told you and for their conscience. Remember that the earth and everything in it belongs to the Lord.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city where a lot of meat was sold after being used in pagan temples. He had already said that eating in itself is not sin, because everything belongs to the Lord. Here he explains that if someone presents that food as something religious, eating it could seem like supporting idolatry. Some understand that the warning comes from a weak believer; others, from an unbeliever. The text does not specify.

Today, before using your freedom, think about how it affects others. If something confuses the faith of someone close to you, give it up out of love, without losing your trust in God.
exp.0:25:
Paul asks the believers in Corinth to consider who they were when God called them. "Calling" means God's call. He reminds them that among them there were not many wise according to the flesh, that is, by human standards, not many powerful, and not many of noble birth.

Paul writes to a church that is divided and proud of its wisdom and of its favorite leaders. He has just said that the cross seems foolish to the world, but it is the power of God. Now he uses the Corinthians themselves as an example: God works through ordinary people. He does not say that none of them were wise or noble, but "not many."

For today: if you ever feel like you are of little worth, remember that your value does not depend on your education, your money, or your family name. God called you by his grace. Serve with humility and do not boast of what you have, because everything comes from him.
exp.14:11:
Paul asks a confronting question. He says that he and the other apostles proclaim that Christ rose from the dead. Then why do some in Corinth claim that the dead do not rise?

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, a church he himself founded. Some of them denied the resurrection of the dead, and scholars are not sure exactly what their reasoning was. Paul reminds them that the message they believed is the same one all the apostles preach. For that reason, denying the general resurrection contradicts the center of their faith.

For today: check whether your hope rests on what Christ has already done. His resurrection gives meaning to your faith and steadiness in the face of pain and death. Reflect on it, and share it with someone who is suffering.
exp.14:10:
It says that Paul and the other apostles, though they are different people, proclaim the same message, and that the Corinthians believed it. The phrase "whether it were I or they" means "whether it is I or whether it is they." "So we preach" means that they announced the good news, and "so ye believed" refers to the faith of the Corinthians.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He has just mentioned that Christ rose and appeared to many witnesses, and he speaks with humility about his own calling. Here he emphasizes that his message is not a personal idea, but the same one the other apostles preached. He does this because some in Corinth doubted the resurrection of the dead, and he reminds them of the foundation of their faith.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith rests on the central message of the gospel: Christ died and rose again. Even though there are different teachers and styles, let us always return to what is essential and stand firm in it.
exp.10:8:
It says that man was not created "for the sake of" woman, but woman "for the sake of" man. "Was created for" means "was created." Paul is referring to the account in Genesis 2, where God forms the woman as a helper for the man.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to correct disorder in their meetings, and here he speaks about wearing a veil or covering on the head when praying or prophesying. He uses Genesis to support his point. Some believe he teaches an order of authority; others, that he speaks of customs of that time. But in verse 11 he clarifies: neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord. They need each other.

For today: value people of the other sex as necessary companions, not as inferiors. Treat everyone with respect and gratitude, seeking to serve the Lord together.
exp.0:14:
Paul says he is glad that he baptized only a few people in Corinth, so that no one could say he was baptized "in my name," that is, as a follower of Paul. "Lest any should say" means "so that no one could claim."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided into groups. Some said they followed Paul, others Apollos or Peter. He reminds them that only Christ died for them and that baptism does not tie them to a human leader. He does not look down on baptism; he wants to correct their pride and their divisions.

For today: value those who teach you, but do not place your identity in a pastor, a ministry, or a group. Your primary loyalty is to Christ. Seek unity with other believers instead of competing with or comparing yourself to them.
exp.13:3:
It says that the one who speaks in a strange tongue builds up only himself in his faith, but the one who prophesies builds up the whole church. The word "edify" in the verse means to build, to raise up, or to strengthen spiritually. Here, "prophesy" means speaking a message from God that everyone can understand.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where great value was placed on striking spiritual gifts. He does not despise tongues, but he corrects the disorder: if no one understands what is said, the congregation receives no help. For this reason he insists that everything serve the good of all.

For today: before you speak or serve in your church, ask yourself whether what you do helps others to grow, and strive to express yourself in a way that is clear and understandable.
exp.9:31:
The passage says that we should live in such a way that we are not a stumbling block or cause offense to anyone. It mentions three groups: the Jews, the Gentiles (those who were not Jews), and the church of God. "Give none offence" means "do not give cause for stumbling or scandal."

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had doubts about eating meat offered to idols. He tells them that, although they have freedom, they must use that freedom with care and love. At the end, in the following verse, Paul sets himself as an example: he seeks the good of many so that they may be saved, not his own benefit.

Today, before doing something that is permitted, we can ask ourselves: "Will this help others draw near to God, or will it make them stumble?" Choosing with love, even giving up something of our own, can be a powerful witness.
exp.12:1:
Paul says that a person can have very great gifts: prophecy, which means speaking on behalf of God; understanding all mysteries, that is, truths of God that were once hidden; having a great deal of knowledge; and a faith able to move mountains. But without love, which here means love, the person is nothing.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride about spiritual gifts, especially speaking in tongues. He does not look down on the gifts, but he shows them that without love they lose their value. This idea continues what he said in the previous verse about tongues.

For today: before you serve, teach, or defend the truth, ask yourself whether you are doing it with love. Today, treat one specific person with patience and kindness, even if it costs you something.
exp.3:17:
Paul says that some in Corinth were "puffed up," that is, full of pride and thinking themselves important. They acted as if Paul were never going to return, and so they believed they would not have to answer to him. The word "soon" that appears later means "quickly."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and boasted of its wisdom and of its favorite leaders. He had sent Timothy to remind them of how to live in Christ. Some felt secure while he was far away and spoke with arrogance. Paul warns them that he will come, if the Lord wills, and that he will not be concerned with their speeches, but with whether there is real power of God in their lives.

For today: live with humility, as if we were always standing before the Lord, whether or not anyone sees us. Let us ask ourselves whether our faith shows in our character and not only in our words.
exp.14:30:
Paul says that he dies every day. He states this emphatically ("Yes"), and he speaks of the pride or boasting he feels about the believers in Corinth, who are his fruit in Christ Jesus. "Concerning you" means "with respect to you." He is not speaking of literally dying each day, but of living always exposed to danger and giving himself completely.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some of them denied the resurrection of the dead. He argues that if there is no resurrection, his daily sufferings for the gospel would make no sense. His risky life is proof that he truly believes in the hope of rising again.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith costs us anything. If we hope in the resurrection, we can serve, forgive, and obey God even when it costs us comfort, time, or reputation.
exp.9:23:
What it says: This verse asks us not to live thinking only about what suits us. Instead, we should also care for the good of the other person, that is, of our neighbor.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who were debating whether they could eat meat that had been offered to idols. Paul says they have freedom, but that freedom is not the only thing that matters. What counts is whether something builds up, that is, whether it helps others grow in faith and does not make them stumble. The following verses show that, in most cases, eating was fine without any problem.

For today: Before using your freedom in something, ask yourself: "Does this help the people around me, or could it confuse or hurt them?" Choose love over your own comfort.
exp.0:19:
Paul asks three questions: "Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this world?" The word "disputer" refers to someone who examines and argues with great cleverness; "world" here means this age or this present world. The phrase about God making something foolish means that God exposed human wisdom as foolishness.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, divided by pride and by admiration for certain teachers. He has just quoted Isaiah (29:14) to show that God does not depend on human intelligence. His point is that no wise person, whether Jew or Greek, reached God through their own reasoning; God chose to save through the message of the cross.

Today we can study and value knowledge, but without boasting in it. Before we debate or compete with arguments, let us remember that no one draws near to God by being cleverer, but by humility and faith in Christ.
exp.10:11:
This verse says that woman came from man, since Eve was formed from Adam, and that now man is born through woman. Neither is superior in origin, because both depend on each other. And the word that appears in the verse as "but" means "but": the source of everything is God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was disorder in the worship meetings. Earlier he spoke about the order of creation and the customs about covering the head. Here he balances his argument: no one should feel superior. Scholars discuss the exact meaning of the word for authority and of the phrase about angels, so it is wise to be humble when interpreting them.

Today we can treat people of the other sex with respect and gratitude, knowing that we need one another. In the family and in the church, let us recognize that every gift and every person comes from God, and let us serve one another with humility.
exp.14:4:
It says that the risen Jesus was first seen by Cephas, who is Peter (his name in Aramaic), and then by the group of disciples known as the Twelve. "Was seen" means that he truly let himself be seen. The word "was seen" in the verse above is the one this comment explains.

The apostle Paul is speaking, writing to the Christians in Corinth. Some of them doubted the resurrection of the dead. Paul reminds them of the essentials he himself received: Christ died, was buried, and rose again. He lists witnesses who saw him alive. That he mentions "the twelve" even though Judas was no longer among them is a way of naming the group; some explain it this way, though the text gives no further detail.

Our faith rests on witnesses and on events, not only on ideas. If you have doubts, read the accounts of the resurrection calmly and speak to God with sincerity. And remember that Peter, who had denied Jesus, was among the first to see him: Christ seeks out those who have failed.
exp.11:12:
This verse says that all believers, regardless of their background or position, were united into one body by the work of the Holy Spirit. "Baptized" here speaks of being immersed into or joined to that body. Where it says "whether... or," it means "whether... whether." "Bond" refers to slaves. And the words "we have all been made to drink into one Spirit" show that we all receive the same Spirit.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride over spiritual gifts. He reminds them that the gifts come from one Spirit and that the church is like a body with many members. Some debate whether the "baptism" refers to water or to the inner work of the Spirit; the text emphasizes above all the unity.

Today, do not look down on another believer because of their culture, their money, or their gifts, and do not feel inferior yourself. If the same Spirit lives in both of you, you are part of the same body. This week, look for a way to serve or reach out to someone in your church who is different from you.
exp.10:21:
Paul asks the Corinthians several sharp questions. He says to them: if what you want is to eat and drink to your own liking, do you not have houses for that? If you do it at the gathering, you are looking down on the church and shaming those who have nothing. To look down on someone is to treat them as unimportant. In the end he says that he cannot praise them for this.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. At those gatherings a meal was shared together with the Lord's Supper. The better-off ate and drank without waiting for the others, and the poor were left hungry. Paul corrects this because it contradicts the meaning of the Supper, as he explains right after.

For today: when we gather together as a church, we should think of others and not only of ourselves. We can ask ourselves whom we are leaving out and how we might share with those who have less, so that no one feels ashamed.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that the Lord commanded that those who preach the gospel should live from the gospel. In other words, they have the right to receive support from those who receive their teaching. The word "ordained" means that he arranged or established it this way.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and defends his right as an apostle to be supported. He gives examples from the priests of the temple, who ate from what was offered there. However, Paul makes clear that he did not use that right, so as not to put obstacles in the way of the gospel. Many understand that his words are similar to what Jesus said in Luke 10:7.

Today we can support with generosity and gratitude those who teach us the Word, and they can serve with humility, without seeking gain.
exp.15:9:
This verse says that if Timothy comes to Corinth, the believers should make sure he is at ease and without fear among them. Paul explains the reason: Timothy works in the work of the Lord, just as he himself does.

Paul writes from Ephesus, where he faces much opposition, but also a great opportunity to preach. He plans to send Timothy, a younger co-worker, to a church marked by divisions and tensions. For this reason he asks that Timothy be received well and that no one look down on him, as the following verse says.

Today we can encourage and support those who serve in the church, especially the younger or less experienced ones. A kind word, a respectful manner, and a prayer for them give them confidence to serve without fear.
exp.11:27:
He says God himself placed different people with different tasks within the church. He mentions apostles (those sent out with authority), prophets (those who speak a message from God), teachers, workers of miracles, gifts of healings, helps (serving those in need), governments (leading and organizing), and various kinds of tongues.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church with divisions and with pride in the most visible gifts. Earlier he compared the church to a body, where all the members need one another. The verses that follow ask whether everyone has the same gift, and the expected answer is no.

Today: discover what your place is in your church and serve others with that gift, without envying or looking down on the gifts of others. Both the one who teaches and the one who helps are valuable to God.
exp.9:26:
This verse says that if someone who does not believe in Christ invites us to their home and we decide to go, we may eat whatever is served to us without asking questions. The word "unbeliever" here simply means someone who is not a believer. The phrase "sets before you" means "serves you." Asking "for the sake of conscience" would mean investigating where the food came from out of fear of offending God.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city where much meat came from pagan temples. Some were asking whether eating it was a sin. Paul answers that the earth and everything in it belongs to the Lord, so the food itself is not the problem.

For today: we can accept the hospitality of those who do not believe with freedom and gratitude, but we should always take care that our freedom does not cause others to stumble or harm our witness.
exp.11:19:
This verse says that, in truth, the church has many parts or members, yet all of them form one single body. The dual wording is handled as follows: the phrase "in truth" means "truly," and the word for "yet" means "but." In other words: there is variety, and at the same time there is unity.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a church marked by divisions and by people who boasted of their spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the human body to show that God himself distributed the gifts and the place of each person. No one is unnecessary, and no one is worth more than another.

Today, instead of comparing yourself to others, thank God for the place he has given you and serve with your gift. Value also those who are different from you, because the church needs them just as it needs you.
exp.6:3:
In marriage, the wife does not have exclusive ownership of her own body, because her husband has a claim on it; and the same goes the other way: the husband does not have exclusive ownership of his own body, because it also belongs to his wife. The verse says the wife "hath not power of her own body," so the word "power" here means authority or control. What matters is that the right is mutual and equal.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and sexual life. Corinth was a city with a great deal of immorality. Paul teaches that marriage is a healthy place for intimacy, based on mutual service rather than demand.

For today: instead of thinking about what I deserve, ask yourself how you can care for and honor your spouse. Speak to each other with respect and affection about your needs, without imposing or manipulating.
exp.13:19:
Paul asks the brothers not to be like children in their way of thinking and understanding. Instead, they should be like children in malice, that is, innocent and without any desire to harm others.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which placed great value on speaking in tongues, even though no one understood what was being said. He corrects this disorder with care: what matters is that everyone understands and is built up. That is why he says he would rather speak a few clear words than many that no one can understand.

For today: Seek to grow in understanding of the Bible and think with maturity before following trends or emotions. At the same time, guard your heart: do not hold on to resentment or wrong intentions, and live with simplicity and innocence.
exp.1:14:
The spiritual person, guided by God's Spirit, is able to evaluate the worth of all things. But no one who does not have the Spirit can examine that person rightly.

Context: Paul writes to the Corinthians, who boasted of human wisdom and were divided. He explains to them that God's truths are understood only through the Spirit. The "natural man" is the one who depends only on his natural reasoning. Paul is not speaking of personal superiority, but of the mind of Christ that God gives to believers.

For today: Before deciding something important, ask the Spirit to guide you through the Bible and prayer. And if others do not understand your convictions of faith, respond with humility and not with pride.
exp.1:6:
Paul says that what he proclaims is the wisdom of God, which had been kept hidden, like a secret.
