Here "mystery" does not mean something strange, but something God planned from the beginning and is now making known. "Predestined" means that God decided it beforehand. "Before the ages," that is, before the world existed. And he did it "for our glory": to bring his people to share in his honor.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who greatly admired eloquence and human wisdom. He reminds them that the message of Christ crucified does not come from philosophers or rulers, but from God. For that reason their faith must rest on the power of God.

Today we can stop looking for security only in what sounds clever or popular. Ask God to show you his truth in his Word, and trust that his plan for you began with love long before you understood it.
exp.0:6:
He says that the believers in Corinth lacked no gift, that is, no ability given by God through his grace. Meanwhile, they eagerly awaited the coming of Jesus Christ, which means his appearing or return, when he will be seen by all. "Coming" here means that they were waiting for the Lord to arrive.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with many gifts but also with divisions and disorder, as he will point out later in the letter. Before correcting them, he acknowledges the good that God has done in them. He reminds them that their final hope is placed in Christ, and not in their own abilities.

For today: give thanks for the gifts God has given you and use them to serve others with humility. At the same time, live with your eyes fixed on the return of Jesus, trusting that he will sustain you.
exp.15:12:
It says we should be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act with courage, and be strong. "Watch" means to stay awake and alert. "Quit you like men" means to act with courage and maturity; it does not refer only to men, but to brave conduct. "Be strong" means to be strong and take heart.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with divisions and problems. As he ends his letter, he gives several brief and direct instructions. After speaking of his plans and of co-workers like Timothy and Apollos, he encourages them to remain faithful. In the next verse he adds that everything should be done in love, so the courage he asks for is not separate from charity.

Today, this invites us not to be carried away by distraction or by fear. You can choose one concrete decision this week, such as praying with persistence or speaking the truth with respect, and do it with firmness and love.
exp.14:47:
It says that we human beings are like the one from whom we came. The "earthy" ones are those who belong to the earth, like Adam, made from dust, and all his descendants. The "heavenly" one is Christ, and the "heavenly" ones are those who belong to him. "Earthy" means made of earth, and "heavenly" means of heaven.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to explain what the resurrection will be like. Some doubted that the dead would rise with a body. He compares Adam with Christ: from the first we inherit a frail and mortal body, and from the second we will receive a glorious and incorruptible body, as the following verses say.

Today we can remember that our final identity does not depend on our present frailty. If you belong to Christ, your future is his. Live with hope, and let his character shape you from now on, even in your weaknesses.
exp.5:6:
Paul tells the believers in Corinth that it is already a defeat for them to have lawsuits between brothers and sisters. He asks why they do not prefer to bear the wrong, that is, the harm or offense, and why they do not prefer to be cheated, meaning to be deceived or to have something taken from them unjustly.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and problems. Some brothers and sisters were suing one another before unbelieving judges. Paul says this to shame them, because the church should have been able to settle its conflicts with wisdom. Then he reminds them that they themselves were also doing harm.

For today: before entering a dispute with another believer, ask yourself whether you can forgive or give something up. If that is not possible, seek the help of mature brothers and sisters who can guide you in peace.
exp.14:33:
Paul says: "Awake to righteousness, and sin not". He adds that some do not know God, and he says this so that they will be ashamed. "Awake to righteousness" means to wake up fully and think clearly, the way a person does after drunkenness, and then to stop sinning.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul warns that this idea, together with bad company, was opening the door to living without restraint: "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die". His rebuke is strong, but he seeks to correct them with love.

For today: what we believe about the future affects how we live now. Think about who you associate with and which ideas you accept. Choose friendships and teachings that draw you closer to God, and live with the hope that Christ has risen.
exp.9:3:
Paul says that all the Israelites in the desert drank the same "spiritual" drink, that is, one given by God in a supernatural way. That water came out of a rock, and Paul states that the rock was Christ. The phrase "followed them" can be understood as meaning that the provision of water accompanied them, or that Christ himself was present with them. Some believe Paul is drawing on a Jewish tradition about a rock that moved; that is not certain.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, believers who felt secure because they had been baptized and took part in the Lord's Supper. He reminds them that Israel also received great blessings, but many fell into sin. It is a warning.

Today we can remember that receiving God's blessings is not enough if we stop obeying him. Seek Christ as your daily source, and do not trust in your spiritual past.
exp.6:18:
It says that being circumcised or not being circumcised is not what matters most before God. What truly counts is obeying what God commands. Circumcision was the physical sign of belonging to the people of Israel. The phrase "keeping" means carrying out with care, and "commandments" refers to God's instructions.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were both Jews and non-Jews who believed in Jesus. There were questions about whether they should change their condition when they became Christians. Paul answers that each person can live out their calling to God in the situation they were already in. What is essential is obedience, not cultural or religious identity. How this relates to the law of Moses he explains in his other letters.

For today: do not let your background, your culture, or your customs make you feel superior or inferior. Instead, ask yourself each day: am I obeying God in what He asks of me now?
exp.10:15:
He says that if anyone wants to argue and fight over this subject, Paul and his companions have no other custom than the one he has just explained, and neither do the churches of God. "Contentious" means someone who looks for a quarrel or enjoys arguing. "Custom" here refers to a practice accepted in the churches.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church with many divisions. He has just spoken about how men and women should present themselves when praying and prophesying in the congregation. Scholars disagree about which exact custom is meant, since it concerned either the veil or the hair according to the culture of that time. With this verse he closes the topic and appeals to the common practice of the churches.

For today: when differences arise over matters of custom, let us seek order and unity among brothers and sisters, without turning every issue into a fight.
exp.13:16:
This verse says that the person who prays or gives thanks to God in a tongue no one understands does it well, and their thanksgiving is sincere. But the one who listens receives no benefit. The phrase "For thou verily givest thanks well" means that the thanks given is genuine, and "but the other is not edified" means that the listener is not strengthened or encouraged in their faith.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the gatherings had become disorderly. Some were speaking in tongues without anyone interpreting, and the others were left without understanding. Paul does not despise that gift, since he practices it himself, but he insists that what matters in the congregation is that everyone be helped.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we say, sing, or teach in the church helps others to understand and to grow. Speaking clearly and thinking about those who are listening to us is a way of showing love.
exp.12:8:
It says that our knowledge and our prophecies are limited. "In part" means incompletely: we know something, but not everything. "We prophesy" refers to communicating messages on behalf of God. Even the spiritual gifts do not give us the complete picture.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some boasted about their spiritual gifts and neglected love. For this reason he shows that those gifts are temporary and partial, while love remains. Christians do not agree about when the "perfect" thing mentioned in the following verse will come; many think it is the return of Christ.

For today: let us be humble when we speak about what we know of God. Recognizing that we understand only in part helps us listen better, treat with patience those who think differently, and put love first.
exp.12:7:
This verse says that love never ends. The word "charity" here means generous, self-giving love, the kind that seeks the good of others. By contrast, prophecies, tongues (speaking in languages one has not learned), and "knowledge" (understanding) will come to an end or be taken away. "They shall fail" means they will reach their end.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some boasted about their spiritual gifts and caused divisions. He shows them that those gifts are partial and temporary, and that love is more important. Christians interpret in different ways when the gifts cease: some say it will be when Christ returns, others think of an earlier moment.

For today: before seeking to stand out for what you know or do, ask yourself whether you are using it to love others. Today, listen patiently to someone or help them without expecting anything in return.
exp.9:21:
It says that we should not make God angry by stirring up jealousy. The word "provoke" means to make someone become upset, and "jealousy" refers to the jealousy of one who demands exclusive loyalty. "Are we stronger than he?" is a rhetorical question: the answer is no. No one can challenge God and come out ahead.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city where there were many temples and festivals with idols. Some believed they could take part in those religious meals and also in the Lord's Supper. Paul warns them that one cannot share the table of God and the table of demons. He also recalls how Israel provoked God in the wilderness (vv. 1-12), although some scholars debate how closely this connects to the phrase.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something in my life that competes with God for my loyalty? It is wise to be honest with him and to turn away from it.
exp.14:44:
This verse compares two men: Adam and Christ. Paul quotes Genesis 2:7, saying that Adam was made a living soul, that is, a being with natural life, who breathes and depends on what God gave him. Christ, the last Adam, is a quickening spirit, that is, someone who gives life to others.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. He explains that the present body is natural and fragile, but the risen body will be transformed by the power of Christ. Just as we inherit a weak life from Adam, we receive a new life from Christ.

For today: if you are tired or limited, remember that your frailty is not the end. Trust in Christ, who gives life, and live with hope.
exp.6:25:
Paul says that, because of "the present distress," it is good for a person to remain as they are. The word "distress" means pressure or urgency that presses in on a person. "To be so" refers to remaining in the state one is in, especially being unmarried. It is his own judgment, not a command.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage. Earlier he makes clear that he has no command from the Lord about virgins, but only his own opinion. Scholars debate what "distress" refers to: perhaps the hardships of that time, or the shortness of the time that remains. He himself says that marriage is not a sin.

For today: before deciding about marriage or any major change, ask what will allow you to serve God better in your situation. Seek counsel calmly and without pressure.
exp.11:30:
It says that we should earnestly desire the spiritual gifts that are most useful for everyone. "But" is the plain meaning of the word, and "eagerly seek" means "pursue with determination." Paul adds that he is going to show them something better than any gift: a more excellent way.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over gifts, such as speaking in tongues. He reminds them that the church is one body with many members and that no one has all the gifts. With this verse he prepares chapter 13, where he speaks about love. Some understand "eagerly seek" as a command, others as a description of what they were already doing.

For today: use your gifts to serve others, not to stand out. Before asking what gift you have, ask how you can love someone better today.
exp.15:23:
Paul closes his letter by saying that his love is with all the Corinthians, and he says it "in Christ Jesus," meaning a love that springs from their union with Christ. The words "in Christ Jesus" refer to that union. The closing word "Amen" in the King James text is the affirmation that means "so be it." The second sentence, about Philippi and Stephanas, is not part of what Paul wrote: it is a note added by later copyists, and many scholars doubt its accuracy, since Paul was writing from Ephesus.

Paul writes to a church full of divisions, pride, and moral problems, and he corrected them firmly throughout the letter. Before saying goodbye, he wants them to know that the correction does not come from rejection, but from affection.

Today, when we have to correct someone or say a hard truth, let us do it as Paul did: making it clear, in words and deeds, that we do it out of sincere love.
exp.13:14:
Paul says that he will pray and sing in two ways: with the spirit and also with the understanding. That is, he does not want his prayer to be only an inner experience, but also something the mind grasps. The phrase "What is it then?" means "So what am I to conclude?" "Spirit" here is usually understood as the spirit of the person praying under the impulse of God, although some interpret it in other ways.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where speaking in tongues was very common in the meetings, but without anyone interpreting it. He does not forbid that gift, but he insists that what is done in the community must build up everyone. For this reason he asks for order and understanding.

For today: when you pray or sing, try to understand what you are saying. Think about the words of the songs and about your words to God, so that your heart and your mind worship together.
exp.7:8:
Take care, he says: the liberty you have must not become a stumbling block to the ones who are weak, that is, those weak in faith or in conscience. The phrase "take heed" means "take care," a stumbling block is something that makes a person fall, and the weak are believers whose conscience is easily troubled.

The apostle Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some were debating whether it was right to eat meat that had been offered to idols. Those who had knowledge understood that idols are nothing and ate without guilt. But others, who had formerly worshiped idols, felt defiled when they saw this. Paul asks that knowledge be used with love.

Today, even if something is not a sin for you, ask yourself whether it could hurt or confuse a weaker brother. Sometimes love means willingly giving up a right in order to protect another person's faith.
exp.5:15:
This verse asks whether you do not know that the one who joins himself sexually with a prostitute becomes one body with her. Paul supports this with a quotation from Genesis 2:24: "the two shall be one flesh." A "harlot" is a prostitute, and "joins himself" means uniting intimately. For Paul, sexual union is not something fleeting or unimportant.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city with much sexual immorality. Some believers thought that what they did with their bodies did not affect their spiritual life. Paul reminds them that their bodies belong to Christ and will be raised, so they matter greatly to God.

For today: take care of your body and your relationships as something that belongs to Christ. Before deciding on matters of sexuality, ask yourself whether it honors God and respects the other person. If you have failed, God offers forgiveness and a new beginning.
exp.0:12:
Paul asks three questions to show how absurd it is to divide into groups. "Is Christ divided?" means that Christ is one and is not split among factions. He then asks whether Paul was crucified for them, or whether they were baptized in Paul's name. The answer to all of these is no.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. People from the household of Chloe told him there were quarrels, since some said they belonged to Paul, others to Apollos, others to Cephas (Peter), or to Christ. Paul reminds them that only Christ died for them and that baptism is in his name.

For today: before we defend a leader, a group, or a way of thinking, let us remember that our primary loyalty is to Christ. We can value those who teach us, but without separating ourselves from other believers because of them.
exp.15:19:
All the brothers and sisters who are with Paul send greetings to the Corinthians. Then Paul asks them to greet one another with a holy kiss. This is a respectful and pure kiss, not a romantic one, as a sign of affection between brothers and sisters in the faith.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus, near the end, and closes with greetings from the churches and from friends such as Aquila and Priscilla. The Corinthians had divisions and arguments, so this greeting reminds them that they are one family. Kissing or embracing as a greeting was a common custom in that culture.

Today we do not have to copy the exact form, since every culture greets differently. What matters is expressing sincere affection: give a hug or a warm greeting to someone in your church, especially to someone you have been distant from, and seek peace with that person.
exp.2:21:
This verse says that everything God has placed in the lives of believers is for their good: teachers such as Paul, Apollos and Cephas (this is Peter), the world, life, death, the present and what is to come. "Yours" means "of you," and "those to come" refers to future things. It does not mean we can possess everything, but that nothing is foreign to us or can separate us from God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided because some followed Paul, others followed Apollos, and others followed Cephas. He tells them not to boast in human leaders. They are not owners of the church; they are servants who help the church. The following verse explains it: you are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

For today: value teachers and pastors as gifts from God, without competing or taking sides. And if you face change, loss or fear, remember that you belong to Christ.
exp.14:21:
This verse compares two men: Adam and Christ. Because of Adam's disobedience, death came upon all human beings. Through Christ, who rose from the dead, new life comes. "Made alive" means that they receive life, that is, they are raised.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom denied the resurrection of the dead. He answers that Christ's resurrection is the beginning and the guarantee of ours. The verses that follow say that this happens "in order": first Christ, then those who belong to him when he comes. Some debate whether "all" means that everyone will be raised or that everyone who is in Christ will receive life. The context points strongly to those who belong to Christ.

For today: if your hope is in Christ, death does not have the last word. You can face grief, illness and fear with confidence, and live today as someone who belongs to the life God promised.
exp.5:8:
This verse asks whether believers do not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God. Paul warns them not to be deceived, and gives a list of unrighteous behaviors: sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, and sexual practices that Paul rejects. The word "fornicators" refers to those who have sexual relations outside of marriage. The word "inherit" here means to receive as one's own. As for "effeminate," scholars debate its exact meaning.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had lawsuits between brothers and sisters and cheated one another. He reminds them that injustice is a serious matter. But he immediately tells them that some of them used to be like this, and that God washed, sanctified, and justified them through Jesus.

For today: do not use grace as an excuse to remain in what God calls unrighteous. Examine your life with humility, leave behind what distances you from God, and trust that his forgiveness and his Spirit give you a new beginning.
exp.0:24:
It says that what seems to men to be the "foolishness" of God is wiser than all human wisdom. And what seems to be the "weakness" of God is stronger than human strength. "Foolish" means senseless or absurd; "weak" means frail. Paul does not say that God is really foolish or weak, but that this is how the world sees him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and proud of its wisdom. He reminds them that the message of Christ crucified seemed ridiculous to the Greeks and offensive to the Jews. Yet in that cross God showed his wisdom and his power to save.

For today: do not be ashamed if your faith seems foolish or weak to others. Trust that God works in ways we do not always understand. When you feel small or without resources, remember that God can do something great through you.
exp.12:11:
Today we see as in a mirror, dimly, but one day we will see "face to face," that is, directly. Today we know only in part; then we will know fully, just as God already knows us. "Obscure" means something unclear, and "charity" is love.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and boasted about its spiritual gifts. He reminds them that those gifts are partial and temporary, while love is what endures. Ancient mirrors were usually polished metal, and they gave an imperfect image. Interpreters debate when "that which is perfect" arrives, though many see it in the return of Christ.

For today: accept with humility that you do not understand everything. Faced with what you do not comprehend, trust God and treat others with love, instead of arguing as if you knew it all.
exp.9:17:
Paul invites the Corinthians to look at Israel "according to the flesh," that is, the people of Israel in their natural sense, as a nation. He reminds them that those who ate of what was sacrificed on the altar were joined to that altar and to what it represented. "Partakers" means that they shared or had fellowship.

Paul is writing to a church where some believers were attending feasts in pagan temples. First he speaks of the Lord's Supper, where there is fellowship with Christ. Then he uses the example of Israel to show that eating at an altar creates a real union. That is why one cannot be with Christ and with idols at the same time.

For today: examine what things bind you spiritually. If something competes with your loyalty to Christ, step away from it and seek fellowship with Him and with His people.
exp.6:17:
Paul asks whether anyone was called by God while already circumcised, that is, a Jew. In that case, he should not try to hide it or change his condition. And if someone was called without being circumcised, that is, a Gentile, he should not get circumcised. The phrase "let him remain circumcised" means that he should stay as he is.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. Earlier he has said that each person should live as the Lord assigned to him and called him. For Paul, being a Jew or a Gentile does not make anyone better before God. What matters is obeying God, as he says right after this.

For today: you do not need to change your background, your culture, or your situation to be valued before God. Serve the Lord faithfully where you are, and ask Him for wisdom if He opens another path for you.
exp.11:7:
It says that the Holy Spirit gives different gifts to different people. To one he gives the "word of wisdom," which is usually understood as the ability to give good counsel or to apply the truth of God wisely. To another he gives the "word of knowledge," that is, spiritual understanding and insight. Here "knowledge" means understanding, not modern science.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over spiritual gifts. He reminds them that all the gifts come from the same Spirit and are given for the common good, that is, for the benefit of everyone. Scholars debate exactly how these gifts operated, but the purpose is clear.

For today: do not boast about what God has given you, and do not envy what he has given to others. Ask God how you can use your gift to serve your church, and give thanks for the gifts of others.
exp.8:20:
Paul speaks of those "without law," that is, the Gentiles, who had not received the law of Moses. He says he approached them as one of them, without imposing Jewish customs on them. He clarifies that he was not without God's law, since he was under the law of Christ, which many understand as the command of love and the teachings of Jesus. His aim was to win those people over to Christ.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a varied city full of differences. He explains that, though free, he chose to serve everyone so that the gospel would reach more people. He adapted his customs, but never his faithfulness to God.

For today: approach people with respect, understanding their world and their customs, without making them feel they must change everything in order to listen to you. Always take care that your love for Christ and your obedience to Him are never bargained away.
exp.13:12:
This verse says that whoever speaks in a tongue that others do not understand should pray that they will be able to explain what was said. The phrase "unknown tongue" refers to a language the listeners do not know, and the word for explaining what was said means making it clear so that everyone can understand it.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some people often used the gift of tongues in their meetings, but without anyone understanding them. He reminds them that what matters most is building up the whole church. So if you speak in a tongue, you should also seek to make it understood, so that others are strengthened and not left confused.

Today, when you serve in the church, whether by speaking, singing, or teaching, try to be clear. Use simple words and ask God that what you share will help others understand and grow in their faith.
exp.3:14:
What it says: Paul explains that the Corinthians may have countless instructors in Christ, but only one spiritual father. Those who guide and look after children were the ones who cared for and directed them; "begotten" means that he was the one who brought them into the life of faith through the gospel.

Context: Paul writes to the Corinthians after describing the sufferings of the apostles. He clarifies that he does not want to shame them, but to correct them with affection, as a father would. He founded that church, and that is why he speaks to them with such tenderness and authority. He will ask them to imitate him and will send Timothy to remind them of his way of life.

For today: Thank those who guided you in the faith, and let them correct you with love. If you teach others, do it with family affection, not with pride or a desire for control.
exp.13:15:
Paul says that if someone praises God "with the spirit," that is, in a tongue others do not understand, the person present who is an ordinary listener (someone without that gift or that knowledge) will not be able to say "Amen" to the prayer of thanks. The reason is simple: that person does not know what was said.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the use of tongues in the gatherings was causing disorder. His concern is that everything should build up the others. He himself speaks in tongues, but he wants public prayer to be understood. Some scholars think the "unlearned" person is a listener without the gift; others think he is simply a visitor or a new believer.

For today: when we pray or take part together in a group, let us do it so that everyone can understand and join in with their "Amen." Loving others includes being clear.
exp.3:12:
They say that Paul and the other apostles are slandered (here "defamed" means speaking badly of someone, damaging their name), and yet they answer with gentle pleas. "The filth of the world" refers to the dirt or sediment that settles at the bottom, and "the offscouring of all things" is what everyone throws away. That is how they were treated, and it is how they are still treated today.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who felt proud and wise. With irony and sorrow, he shows them the real life of an apostle: suffering and contempt. Then he makes clear that he does not seek to shame them, but to correct them as a father corrects his beloved children.

For today: when someone insults you or looks down on you for following Christ, you do not have to repay evil with evil. You can respond with kindness and prayer, trusting that the worth of your life does not depend on the opinion of others.
exp.0:22:
Paul says that he and his companions proclaim Christ crucified. For the Jews this is a stumblingblock, that is, something that makes them stumble or takes offense. For the Gentiles, meaning the non-Jews, it is foolishness, a meaningless nonsense.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and greatly admired human wisdom. The Jews asked for miraculous signs, and the Greeks looked for brilliant philosophy. A Messiah who died on a cross fit neither of these. But Paul goes on to say that, for those who are called, Christ is the power and wisdom of God.

For today: do not be ashamed of a simple message that others do not understand. Trust that the cross has power, and share Christ with humility, without dressing him up to please everyone.
exp.7:1:
He says that the one who thinks he already knows everything in fact does not yet know as he ought to know. The phrase "thinks that he knoweth" refers to presuming or believing oneself to be very wise. "Knowledge" here means understanding. True wisdom includes humility and recognizing that there is always more to learn.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some were debating whether it was right to eat meat that had been offered to idols. Those who considered themselves more knowledgeable looked down on the brothers and sisters whose conscience was weak. Paul reminds them that knowledge without love becomes pride, and that love is what builds others up.

For today: before correcting or arguing with someone about matters of faith, ask yourself whether you are doing it with humility and love. Knowing a great deal about the Bible is not enough if I treat others badly. Ask God that your knowledge may lead you to serve, not to boast.
exp.11:15:
This verse imagines the ear feeling less important than the eye and reasons that, because it is not an eye, it no longer belongs to the body. Paul responds with a question: does feeling that way mean it stops being part of the body? The answer is no.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and comparisons between those who had more visible gifts and those with less showy ones. He uses the image of the human body to explain that the church is one body with many members. What makes someone belong is not their function or talent, but that God placed them there.

For today: if you feel unimportant because your service is quiet or different from others', remember that you belong to the church by God's will. Do not compare yourself; serve with joy where He has placed you.
exp.14:28:
It says that some people were baptized "for the dead." Paul asks what purpose that would serve if the dead never rise. "Else" means "otherwise," and "at all" means "in any way."

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who doubted the resurrection. He uses this practice as an argument: if they themselves did it, they basically expected a resurrection. It is not known with certainty what that baptism consisted of; there are several interpretations, and Paul neither recommends it nor explains it. The following verses strengthen his point: he risks his life every day because he believes in the resurrection.

For today: examine why you do what you do in your faith. If Christ rose and we too will rise, then obedience, service, and even sacrifice make sense and carry hope.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that God gives each believer a visible demonstration of the work of the Holy Spirit, and that he does so "to profit withal," that is, for the good of everyone. The word "but" is used here to mark a contrast, and the word "manifestation" means that something of the Spirit becomes noticeable in the life of each person.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and gave too much importance to the most striking gifts. Earlier he has said that there are diversities of gifts, ministries, and operations, but one Spirit, one Lord, and one God. Afterward he will list several specific gifts.

For today: do not despise what God has given you, nor envy what others have. Ask yourself how you can use your gift, whether great or simple, to help and encourage others in your church and in your community.
exp.2:4:
Paul asks what Paul and Apollos are. He answers that they are "ministers," that is, servants or helpers, through whom the Corinthians came to believe. Each one did only what the Lord assigned to him.

Paul is writing to the believers in Corinth, who were divided and boasted of following one leader or another. He corrects that attitude by showing that the leaders are not the center: they are servants. Apollos was another teacher who worked in that church after Paul.

Today we can give thanks to those who teach us the faith, but without putting them in the place of Christ. Let us avoid comparing pastors or groups, and instead serve with humility in what God has given us.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that love (the "charity" in this version) does not rejoice when someone does something unfair or wrong. The word "rejoiceth" in the verse above means "is glad" or "takes delight." Instead, love rejoices when the truth wins out and comes to light.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, pride, and a great deal of attention to spiritual gifts. In this chapter he shows them that without love, every gift loses its value. He describes what true love is like, with simple examples from everyday conduct.

For today: think about whether you have ever taken pleasure in gossip, mockery, or someone else's downfall, even silently. Ask God to help you delight in what is honest and just, and to speak the truth with respect and kindness.
exp.13:0:
It tells us that we should "follow after charity," that is, pursue love with real effort, like someone chasing after something important. It also urges us to "desire" the spiritual gifts, meaning to want them eagerly. And "rather" it asks us to desire the gift of prophesying, which here means speaking words from God that help others.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings had become disorderly. Some were showing off by speaking in tongues when no one could understand them. Following chapter 13, on love, Paul joins the two themes: the gifts must be used with love and for the benefit of everyone.

For today: before you serve or speak in your church, ask yourself whether what you are doing will help others understand, grow, and receive encouragement. Seek love first, and then use your gifts to strengthen others, not to draw attention to yourself.
exp.15:6:
Paul says he does not want to visit the Corinthians only in passing, a quick stop with no time to talk. He hopes to stay with them for a good while, if the Lord permit, that is, if God allows it or sees it as good.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, which had problems and needed close attention. He plans to pass first through Macedonia and then reach Corinth, perhaps to spend the winter there. A brief visit would not be enough to help them grow and work through their differences.

For today: make your plans with seriousness and with care for people, but with a heart ready to depend on God. Give quality time to those you love and serve, and remember that the future is in the Lord's hands.
exp.14:53:
This verse says that when God transforms our weak, mortal bodies into bodies that can never be damaged or die, what the Scripture said will come true: death is swallowed up, completely consumed, and the victory belongs to God. "Put on" is an image: the perishable puts on the imperishable like new clothing.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. In this chapter he explains that Christ rose and that believers will also rise. Here he quotes the prophet Isaiah (25:8), and in the next verse he mocks death, which no longer has the last word.

For today: if you have lost someone dear or fear death, you can hold on to this hope. Pray with confidence and live without fear, serving God and others, because your labor in the Lord is not in vain.
exp.6:8:
He says that whoever cannot control their desires and lives in constant struggle would do well to marry. "Self-control" is the word in the verse above that matches the idea of mastering oneself, especially in sexual matters. The verse's phrase "to burn" is usually understood as burning with desire, though some scholars think it refers to a wider anguish over not being able to live unmarried.

Here the apostle Paul is answering questions the Corinthians had written to him about marriage and singleness. He had said that singleness is good, but he clarifies that each person receives a different gift from God: some to remain single and others to marry. Marrying is not something lesser.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or pressure yourself. Ask God sincerely which path is yours, whether singleness or marriage, and live it with honesty, self-control, and gratitude.
exp.5:3:
Paul says that if believers have disputes about matters of everyday life (the things of this present life), they should ask people from the same church to settle them. Quoted phrases from the source are not present in the English verse, so the earlier comments about the old wording are omitted here. The phrase "those who are least esteemed" is understood in two ways: some think Paul speaks with irony, as if to say, "not even the most simple people in the church would do so poor a job," while others believe it refers to those whom the world does not value.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were taking one another to pagan courts. He tells them this is shameful, because if they will one day take part in judging the world, how can they fail to settle small matters among themselves?

Today, before going to court against another believer, seek the counsel of leaders or mature brothers and sisters in your church who can help you reconcile with humility and truth.
exp.2:10:
Paul says there is only one possible foundation for life and for the church: Jesus Christ. No one can lay a different one. A foundation is the firm base on which a house is built. It is a base that God has already laid, not one invented by people.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who were divided and gathered around different leaders. He reminds them that teachers are only God's fellow workers. Paul laid the foundation when he proclaimed Christ to them, and others keep building on top of it. What matters is that each person takes care in how they build.

For today: examine what you are building your life, your family and your service on. If you rely on reputation, success, or some leader, return to Christ and let Him be the foundation of your daily decisions.
exp.14:17:
It says that, if Christ was not raised, the believers who have already died have also perished. "Fallen asleep" is a gentle way of saying they died, and "perished" means they would have no salvation or hope after death. Without resurrection, their faith in Christ would have led them to nothing.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul shows them that denying this has serious consequences: if the dead do not rise, then Christ did not rise either, and the whole gospel falls apart. He then makes clear that Christ did rise, and that his resurrection is the guarantee of ours.

For today: when you say goodbye to a loved one who trusted in Christ, or when you think about your own death, rest on the resurrection of Jesus. Your hope is not a pleasant idea but a fact you can lean on, one that gives you comfort and encouragement to live.
exp.11:24:
It says that God arranged the body so that there is no division or quarreling among its parts. Instead, each member should genuinely care for the others. "Schism" means disagreement, division, or lack of unity. "Have the same care one for another" means that they look out for one another.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and pride, especially about spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the human body: the parts that seem less important receive greater honor, because all of them are necessary. The church is the body of Christ, and God ordered it this way so that there would be unity and mutual care.

Today we can look out for someone in our church or family who seems to go unnoticed. This week, call them, listen to them, or help them with something specific, and so we practice that mutual care.
exp.13:26:
This verse says that if anyone speaks in a "foreign tongue" (another language or speech that the others do not understand) in the meeting, only two, or at the most three people should speak, one after another, and someone should interpret what is said. "At the most" means "at most," and "one after another" means one at a time.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whose meetings were disorderly, with many people speaking at once. He does not forbid the gift of tongues, but he asks for order so that everything serves "for building up," that is, for strengthening everyone. Christians have understood in different ways what these tongues were exactly.

For today: when we take part in the church, let us seek for what we do to help others understand and grow, and not only to express ourselves. Order and respect are also a way of loving.
exp.14:26:
This verse says that God placed all things under the feet of Christ, quoting Psalm 8:6. But it makes an important clarification: when it says "all things," God the Father is excepted, since he was the one who gave that dominion.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend the resurrection. He explains that Christ reigns until he defeats every enemy, and that the last enemy will be death. Here he makes clear that Christ reigns with the authority of the Father, and that in the end everything will be fulfilled in harmony between the two. How the relationship between the Son and the Father is understood here has been widely discussed, but the central point is the triumph over death.

Today we can rest in the fact that Christ has the last word. In the face of fear, grief, or injustice, we can pray with hope, knowing that death will not win.
exp.3:0:
Paul says that people should see us as "ministers of Christ," that is, servants or helpers who obey their Lord. He also calls us "stewards of the mysteries of God": managers entrusted with carefully distributing the divine truths that God has revealed, especially the gospel. The word "account" means "consider."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions because some were proudly following different teachers. He corrects that attitude by explaining that leaders are not celebrities or bosses, but servants and managers. That is why, in the next verse, what matters most is that they be faithful to the one who placed them in that work.

For today: if you serve God in something, whether teaching, helping, or leading, do not seek applause or compare ministries. Ask yourself whether you are being faithful with what God has entrusted to you, and do it with humility.
exp.3:5:
Paul says that he has used his own case and that of Apollos as an example, out of love for the Corinthians. The sense of "but" is set aside here, and "puffed up" means being filled with pride. The purpose is that they learn not to go beyond what the Scripture teaches, and not to become arrogant by favoring one leader over another.

Paul writes to a divided church, where some were boasting that they followed Paul, Apollos, or others. Earlier he has said that only the Lord judges truly. Here he shows them that not even the apostles are grounds for pride, since they are servants.

Some understand "what is written" as the Scriptures in general; others understand it as earlier quotations from the letter itself.

Today: before you praise or criticize a pastor or teacher, ask yourself whether what you are saying rests on the Bible. Avoid competing between leaders, and remember that everything good comes from God.
exp.8:9:
Paul asks whether the law about not muzzling the ox was said only for the animals. He answers that it was also written for us, that is, for people. "Plow" means preparing the ground, and "thresh" means separating the grain from the straw. Those who do this work do it in the hope of receiving a share of the harvest.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and defends his right, as an apostle, to receive support from them. He uses the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 25:4) to show that the one who works deserves to live from his work. However, he immediately says that he did not use that right, so as not to hinder the gospel.

Today, we can generously support those who serve us spiritually, such as pastors or missionaries. We can also work by serving others with hope, trusting that God sees our effort.
exp.6:19:
This verse says that each person should remain in the condition of life they were in when God called them to faith. The word "calling" here does not mean profession, but God's call and the situation a person was in when they received it. The word "abide" in the verse means to remain in that same condition.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. Some believed that, upon believing in Christ, they had to change their status: be circumcised or cease to be circumcised, or change their social condition. Paul answers that what matters is obeying God, not changing one's outward position. Even so, he clarifies that if a servant can become free, it is good to pursue it.

Today we can serve God faithfully where we are: at work, in the family, or at school. There is no need to change place to please him; we can live with honesty and love right there.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that those who are entrusted with something that does not belong to them are asked for one thing only: that they be found faithful. "Stewards" are managers or caretakers, people who look after and distribute another's goods. "Is required" means "is demanded" or "is expected." "Found faithful" means that, when their work is examined, it proves trustworthy.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were dividing into groups and comparing their leaders. He presents himself, together with the other apostles, as a servant of Christ and a steward of the "mysteries of God," that is, the truths of the gospel. For this reason he says that the judgment of people matters less; the one who truly evaluates is the Lord.

For today: whatever you have, whether time, gifts, or responsibilities, is a charge from God. Seek to carry it out with honesty and perseverance, without looking for applause, trusting that He sees everything.
exp.5:4:
Paul says that what he is about to say is meant to make the Corinthians feel ashamed. He asks them with irony: is it really true that there is not even one wise person among you who can settle a dispute between brothers? The word "judge" here means to arbitrate or settle a dispute.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with many problems. Some believers were taking one another to court before tribunals of people who did not believe in Christ. Paul reminds them that Christians will one day take part in judging the world, so they ought to be able to settle everyday matters among themselves.

Today, when there is a conflict with another believer, let us first seek the counsel of mature and prudent brothers and sisters in the church. Resolving differences with humility and in private protects the witness of the community and cares for the relationship.
exp.10:26:
It says that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord "unworthily," that is, in a way that does not match what they mean, will be "guilty": they become responsible for showing disrespect to the body and blood of Christ. The words "eat" and "drink" in the verse above are the plain forms of what the verse is describing.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the Lord's Supper had become disorderly. According to the earlier verses of this chapter, there were divisions, and some were eating without waiting for or sharing with others. He reminds them that this meal proclaims the death of Jesus. Scholars agree that the problem was attitude, not that anyone had to be perfect.

For today: before taking part in the Lord's Supper, take a moment to examine your heart. Ask for forgiveness, be reconciled with anyone you have offended, and remember with gratitude what Christ did for you.
exp.13:11:
Paul says that the Corinthians are very eager for spiritual gifts, that is, the abilities that the Holy Spirit gives. But he asks them to seek to abound and excel in those that serve to build up, that is, to strengthen and help grow the whole church. "Ye" means "you," and "seek" means "be eager."

Paul is writing to a church that is very enthusiastic about the gifts, but somewhat disorderly. Some were speaking in tongues that no one understood, and that did not help the others. Earlier, he compared this to languages: if you do not understand what someone is saying, that person becomes a stranger to you. For this reason he insists that what matters is that everyone understands and is helped.

For today: before you use your gifts or abilities in the church, ask yourself: "Does this help others know and love God better?" Serve with clarity, humility, and a concern for the good of everyone.
exp.10:4:
He says that a woman who prays or prophesies in the congregation without covering her head dishonors her "head." That word can refer to herself or to the man, and scholars debate which sense is dominant. "Would be shaven" is an older way of saying "would have her head shaved" or "would have her head shorn": for Paul, going uncovered was as shameful as having the head shaved. Here it is taken for granted that women also pray and prophesy in public.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorders in its meetings. He responds to matters of decorum according to the customs of that city. Scholars discuss whether the covering was a veil or the hair itself, and what it meant exactly in that culture. That is not known with certainty.

For today: in worship, let us seek to have our conduct honor God and not scandalize others, and distinguish between the principle of order and respect and the customs of an era.
exp.8:14:
Paul says that he never used the right he had to receive support for preaching the gospel. He does not write this to ask that they now give it to him. He would rather die than have anyone take away his "glorying," that is, the reason for pride and joy he has in preaching for free. Making it "void" means leaving it without value or cancelling it.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and earlier he argued that those who work for the gospel have the right to live from their service. Here he clarifies that, although that right is real, he chose not to use it, so that no one would think he preached for money or that the message would be hindered. Some scholars think he was also responding to criticism in Corinth about the way he supported himself.

For today: sometimes it is good to give up something that is rightfully ours out of love for the gospel and for others. Ask yourself what right you could let go of in order to serve better, without boasting or demanding recognition.
exp.13:36:
It says that if anyone thinks of himself as a prophet or as a person guided by the Spirit, he should acknowledge that what Paul writes comes from the Lord. The words "according to their own opinion" would be "in their own view," and the verse's word "think" covers that sense. The word "acknowledge" means "accept" or "admit."

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where the gifts were being used in disorderly ways, especially in the gatherings. He firmly corrects those who considered themselves very spiritual and did not want to accept his instruction. The verses before this one about women have been understood in various ways, and Christians debate their scope. Even so, the point of this verse is the authority of apostolic teaching.

For today: true spirituality shows itself in humility. Whoever says he is guided by God must be willing to be corrected by Scripture.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that Paul preached in a plain way so that the faith of the Corinthians would not depend on people's intelligence or arguments, but on the power of God. The word "stand" means to rest or be built upon a foundation. "Wisdom of men" is human reasoning.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city where fine speaking and philosophy were greatly admired. There were divisions and pride among them. He recalls that he came to them weak and fearful, without brilliant speeches, but with the work of the Spirit. He then makes clear that there is indeed a wisdom of God, which is not of this world.

For today: examine what your faith rests on. Appreciate what you are taught, but trust in what God does, not in a preacher's talent or in your own arguments. Pray, asking that the Spirit sustain you.
exp.2:22:
It says that believers belong to Christ, and that Christ belongs to God. The word "ye" means "you." It is a short phrase that closes a list: everything Paul has mentioned belongs to you, but you belong to Christ. Christians understand that "Christ is God's" speaks of Christ's relationship with the Father; interpreters explain in various ways how to understand that order, but the general sense is an order of belonging and love.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided, since some said they followed Paul, others Apollos, and others Peter (Cephas). He corrects them: do not boast in human leaders, because those leaders are a gift to them, not their owners.

For today: stop comparing yourself with or competing against others over their leaders or followers. Rest in this: you are Christ's, and that gives you security. Value those who teach you as a gift from God, but follow Christ.
exp.8:5:
Paul says that he and Barnabas also have the right to stop working with their hands and to live on support from the church. "Power" means right or authority. "Forbear working" refers to not earning one's living through one's own trade, in order to devote oneself only to the ministry. It is a rhetorical question: the expected answer is that they do have that right.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his ministry as an apostle. He has already mentioned that other apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Peter (Cephas) receive support. Paul and Barnabas, by contrast, chose to work with their hands. He does not claim the right in order to demand it, but to show that he gave it up willingly out of love for the gospel.

For today: value and generously support those who serve in ministry. And if you have some right, consider whether it is sometimes wise to set it aside in order to help others believe.
exp.3:2:
Paul says that it matters very little to him whether he is judged by the Corinthians or by any human court. The phrase "human judgment" is, literally, "human day," meaning a verdict from men. And he adds something surprising: he does not even judge himself, meaning he does not declare himself approved or condemned by his own opinion.

Paul is writing to a divided church, where some were comparing and criticizing their leaders. He has just said that ministers are stewards of the mysteries of God, and that a steward is required to be faithful. That is why the final judge is neither the Corinthians nor Paul, but the Lord, who will judge in his time.

For today: serve God faithfully without living on the lookout for applause or criticism. Listen to advice with humility, but leave the final verdict in the hands of the Lord, who sees the heart.
exp.15:8:
Paul says that in Ephesus a great and effective door has been opened to him, that is, a great opportunity to preach the gospel with real results. But he also says there are many adversaries, that is, people who oppose him. "Effective" means that it bears fruit, that it works.

Paul writes this letter to the Corinthians from Ephesus. He explains to them why he will stay there until Pentecost: the work is moving forward, though there is opposition. He also tells them about his plans to visit them at a more relaxed pace, "if the Lord permits." Commentators see in this his humility before the plans of God.

For today: a good opportunity does not always come without difficulties. If God opens a door for you to serve, do not be discouraged by opposition. Pray, ask for wisdom, and continue with patience and love.
exp.15:7:
Paul says that he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost. The word "but" is used here to show a contrast, and "Ephesus" is the city of Ephesus. Pentecost was the Jewish feast celebrated fifty days after the Passover, and Christians later remembered it for the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Paul writes from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, and he explains his travel plans. He wants to visit them unhurriedly, not just in passing. But first he stays in Ephesus because there he has a great opportunity to preach, although there are also many opponents, as the following verse says.

For today: sometimes God asks us to remain where we are, even when there are difficulties, because there is work to be done there. Before you move, ask God whether your present place is still your door of service.
exp.9:2:
It says that all the Israelites, the ancestors of the Jews, ate the same spiritual food in the desert. Paul is referring to the manna that God gave them from heaven each day. He calls it "spiritual" because it came from God and not from the earth, and perhaps also because it pointed to something greater.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who felt secure because they had been baptized and took part in the Lord's Supper. He reminds them that Israel also received great blessings from God, and yet many fell into sin and were judged. It is a warning not to become complacent.

For today: receiving blessings from God and taking part in the life of the church is not enough. We need sincere and constant obedience. Be thankful for what God gives you, but guard your heart so that you truly follow him.
exp.14:2:
Paul says that the first and most important thing he taught the Corinthians was what he himself had received: that Christ died for our sins, just as the scriptures foretold. The word "first of all" in the verse can be understood as "in the first place" or "as the most important thing."

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. To answer them, he reminds them of the basic gospel they had already received. Here he quotes a summary of the Christian faith that had been circulating since the earliest days. Scholars believe the "scriptures" refer to the writings of the Old Testament, although he does not point to one exact passage.

For today: when your faith feels confused or weighed down by debates, return to what is essential. Christ died for your sins, and that is good news to receive with gratitude and to share with simplicity.
exp.9:16:
It says that, since there is one loaf on the Lord's table, all of us who take part in it, though we are many, form one body.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and was tempted to join in feasts held in honor of idols. He reminds them that the Lord's Supper is a communion with Christ and also among brothers and sisters. For this reason one cannot share the Lord's table and the table of idols at the same time. Christians have understood in various ways what happens exactly at the Supper, but all of them see here a real union.

Today, when you take part in the Supper, remember that you do not come alone. Before taking it, try to make peace with some brother or sister, and treat them with the affection of someone who shares the same bread.
exp.13:8:
Paul says that if we speak in a tongue without uttering clear, understandable words, no one will be able to understand what is being said. It would be like speaking into the air. A "clear meaning" in the sense of a message with understandable significance is what he has in mind, and "shall utter" means to speak out or pronounce.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where several people used the gift of tongues in meetings with no one interpreting. Earlier he gave the example of the flute, the lyre (a stringed instrument), and the war trumpet: if they do not sound clearly, no one knows what is being played or when to get ready. His aim is that the church be built up.

For today: when you speak, teach, or pray in a group, use simple, clear words so that everyone can understand and be encouraged. Ask yourself: "Is what I am saying being understood?"
exp.0:4:
It says that the believers in Corinth were enriched in Christ in every way. "Utterance" refers to the ability to speak and express oneself, and "knowledge" to understanding. "You are enriched" means they have received abundance, not because of their own merit, but because they are united to Jesus.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with remarkable gifts, but also with divisions and serious problems, which he corrects later on. Before rebuking them, he begins by thanking God for what He has already done in them. Some think that "utterance" also points to spiritual gifts of speaking, but the text does not specify this.

For today: before criticizing others or yourself, acknowledge with gratitude what God has already given you in Christ. Use your words and your knowledge to serve and build up others, not to boast.
exp.7:11:
Paul says that when someone causes a brother or sister with a weaker faith to act against what their conscience allows, that person is sinning against the brother or sister. Wounding their weak conscience means hurting or harming the conscience of someone who is still unsure in their faith. And since that person belongs to Christ, wounding them is sinning against Christ himself.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city where meat that had been offered to idols was sold. Some believers, who had more knowledge, knew that idols are nothing and ate without any problem. But others, who came out of paganism, felt that eating was worshiping the idol. Paul asks them that their knowledge not make them insensitive.

For today: before using my freedom in something doubtful, I can ask myself how it will affect the one who is watching me and is still growing in faith. Loving my brother or sister is worth more than being right or exercising my right.
exp.6:15:
This verse asks: how do you know, wife, whether you will bring your husband to salvation? And the same question is put to the husband about his wife.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage. He speaks of couples where only one of them believes in Christ. He has just said that if the unbeliever chooses to leave, the believer should let them go, because God has called us to live in peace. Interpreters debate whether this verse offers hope that the spouse will be converted, or whether it instead warns that no one can be sure of this and so a person should not hold back by force someone who wants to leave. Both readings are possible.

If you live with someone who does not believe, live with love, patience, and peace. Do not press or despair: salvation is the work of God, and your good witness can be a seed.
exp.9:22:
It says that although there are many things that are permitted to me, not all of them are good or help me. "Lawful" means allowed. "Expedient" means that it is beneficial, that it is the best course. "Edify" means that it builds up, that it strengthens one's own faith and the faith of others.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who lived surrounded by temples and by meat offered to idols. Just before, he warned them not to become involved in the worship of demons. Here he clarifies that, in matters where there is freedom, it is not enough to ask whether something is allowed, but whether it helps others. Then he adds that no one should seek only his own good, but the good of his neighbor.

For today: before doing something that is permitted, such as a form of entertainment or a way of spending your time, ask yourself whether it draws you closer to God and whether it strengthens those around you.
exp.13:31:
They say that those who receive and pass on a message from God must keep control of themselves. The word "spirits" here refers to the gift or prompting of prophecy in each person, and the phrase "are subject" means that they submit, or allow themselves to be put in order. The prophet is not swept along by a force he cannot stop; he can wait for his turn and be silent.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly and several people spoke at the same time. He wants the messages to build up everyone. Some understand that "the prophets" are the others who weigh what is said; others, that each prophet controls himself. Both ideas point to order.

For today: before you speak or serve in the church, ask yourself whether you are doing it with respect, waiting your turn, and whether what you say helps others grow. Self-control is also a fruit of the Spirit.
exp.10:14:
It says that for a woman it is fitting and beautiful to let her hair grow long, because her hair was given to her as a kind of covering. Letting the hair grow long means leaving it uncut. Fitting means worthy of respect. Indecorous, as the older wording puts it, means improper or shameful.

Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about order in worship. He uses the custom of his time and nature as an argument. Scholars debate whether the "covering" refers to a cloth or only to the hair, and what local customs Corinth had. This is not entirely clear.

For today: take care to show respect and order when you worship, and do not turn cultural customs into a cause for quarrel. Ask yourself how you can honor God and others with humility and simplicity.
exp.8:1:
Paul says that other people may not recognize him as an apostle, but the believers in Corinth should. A "seal" was a mark that guaranteed something was genuine, like a signature. "Apostleship" is the work of an apostle, a sent one of Christ. For Paul, the church in Corinth is the proof of his calling.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some of them doubted his authority. He had preached there and a church had been born. So he reminds them that their own faith is evidence that God sent him. With this he begins to defend his right to receive support for his work, although he had chosen not to use it.

For today: God often shows his work in changed lives. When someone points something out to you, do not defend yourself with empty words; let your testimony and your love speak. And remember that whoever serves faithfully leaves marks on others.
exp.11:28:
Here Paul asks a series of questions whose obvious answer is "no." Not everyone in the church is an apostle, a prophet, or a teacher. The verse of "teachers" and of "workers of miracles" is given in the verse itself, so no extra word needs to be explained here.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who were divided and thought themselves superior because of the gifts they had. He reminds them that the church is a body with many parts, and that God himself distributed the gifts as he chose. For that reason no one should feel more important or less valuable. Then he leads them to love, the way of love described in chapter 13.

For today: instead of comparing yourself with others, be thankful for the place God gave you and serve with what you have. And value those who serve in other ways.
exp.13:20:
The verse says that in the Law, meaning the Scriptures of the Old Testament, God announced that he would speak to his people through other tongues and through foreign lips. Even so, the people would not listen to him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued speaking in tongues too highly during the gatherings. He quotes Isaiah 28:11-12, where God warned a hardened people that they would hear foreign languages, and even then they would not believe. Paul wants the Corinthians to think with maturity: what matters is that everyone understands and is built up.

For today: before you speak, pray, or sing in church, ask yourself whether others will be able to understand and receive help. Let your way of serving always seek the good of others, not merely to impress.
exp.6:13:
It says that when a believer is married to someone who does not believe, that marriage is not something defiled. The unbelieving spouse is made holy, meaning they are joined in some way to what is holy through their relationship with the believer. For that reason the children are not unclean (impure, set apart from God), but holy (set apart, close to God). Here "unbelieving" simply means one who does not believe.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage. Some believers feared that staying married to an unbeliever would spiritually defile them. Paul tells them not to separate. Scholars discuss how far this holiness reaches: the verse does not say that the spouse is automatically saved.

For today: if you live with someone who does not share your faith, do not see them as a burden. Love with patience, be steadfast, and pray for that person, trusting that God can work through your life.
exp.14:34:
Here Paul presents the questions someone might ask: "How are the dead raised up?" and "With what body do they come?" The phrase "But some man will say" means that someone will ask. These are sincere or mocking doubts about what the resurrection would be like.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, where some denied the resurrection of the dead (verse 12). Earlier he had warned them against bad influences and a lack of knowledge of God. Now he answers with an image from the field: a seed that dies and produces a different plant. The exact details of how the resurrected body will be are not fully explained.

For today: when you have doubts about the faith, bring them to God and to his Word with humility, without mockery. And trust that God, who gives life to the seed, can fulfill his promise.
exp.10:19:
Paul tells the Christians in Corinth that, although they gather as a church, what they are doing cannot be called eating the Lord's supper. "When you come together in one place" means that they meet in the same location. With these words, Paul points out that their gathering does not match what Jesus established.

Paul writes because there are divisions among them. According to the verses that follow, each person was eating his own meal without waiting for the others. As a result, one went hungry while another became drunk. The poor were left feeling ashamed. Scholars generally agree that this happened during the ordinary meal that accompanied the Supper, although the exact details are debated.

For today: before taking part in the Lord's Supper, let us examine how we treat our fellow believers. Sharing the table with Christ calls us to wait for one another, to serve, and to care for the most needy in the community.
exp.6:24:
Paul speaks about the unmarried, that is, people who have never married. He says he has no direct command from the Lord about them, meaning Jesus left no specific teaching on this subject. For that reason he gives his opinion, his honest judgment. He can be trusted in his advice because God showed him mercy and made him faithful.

Paul is responding to questions the Corinthians had written to him about marriage and remaining single. He distinguishes between what Jesus taught and his own counsel as an apostle. According to the verses that follow, he advises with an eye to the present distress, a difficult situation that scholars explain in various ways.

Today we can learn to give and receive advice with humility, without presenting our opinions as commands from God. And when deciding whether to marry or not, it is wise to pray, ask for wisdom, and serve the Lord faithfully in whatever stage of life we are in.
exp.4:5:
It is not good that the Corinthians take pride in themselves. Their boasting is presuming to be above others. Paul reminds them of something they already know: a little yeast makes the whole batch of dough rise.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. They were tolerating a man who was living in serious immorality, and yet they felt proud. Paul uses leaven as an image: sin that is not confronted can affect the whole community. Some understand the handing over to Satan as expelling the man from the church, although its exact scope is debated.

Today we can ask whether we are ignoring some sin, in ourselves or in our community, while we boast about how good we are. With humility and love, it is wise to face it, always seeking the restoration of the person and the purity of the church.
exp.15:10:
Paul says that no one should look down on Timothy. The phrase "look down on" means to think little of him or not give him proper honor. Instead, the Corinthians should help him continue his journey "in peace," that is, with good treatment and without conflict, so that he can return to Paul. Paul is waiting for him along with the brothers who are accompanying him.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth from Ephesus. He has just said that Timothy does the Lord's work just as he does. Timothy was young, and Paul does not explain why he asks for this care; some think he feared Timothy would be treated with contempt because of his age or his character, but that is an interpretation.

For today: value and support those who serve God, regardless of their age or experience. A word of encouragement or a concrete help can strengthen them greatly.
exp.4:3:
It says that when the church gathers in the name of Jesus, Paul will be united with them in spirit, even though he is far away. The phrase "when ye are gathered together" means "when you are gathered together." The word "power" means strength or authority. So the decision is made under the authority of Jesus, not by human opinion.

Paul writes from Ephesus, as is commonly understood, to the church in Corinth. There was a serious case of sexual immorality among them, and the church was doing nothing; they were even proud of it. Paul asks them to act together as a community. How exactly to understand being "handed over to Satan" is interpreted in several ways, but the stated purpose is that the person would ultimately be saved.

For today: when the church faces a serious sin, it should act with humility, unity and prayer, seeking the restoration of the person and not punishment or pride.
exp.13:29:
It says that if, while a prophet is speaking in the meeting, God shows something to another person who is seated, the one who was speaking first should stop and be quiet.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly and many wanted to speak at the same time. He seeks order so that everyone receives encouragement and teaching. The prophets speak in turns, and the others weigh what is said. Scholars understand in different ways how this "revelation" worked, but the purpose of building up everyone is clear.

Today we can practice listening well and making room for others. Even when we have something valuable to say, in the church and in small groups it is wise to speak with humility, without monopolizing the conversation, so that everyone is encouraged.
exp.14:15:
What it says: Paul repeats a logical argument. If it is true that the dead never rise, then Christ was not raised either, because his resurrection would be an impossible exception. The two things are bound together: the resurrection of Christ and the resurrection of believers.

Context: Paul is writing to the church in Corinth. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead (v. 12). Paul shows them where that idea leads: if there is no resurrection, the preaching, the faith, and the forgiveness of sins are left without foundation. He does not doubt that Christ was raised; he only exposes the absurdity of denying the resurrection.

For today: Our hope is not just a pleasant idea, but rests on a fact: Christ lives. When you face loss, fear, or grief, lean on that certainty. You can pray: "Lord, strengthen my faith in your resurrection and in the promise that we too will live."
exp.11:23:
It says that the parts of the body that look good and seem worthy do not need special attention. "Presentable" here means proper and becoming. Instead, God put the body together so that the part that had less honor was given more honor and care. In this way, no one is forgotten.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and valued showy gifts more, such as speaking in tongues. He uses the picture of the body to show that every believer is necessary. Some understand the parts that are "less presentable" to mean the private parts we cover with clothing, but the central point is mutual care.

For today: notice who in your church goes unnoticed, such as someone older, sick, or shy. Look for that person this week, greet them, and give them a place. In this way you reflect God's care.
exp.14:51:
It says the change will happen suddenly, "in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye," when the last trumpet sounds.
