Then the dead in Christ will be raised with a body that does not decay, and believers who are still alive will also be changed. "In the last trumpet" is the same as "at the last trump." "Incorruption" refers to what breaks down and dies.

The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection. He explains a "mystery," that is, a truth that God reveals. Our present body cannot enter the kingdom of God as it is, so it needs to be transformed. Christians understand in different ways when and how this will happen, but all agree that God will do it.

For today: if in Christ death does not have the final word, we can face sickness, grief, and fear with hope. Today you can comfort someone with this promise and live trusting in God.
exp.6:5:
Paul makes clear that what he has just said is not a command from God, but a concession. "Permission" means that it gives freedom or leave to do something; "commandment" is a binding order.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage. He is referring to what came before: that spouses may separate for a short time, by mutual agreement, to pray. Interpreters differ a little: some believe "this" points only to that temporary pause; others, to the whole of the earlier advice. In either case, Paul offers wise guidance, not a law.

Today we can distinguish between what the Bible commands and what it leaves to our freedom. In marriage, couples should decide together, with respect and mutual agreement, how to give time to prayer, without imposing it on one another.
exp.6:14:
If the unbelieving spouse decides to leave and end the marriage, the believer may let them go. "Unbelieving" here means someone who does not believe. A believer is not bound, like a slave, to that marriage in such a case. God has called us to live in peace.

The apostle Paul is answering questions from the Corinthians about marriage. Earlier he asked that a believer not abandon an unbelieving spouse if that spouse wants to stay. Here he speaks of the opposite case: when it is the unbeliever who leaves. Christians interpret differently whether this also allows a new marriage; the text does not say so clearly.

For today: work to keep your marriage with love and patience, but if the other person decides to leave, do not carry a guilt that is not yours. Seek God's peace and the counsel of a pastor.
exp.6:10:
She says that a wife who has separated from her husband has two paths: to remain unmarried, or to be reconciled to him. She also commands that the husband not send away his wife. "Separate" means to part from one another; "send away" means to leave or divorce; "unmarried" means single.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth and answering questions about marriage. Before this verse, he recalls a teaching of the Lord Jesus: the wife should not separate from her husband. Then, for new cases, such as couples where one does not believe, he gives his apostolic counsel. Some scholars think Paul is speaking of difficult situations, and Christians interpret differently how to apply it in cases of abuse.

For today: if there is a conflict in the marriage, first seek reconciliation, through dialogue, humility, forgiveness, and the help of a counselor or pastor. If there is danger or violence, seek protection and wise support.
exp.13:6:
Paul says that even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp (a stringed instrument similar to a guitar), need clear and distinct sounds. If they only make noise without rhythm or distinct notes, no one can recognize the tune.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued speaking in tongues very highly in their gatherings, but without anyone understanding it. He uses this example to show that a confusing message helps no one. He prefers what builds up the whole church.

For today: when you teach, pray aloud, or serve in your church, try to speak with clarity and simplicity, so that others understand and are encouraged in their faith.
exp.14:27:
It says that when Christ has conquered everything, including death, the Son himself will place himself under the authority of the Father, who gave him that dominion. "Subdued" here means placed under authority. "But when" is the sense of the phrase in question. The final goal is that God be all in all, that is, that God reigns fully and his presence fills everything.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some denied the resurrection of the dead. He explains that Christ's resurrection begins the final victory over death. That subjection of the Son does not mean he is lesser in worth; Christians have understood it in different ways. The theme is the order and purpose of the work of redemption.

For today: the story ends with God at the center and with death defeated. That hope helps us live with peace, serve without fear, and put God first in every area of life.
exp.10:2:
It sets out an order of relationship: Christ is the head of every man, the man is the head of the woman, and God is the head of Christ. "But I would have you know" means "I would have you know." The word "head" is understood in several ways: some see authority, others see origin or source.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its gatherings. He has just praised them for following his teachings, and now he introduces a subject about how men and women prayed and prophesied in public. Scholars debate the exact meaning of the customs of that time regarding covering the head.

For today: the verse reminds us that all relationships, even the closest, are lived under Christ. We can ask ourselves whether our conduct at home and in the church reflects humility, respect and service, like that of Christ toward the Father.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that if a Christian woman is married to a man who does not believe, and he agrees to keep living with her, she should not leave him. The word "unbelieving" here does not mean being unfaithful in the marriage, but having no faith in Christ. "Agrees" means that he is willing and accepts it.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage. Some believers may have thought that staying married to an unbeliever made them unclean. Paul makes clear that this is not so: one person's faith can bring blessing to the home, and God desires peace in the family. He himself says that he gives this advice "I, not the Lord," meaning that there is no direct word from Jesus about this case.

Today, if your spouse does not share your faith but wants to stay with you, try to live with love, respect, and patience. Your daily example can speak louder than your words.
exp.15:0:
Paul is speaking to them about the offering being gathered for poor Christians, whom he calls "the saints." The word "collection" in the verse refers to a gift of money gathered from the people. He asks them to do the same thing he has already instructed the churches of Galatia to do.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth. The believers in Jerusalem were in need, and Paul was organizing help from churches in other regions. For that reason he gives practical instructions, so that everything will be ready before he arrives. The verses that follow show that he wanted order, not pressure at the last minute.

For today: giving with order and planning is a good way to practice generosity. Instead of waiting for an emergency to arise, we can set something aside regularly, according to what God allows us, to help whoever is in need.
exp.1:0:
Paul reminds the brothers in Corinth that when he came to them, he did not present himself with lofty words or with a speech full of human wisdom. "Pompous speech" means talking in a showy way, aiming to impress. "Declaring to you the testimony of God" means proclaiming to them what God did and revealed in Jesus.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city that greatly admired eloquence and wisdom. There were divisions among the believers, and some boasted of brilliant leaders. Paul reminds them that his first visit was simple, so that their faith would rest on God and not on human abilities.

For today: when you speak about Jesus to others, you do not need impressive words. Be simple, honest, and faithful to the message; God works through him.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that what Paul has just explained is his defense before those who question him. The word "answer" means defense or explanation. The phrase "to those who examine me" refers to those who test or judge him, perhaps with doubts or criticism.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some were doubting his authority as an apostle. He responds by reminding them that he saw Jesus and that the church itself, the fruit of his work, is proof of his calling. Then, in the verses that follow, he will defend his right to receive support for his service, though later he will explain that he chose not to use it.

For today: when someone questions your faith or your service, respond with calm and with facts, not with anger. A life that bears fruit speaks better than words. And it is good to give explanations with humility, without losing the desire to serve others.
exp.15:13:
This verse says that everything we do, great or small, must be done with love. In this older version, the word "charity" does not mean giving alms, but the generous love that seeks the good of the other. "All your things" refers to everything: words, work, decisions and service.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, pride and arguments. At the end of his letter, he gives brief commands: watch, stand firm and be brave. Then he sets this limit: firmness and courage must go together with love. In this way he returns to what he taught in chapter 13.

Today, before you respond in an argument or make a decision, ask yourself: "Am I doing this with love?" You can be right and still speak harshly. Today, try to make your tone, your patience and your actions reflect the love of Christ.
exp.2:13:
It says that if what someone built on the foundation holds up under testing, that person will receive a reward. To "build upon" means to keep building on top of something already laid. To "abide" means to remain standing. God rewards work that proves firm and valuable.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, who were divided and boasted in their leaders. He laid the foundation, which is Jesus Christ, and others keep building on it. Paul reminds them that each worker will give an account, and that the fire of the Lord's day will test the quality of what has been done. Christians interpret in different ways what that reward will be, but all agree that God will judge with justice.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we do for God, in the church, at home, or at work, we do with love, truth, and humility, and not to show off, because that is what endures.
exp.6:30:
Here Paul says that those who "use this world," that is, those who enjoy or handle the things of this life (money, work, possessions), should do so without clinging to them, as if they were not fully using them. The reason is that "the fashion of this world passeth away": the present form of things is passing.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. He says that "the time is short," and for that reason he invites them to live with inner freedom. Scholars debate whether he is speaking of a present difficulty or of the nearness of Christ's return. In either case, his desire is that they live "without anxiety."

For today: enjoy what God gives you, but do not let your possessions, your work, or your worries take the place of God in your heart.
exp.1:8:
It says that God has prepared things so great for those who love him that no one could see them, hear them, or imagine them by their own means. The word for "ear" here means hearing, and the phrase about things "entering the heart" means coming into the mind or imagination. The word "rather" in this sentence is the one that carries the contrast.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who boasted in human wisdom. He reminds them that the rulers of this world did not understand God's plan, and that is why they crucified Jesus. Paul introduces the quotation with the words "as it is written," probably drawing on Isaiah 64:4 and 65:17, though the quotation is not exact. In the verse that follows, he explains that God reveals these things through his Spirit.

For today: do not be content to measure your future only by what you see or understand. Ask the Spirit to teach you, and trust that God keeps something good for those who love him.
exp.11:14:
This verse imagines the foot feeling less important and saying, "Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body." Paul answers with a question: does thinking this way make it stop being part of the body? The answer is no.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, a church marked by divisions and rivalry over spiritual gifts. Some felt superior, and others perhaps felt inferior. Paul uses the image of the body to explain that all believers form one body by the same Spirit, and that each one is necessary.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or think that your service is worth little. If you belong to Christ, you are part of his body. Do with joy what God has given you, without envy and without contempt.
exp.0:0:
Paul presents himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, a messenger sent with authority to carry his message. He says he was "called," meaning chosen, and that this happened "through the will of God," not by his own merit. He also mentions Sosthenes, whom he calls "our brother."

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth, a large and very diverse city. The verses that follow show that this is the opening greeting. Exactly who this Sosthenes was is not known for certain; some connect him with a man mentioned in Acts 18:17, but the Bible does not confirm this. Paul begins by affirming his authority before correcting several problems in the church.

God continues to call ordinary people to serve him, and this does not depend on our being perfect. We can serve with humility, remembering that our place comes from his will and grace. Furthermore, it is good to serve alongside other brothers and sisters, as Paul did.
exp.8:7:
Paul asks two questions. He asks whether what he has just said is only human reasoning, that is, an idea based on the logic of ordinary people. And he answers with another question: God's law says the same thing too. The word "authority" means the right to something, and the phrase "by human standards" means by human judgment.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his right, and that of Barnabas, to receive support from the church for their work in the gospel. He uses everyday examples, such as the soldier, the vineyard worker, and the shepherd. Then he shows that Scripture teaches the same thing, by quoting the law of Moses about the ox that treads out the grain. Although he had that right, he later explains that he chose not to use it.

For today: it is right to value and support those who serve in the church, without taking advantage of them. And the one who serves may, out of love, give up what is rightfully theirs.
exp.8:15:
Paul says that preaching the gospel is nothing he can boast about. For him it is not an option but a duty that God placed on him. The word "glory" as used here means to boast or take pride in something. "Necessity" here means obligation. And the phrase "woe is unto me" expresses a strong warning: it would be serious if he stopped preaching.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. He has just explained that he had the right to receive financial support for his work, but he did not use that right so that he would not hinder the message. Here he makes clear that his motive is not to seek praise. His calling comes from God, and that is why he feels responsible to carry it out.

For today: when you serve God, examine your motives. Do what He has entrusted to you faithfully and humbly, without seeking applause, remembering that it is a gift of grace to be able to share the good news of Jesus.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that God revealed his secret wisdom to us through the Holy Spirit. The reason is that the Spirit searches all things, even the deepest things of God. "But" is the word the verse uses to connect this thought to the one before it; "searches" means to investigate thoroughly, to know completely.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church that boasted in human wisdom. He reminds them that the rulers of this world did not understand the message of the cross. What God prepared is not discovered by intelligence alone; God himself makes it known.

For today: before you read the Bible or make important decisions, ask the Holy Spirit to give you understanding. Do not depend only on your own cleverness; come with humility, expecting that God will show you his truth.
exp.3:20:
Paul asks the believers in Corinth a question: do they want him to come with a rod, that is, with firm correction, or with love and a spirit of gentleness and humility in how he treats them? The rod is an instrument of discipline, like the one a father or a shepherd would use.

Paul writes to them as a spiritual father, since he founded that church. Some in Corinth were proud and talked a great deal, and some even questioned his authority. He tells them that what matters is not fine-sounding words but the power of God seen in a life. The choice is left to them: their attitude will determine how he deals with them.

For today: when someone corrects us, or when we have to correct someone, let us remember that humility and love open doors. And if we are corrected, let us listen with simplicity, before a harsher correction becomes necessary.
exp.14:25:
What the verse says: Paul affirms that death is the last enemy that Christ will destroy. "Destroyed" means annulled, with its power taken away. "Last" means final. Death does not have the final word; God does.

Context: Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. He explains that Christ rose and that his reign advances until it overcomes everything that opposes God. Death appears at the end of that list, as the hardest enemy. How and when all of this will happen in detail, the Bible does not fully explain.

For today: If you are grieving or afraid of death, this verse invites you to wait with confidence. You can mourn your loved ones without losing hope, because your faith rests on a Christ who has already won and who will complete his work.
exp.10:31:
What he says: Paul explains that when the Lord judges us, he is really correcting us the way a father corrects his children. "Chastened" here means disciplined or trained, not destroyed. The purpose is that believers should not be condemned along with the world that rejects God.

Context: Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some were abusing the Lord's Supper: they ate without waiting for others, and the poor were left humiliated. He says this brought consequences, such as sickness and even death among some. Interpreters debate whether all the illnesses there were caused by this, but Paul does see a discipline from God.

For today: When God corrects you through his Word or your conscience, do not see it as rejection, but as love. Examine yourself with humility, confess what is wrong, and treat your brothers and sisters with respect and consideration.
exp.10:5:
If a woman does not want to cover her head when she prays or prophesies, then she should also have her hair cut off. But since she thinks it is a shame to have her hair cut off or shaved, then let her cover herself. "Shorn" means having the hair cut very short, and "shame" here means something disgraceful or improper.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its gatherings. He speaks of a custom of that time about how men and women presented themselves when praying and prophesying. Scholars discuss exactly what the "covering" was (a veil or hair arranged a certain way) and how much of this was cultural. Paul uses the argument to defend order and respect.

For today: when we worship, let us take care that our manner and our appearance honor God and do not cause stumbling or division, always seeking love and order among brothers and sisters.
exp.1:15:
It says that no one can know the thoughts of God by themselves or teach him anything. But believers, through the Spirit, have "the mind of Christ," that is, a way of thinking and understanding that comes from Him. The question "who has instructed him?" is a question meant to say: no one. It is taken from Isaiah 40:13.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who boasted of human wisdom and divided themselves into groups. He explains that God's true wisdom is understood through the Spirit, not through intellectual pride. The "natural man" refers to a person who is guided only by what is natural, without the Spirit. Paul does not say that believers know everything, but that God has given them understanding.

For today: before deciding or arguing, ask God for His guidance and see how Jesus thought and acted. Study the Gospels with humility, willing for Him to correct your way of thinking.
exp.13:32:
It says that God is not a God of disorder or confusion, but of peace. Here "disorder" is understood as confusion or commotion. It adds that this is so in all the churches of the saints, that is, of the believers.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whose meetings were disorderly: several people spoke at once, using gifts such as prophecy and tongues. He asks them to speak in turns, so that everyone may learn and be encouraged. The sentence that follows about women has been interpreted in various ways among Christians, so it is wise to read it carefully and in its context.

For today: when you take part in your church, or in a group, try to listen and wait for your turn. Seek to speak in a way that builds up others and does not create confusion. Order, rightly understood, is a way of loving.
exp.14:35:
He says that when someone sows a seed, that seed does not come to life unless it first dies.

The apostle Paul is answering those who doubted the resurrection and asked how the dead would be raised and with what kind of body they would come. Paul uses an example from the field that everyone knew. The buried seed seems to come to an end, but from it a new plant grows. With this image he shows that death is not necessarily the end, and that God gives life in ways that surprise us.

For today: when you go through losses or painful endings, remember that God can bring life out of what seems to be nothing. Trust in his power and wait with patience, knowing that he keeps his promises.
exp.6:0:
Paul begins to answer the questions the Corinthians had asked him in a letter. He says that it is good for a man not to touch a woman, an expression from that time that is understood to mean not having intimate relations, or not marrying. The words "in regard to" mean the same as "concerning," and the word you wrote is about the same as they wrote.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, a city with much immorality. Some scholars believe this phrase quotes what the Corinthians themselves thought, and others believe it is Paul's own view about remaining single. The verses that follow clarify that marriage is good and protects against immorality.

For today: whether you are single or married, live your situation as a calling from God, with purity and gratitude, without looking down on others for their choice.
exp.9:18:
Paul asks a question to clarify his point: am I saying that an idol is something real, or that the food offered to idols has power in itself? The phrase "sacrificed to idols" means meat offered in pagan rites. The question expects a "no," but Paul will soon make clear that something more serious lies behind it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, surrounded by pagan temples. Earlier he spoke of communion at the Lord's Supper and of the example of Israel, where those who ate of the sacrifice shared in the altar. Now he avoids two errors: thinking that idols are real gods, and thinking that taking part in those feasts is harmless. He warns that behind those practices there are spiritual forces opposed to God.

Today, let us ask what things receive our loyalty and worship. Even if we have no statues, we must take care that our lives are not divided between Christ and other devotions.
exp.13:28:
It says that in the church gathering two or three prophets should speak, that is, people who communicate what God shows them to help others. The others present should examine carefully what was said to see whether it is true and in line with God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had disorderly meetings, with many people speaking at the same time. He asks for order so that everyone may learn and be encouraged. Some understand that the rest are the other prophets, and others think it is the whole congregation. The text leaves this open.

Today, let us not accept every message just because it sounds spiritual. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, with humility and prayer, and let us do it with respect, seeking the good of everyone in the church.
exp.5:5:
It says that one believer takes another believer before a judge, and that he does so in front of "unbelievers," that is, people who do not believe in Christ.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a church marked by many divisions. He is concerned because their legal disputes were being brought before pagan courts. He tells them this is a shame, since there should be someone among them wise enough to settle these matters. Scholars debate which specific cases he had in mind, but the rebuke is clear.

For today: if you have a conflict with another believer, try first to resolve it with humility, through dialogue, and with the help of mature leaders in the church. Take care that your witness is not harmed before those who do not believe.
exp.0:9:
Paul asks the believers in Corinth, with much affection and in the name of Jesus, to be in agreement with one another. "That ye all speak the same thing" means that they should not divide over opinions that set them against each other. "Divisions" means splits or disagreements. "Perfectly joined together" speaks of being well fitted together, like pieces that fit, with one mind and one purpose.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth. He has just reminded them that God is faithful and called them to share the life of his Son. Then he learns, from people of Chloe's household, that they were splitting into groups, each following the leader they preferred: Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ.

For today: if there is division in your church or family, do not take the side of one person or one faction. First look for what unites, which is Christ, and speak with humility and respect.
exp.11:26:
They say that the believers in Corinth, together, form the body of Christ, and that each one is a member, a part of that body. "In particular" means that each person is a distinct piece, not the whole body.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride over spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the body to teach them that everyone is necessary, that God distributes different gifts, and that no one should despise another or think himself superior.

For today: this week, look for a brother or sister in your church and ask how they are doing. If they are suffering, accompany them; if they receive some joy, celebrate it with them. In this way you live out that you belong to one and the same body.
exp.15:11:
Paul says that he strongly encouraged Apollos to visit the Corinthians together with other brothers. But Apollos did not want to go for now. Paul says that he will come when he has a good opportunity.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, and some preferred Apollos while others preferred Paul. That is why it is remarkable that Paul speaks of Apollos with respect. We do not know for certain why Apollos did not go; the text only says it was his decision, and Paul does not pressure him or criticize him.

For today: we can work with other believers without controlling them. Let us respect that each servant of God has his own time and his own way of serving, and trust that God guides each one.
exp.13:39:
It says that everything done in the church meeting should be done in a fitting and orderly way.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth. In that congregation there was confusion in the meetings: several people spoke at the same time, especially with gifts such as prophecy and tongues. Paul has just encouraged them to use those gifts, and now he closes the chapter with this balance: spiritual freedom, but with order, so that everyone is built up and it is clear that God is not the author of confusion (v. 33).

For today: before taking part in your church, whether by singing, teaching, or praying, ask yourself whether what you are about to do will help others understand and grow. Serving with preparation and respect is also a way of showing love.
exp.3:3:
Paul says that, although his conscience does not accuse him of anything, that does not prove he is right before God. The word "justified" here means declared innocent or approved. In the end, the one who examines him and decides is the Lord, not he himself or other people.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which is divided by preferring some leaders over others. Some were criticizing Paul and Apollos. He reminds them that God's servants must be faithful, and that the final judgment belongs to the Lord, who knows even what is hidden in the heart.

For today: having a clear conscience is good, but it is not the last word. We can ask God to examine our heart, and avoid judging others harshly, trusting that He judges with perfect truth and also knows how to recognize what is good.
exp.1:5:
Paul says that he does teach wisdom, but to those who are "mature," that is, to believers who are spiritually grown in the faith. The word "but" in this verse introduces a contrast. That wisdom does not come from this present age (this era or the present world) nor from its rulers and leaders, who come to nothing, meaning they pass away and lose their power.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and fascinated by brilliant speeches. He has just said that his preaching did not rely on persuasive words, but on the power of the Spirit. Now he clarifies that the gospel is not ignorance: it has a deep wisdom, but that wisdom comes from God. Some understand "mature" as mature believers; others understand it as all who are in Christ.

For today: do not measure your faith by what impresses the world. Seek to grow in maturity, asking the Spirit to teach you God's wisdom in his Word.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that the man and the woman need each other. Neither can live without the other "in the Lord", that is, within the life and order that Christ establishes. The word "man" in the verse is the same word used for a male person, and "Nevertheless" means "still, even so," introducing a correction.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its gatherings. He had been speaking about customs of covering the head when praying, and about the relationship between man and woman. Here he corrects any idea of superiority: he says they are interdependent. Some details of this passage, such as the part about the angels, are interpreted in several ways.

For today: in the home, the church, and the workplace, let us value the other sex as a gift from God, not as a rival or as someone inferior. Today you can thank a person of the other sex for something concrete they contribute to your life.
exp.14:8:
Paul says that he considers himself the least of the apostles. He states that he does not deserve to be called an apostle, and the reason is clear: he once persecuted the church of God. In this older wording, the sense is that he is not worthy of the name, and the word for last means the final one.

Paul writes to the Corinthians when he recalls that the risen Jesus appeared to many witnesses. He was the last to see him. He mentions his violent past against believers to show that his calling is not due to his own merits. He then adds that everything he is comes from the grace of God.

For today: you do not have to hide your past mistakes or live buried in them. You can acknowledge them with humility and trust that the grace of God transforms you and enables you to serve others.
exp.0:3:
Paul says that he always gives thanks to God for the believers in Corinth. The reason is the grace of God, that is, his favor and undeserved gift, which they received through Jesus Christ. The word "always" and the phrase "given you" are the parts of the verse to note here: "always" means at all times, and "given you" means that God has bestowed this grace on them.

Paul writes from Ephesus, according to most scholars, to a church with many problems: divisions, pride, and disorder. Even so, he begins with thanksgiving, not with rebuke. He looks first at what God has done for them, and later in the letter he corrects what is wrong.

Today we can imitate Paul: before criticizing someone in the church, the family, or the workplace, let us ask God to show us the grace already at work in that person, and give thanks for it. This softens the heart to speak the truth in love.
exp.14:36:
It says that when someone sows, they do not put the fully grown plant into the ground, but only a seed that is "bare," that is, a simple grain without its final form. It may be of wheat or of some other seed. "Perhaps" here means "for example." "Shall come up" means "that is going to sprout."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. He answers the one who asks how the dead are raised and with what body. He uses the seed as an example: what is buried is very different from what later comes up. Many understand that in this way he prepares the idea of a risen body that is different, yet with continuity.

For today: when you face losses or painful endings, remember that God can bring life from what you see only as a buried seed. Trust in his power and wait with hope.
exp.14:16:
It says that if Christ was not raised, believing in him is of no use. Where the verse comments on the word "vana," meaning empty, without value or result, rewrite it for "vain" from the verse: "vain" means empty, without value or result. The phrase about being still in sins means that they would remain under the guilt of sin, without true forgiveness. Rewrite that as: the phrase "ye are yet in your sins" means that they would remain under the guilt of sin, without true forgiveness.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. Some among them were saying that the dead do not rise. Paul shows them that denying this leads to denying the resurrection of Christ as well, and then the whole gospel falls apart. For him, the resurrection is the center of the faith, not a detail.

For today: our hope does not rest on feeling good or on being good people, but on a fact in which God acted. When you doubt or feel guilty, remember that Christ lives, and that in him there is real forgiveness and firm hope.
exp.13:21:
This verse says that tongues are a sign, but not for believers; they are for those who do not believe. Prophecy, that is, the word of God spoken to guide and encourage, is for believers. "Unbelievers" here means those who do not believe, and "believers" means those who do.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to correct the disorder in their gatherings. He quotes Isaiah, where God speaks to a people who will not listen. Scholars explain the "sign" in different ways: as a warning, or as a sign that this people was not listening. What is clear is that Paul wants everything in the church to be understood and to build people up.

For today: when you serve in the church, try to speak so that others can understand you and go away strengthened. Let your aim be to help others, not to draw attention to yourself.
exp.15:1:
Every Sunday, each believer was to set aside something at home from whatever money God allowed them to earn. "Set aside" means to keep it back, and "collections" are gatherings of offerings. In this way, when Paul arrived, they would not have to gather everything in a hurry.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He was organizing help for the poor Christians in Jerusalem, and he had already given the same instruction to the churches in Galatia. Many understand "the first day of the week" as the day when Christians met together, although the text gives no further detail. Paul wanted order, and he wanted the Corinthians themselves to choose the people who would carry the gift.

For today: give with planning, not by impulse. Decide in prayer on a regular portion of what God gives you, set it aside faithfully, and use it to help others.
exp.6:38:
A married woman is bound to her husband for as long as he lives. If her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, with one condition: that the marriage be "in the Lord." The words "bound by the law" mean that marriage is a commitment that holds as long as both are alive.

The apostle Paul speaks here, answering questions that the Christians in Corinth had sent him about marriage and singleness. Earlier, he had already taught that marriage is lasting. Here he clarifies the situation of widows. "In the Lord" is commonly understood to mean marrying a fellow believer, though some also interpret it as marrying with an attitude of obedience to God.

For today: if you are thinking about getting married, do not look only at affection; look for someone who loves God and with whom you can grow in faith. And pray before you decide.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that God knows very well what the people considered wise are thinking, and that those thoughts are "vain," that is, empty, without lasting value. "Again" shows that Paul is quoting Scripture once more, here Psalm 94:11.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were divided and boasted of following human leaders, such as Paul, Apollos, or Cephas. They valued eloquence and worldly wisdom greatly. Paul reminds them that before God this wisdom is not what matters most, and so he concludes: let no one boast in men.

Today we can examine what we take pride in: our studies, intelligence, opinions, or the leaders we admire. It is wise to learn with humility, to ask God for wisdom, and not to think ourselves superior to others or to use knowledge to divide.
exp.5:1:
Paul asks whether believers do not know that the saints, that is, those who belong to God, will take part in judging the world. If that is so, he says, how could they be unable to settle matters that are "very small," that is, ordinary disputes among themselves? Here "unworthy" means incapable or not fit.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some brothers and sisters were taking one another to court before judges who did not believe. He is ashamed of this and reminds them of their calling. How and when the saints will judge the world is understood in several ways, but Paul takes it as certain.

For today: when you have a conflict with another believer, first seek to resolve it with humility, through dialogue, and with the help of mature brothers and sisters in the church, before making it public or taking it to lawsuits.
exp.6:29:
It says that those who weep should live as though they did not weep, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, and those who buy as though they owned nothing. These are three examples of not fixing the heart on what passes away.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. Earlier he said that "the time is short," and then that "the form of this world is passing away." Many understand that he is speaking of the urgency of living for God, perhaps also because of the hardships of that time. He does not say that sorrows, joys, or possessions do not matter, but that they should not rule over us.

Today we can enjoy what is good and grieve what is sad, but without placing our hope in them. Ask yourself: what is holding me too tightly today? Surrender it to God in prayer.
exp.6:1:
It says that, because of sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. The word "but" is used to contrast this with the previous verse, and the phrase "because of" means "due to." The verse presents marriage as a good and protected place for sexual life.

Paul is answering a letter from the Corinthians. Some believed the most spiritual course was to avoid all sexual relationships, and he accepts that remaining unmarried can be good (v. 1). But Corinth was a city with a great deal of immorality, and Paul speaks with realism. He emphasizes that husband and wife belong to each other, with equal duties toward one another.

For today: care for your marriage with faithfulness, respect, and honest conversation. If you are married, seek to serve your spouse, not only to receive. If you are single, trust that God also gives you strength and wisdom to live in purity.
exp.15:20:
Paul says that this final greeting is in his own hand. The word "salutation" here means greeting. Up to this point, another person had probably written the letter while Paul dictated it, and now he takes up the pen and writes these words himself.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth from Ephesus. In his time it was common to dictate letters to a secretary. Paul would add a few lines in his own handwriting, perhaps to give authenticity and a personal touch. The text says nothing more here, so we cannot be certain of all his reasons. What follows are serious words of love for Christ and of grace.

For today: put a personal touch into how you care for others. A sincere message, a phone call, or a handwritten note can show that you truly care, and that your affection is not just a routine habit.
exp.9:10:
What happened to the Israelites in the wilderness took place as an example or warning. The word "figure" means an example or pattern, and "admonition" means a warning or teaching meant to correct us. Those stories were written for us, who live in the final age, when what God had been doing across the ages is brought to completion.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who felt secure yet tolerated idolatry and immorality. He reminds them that Israel was delivered by God and yet fell through disobedience, testing God, and grumbling. Some understand "the ends of the ages" as the era that began with Christ.

Today, do not read the Old Testament only as ancient history. Ask yourself what mistake of theirs you might repeat, such as complaining ungratefully or playing with temptation, and ask God for help to obey him.
exp.0:10:
Paul says that someone told him how the Corinthians are doing. "It has been reported to me" means "I have been informed." The people who told him are "those of Chloe," probably members of her household or her group. The news is that there are "quarrels" among them, that is, fights and arguments among themselves.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, whom he calls "my brothers." He has just asked them to live united and of one mind. Now he explains why he says this: it is not a guess, but something he was told. About Chloe we know only this name; it is not known for certain who she was or where she lived. The following verses show that they were splitting into factions according to their favorite leaders.

When we see divisions in the church or in the family, it is good to speak with humility and clarity, as Paul did, and without gossip. Let us make sure that Christ, and not our own preferences, is the center of the unity.
exp.11:17:
God himself, the verse says, placed each part of the body in its position, just as he chose. "Members" means the parts of the body, such as the eye, the ear, or the hand. The word "set" means put in place or arranged. Nothing is there by chance.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and people who felt more important than others. He uses the image of the human body to speak about the church, which is the body of Christ. He wants to show that each believer has a place and a function given by God, and that variety is part of his plan.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or feel worthless because your service is little seen. If God put you where you are, your part matters. Ask him how to serve with what he has given you, and value others as well.
exp.5:9:
This verse continues a list of unjust behaviors. It says that those who live in theft, greed, drunkenness, insults, or cheating will not inherit the kingdom of God. "Revilers" are those who speak with insults and slander. "Thieves" are those who steal by force or take advantage of others. "Covetous" people are those who always want more, without caring about the harm done to others.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, who had lawsuits and cheated one another among brothers and sisters. He warns them that a life of injustice contradicts the kingdom of God. But right away he reminds them that some of them had been like that, and that they had already been washed, made holy, and made righteous in Jesus. He does not speak to condemn without hope, but to call them to change.

Today we can examine our words, our money, and how we treat others. If there is something unjust in us, let us ask forgiveness, make right the harm done, and trust that Christ gives the power to change.
exp.9:14:
He says that Paul speaks to the Corinthians as to people with good judgment. He wants them to be seen as sensible and discerning. He asks them not to accept his words without thinking, but to examine what he says and judge for themselves whether it is true. The word "judge" means to weigh carefully and consider with attention.

Paul, the apostle, writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of pagan temples. He has just warned them to flee from idolatry. Now he is going to give them an argument about the Lord's Supper and its fellowship with Christ. That is why he appeals to their reasoning before explaining why they cannot mix the Lord's table with pagan rites.

Today, God invites us to think, not only to obey. Compare what you hear with the Bible, calmly and in prayer, and your faith will be firm and reasoned.
exp.7:0:
Paul says that, concerning meat offered to idols, believers have a certain knowledge. But he warns that knowledge puffs up, that is, fills a person with pride, while love builds up others, that is, strengthens and constructs them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city where a great deal of meat was sold after it had been used in pagan temples. Some believers felt superior because they knew that idols are nothing, and did not think about fellow believers with a more fragile conscience. Paul responds to questions the church had put to him.

For today: before you show what you know in a debate or on social media, ask yourself whether your words help others grow or only make you look good. Use what you know to serve with humility and to care for someone who is still learning.
exp.0:16:
Paul says that Christ did not send him primarily to baptize, but to proclaim the gospel. And he does so without "wisdom of words," that is, without eloquent speeches meant to impress. The phrase "lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect" is rendered in the verse as "lest the cross of Christ should lose its power," and the cross of Christ is what would lose its power if the message were presented with clever rhetoric.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided into groups that followed different leaders. He is glad that he baptized only a few people, so that no one would think he baptized to form his own group. He does not belittle baptism; he only makes clear that his central mission was to preach the message of the cross, which the world sees as foolishness.

For today: when you share your faith, do not seek to show off or win admiration. Speak simply and sincerely about what Christ has done for us, and trust that God gives power to that message.
exp.6:34:
Paul says that what he has explained he says for their own good. He does not want to put a trap on them or a burden on them. What he seeks is what is "honest and decent," that is, orderly and worthy, so that they can draw near to the Lord without hindrance or distraction.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and remaining single. He had said that, because of the difficulties of that time, being single allowed a person to devote more of themselves to the Lord. Even so, he makes it clear that he is not imposing a rule: marrying or not is a free decision, and both are good.

For today: whatever our situation, let us ask ourselves which things distract us from God and how we can serve him with more attention and without anxiety.
exp.6:36:
This verse says that the father who has firmly decided, without pressure and with full freedom, to keep his daughter unmarried, does well. "Pressure or urgency" is the sense of the word the verse renders as "necessity," and keeping his daughter unmarried is what "keep his virgin" means. Some scholars believe the passage speaks of a man and his fiancée rather than a father; the text allows both readings.

Paul is answering the Corinthians about marriage and the single life. He advises them with their good in mind, not to lay a burden on them, but so that they may serve the Lord without distraction. He recognizes that marrying is not sin and that each person must decide with freedom.

Today we can make important decisions, such as marrying or remaining single, with calm, prayer and personal conviction, without yielding to family or social pressure, and always seeking to serve the Lord better.
exp.14:24:
It says that Christ must reign until all his enemies are placed under his feet. The phrase "must" is a stand-in for what is necessary or required. Placing enemies under the feet was an image of complete victory.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection of the dead. He lays out the order of events: Christ was raised first, then those who belong to him will be raised, and at the end Christ will hand the kingdom over to the Father. Paul uses words from Psalm 110:1 to show that Christ's victory is certain, and that the last enemy to be defeated will be death.

For today: when evil or fear seem stronger, remember that Christ reigns and his final victory is assured. You can live with hope and keep doing good without losing heart.
exp.10:27:
Before taking part in the Lord's Supper, the verse says, each person should examine themselves honestly. "Examine" means to test oneself or look carefully at one's own heart. After that self-examination, the person may eat the bread and drink from the cup.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided. When they gathered for the meal, some looked down on the poorer members and behaved without respect for what that moment represents. Paul reminds them that the Supper proclaims the death of Christ. For that reason he calls them to take part with seriousness, not with carelessness or selfishness.

Before communion, take a moment to pray. Ask forgiveness if you have wronged someone, seek reconciliation, and take part with gratitude, remembering what Christ did for you.
exp.10:0:
Paul invites the believers in Corinth to follow his example, but with a clear condition: he himself follows Christ. Paul's words here mean "be followers," that is, copy his way of living. Christ is the final model.

Paul writes to a church with many problems of division and pride. Just before, in chapter 10, he taught them not to seek their own advantage but the advantage of many, so that they may be saved. Some scholars see this verse as the close of that teaching, and others as the beginning of what follows. There is debate about where the chapter should have begun.

For today: think about who imitates you, such as your children, companions, or brothers and sisters in the church. Try to live in such a way that, by following you, they come closer to Christ. And follow those who truly follow Jesus.
exp.0:29:
This verse says that believers belong to God by being united with Christ Jesus. God himself made Christ to be wisdom for us, righteousness (being declared right before God), sanctification (being set apart for God and transformed), and redemption (being rescued, like someone who pays a ransom).

Paul writes to a church in Corinth that was divided and boasted in human wisdom and in favorite leaders. He reminds them that God chose humble people, so that no one may boast. Everything they have comes from Christ, not from themselves.

For today: when you feel proud of your achievements, or small because of your failures, remember that your worth before God does not depend on you but on Christ. Thank him today for what he has already done for you.
exp.14:3:
This verse says that Jesus was placed in a tomb and that God raised him from the dead on the third day. The reference to the words "that he was buried" and "that he rose again" describes these two events directly, so no word needs special comment here. The phrase "according to the scriptures" means that this agreed with what the sacred texts of the Old Testament had already announced.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. For that reason he reminds them of the essentials of the gospel that he himself received and taught them: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again. He then mentions witnesses who saw him alive, many of whom were still living at that time.

For today: our hope does not rest on an idea, but on a fact. If Christ rose again, we can face pain, failure, and even death with confidence. Today, thank God for that victory and place your fears back in his hands.
exp.6:2:
This verse says that the husband should give his wife what is due to her in marriage, and that the wife should do the same for her husband. "Benevolence" here means the affection and intimacy that belong to marriage. "Due" means that it is something owed, that is, a duty of love.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. In a city with much sexual immorality, he makes clear that marriage is good. What stands out is that he treats both spouses equally: the duty is mutual, not only from one toward the other.

For today: instead of demanding, seek to serve each other with tenderness and respect. Speak honestly about your needs, and care for the other as you would care for yourself.
exp.4:10:
Paul clarifies what he meant in his earlier letter. He is not asking them to pull away from every sinner in the world, but from someone who calls himself a "brother" in the faith and lives in serious sin without repentance. "Keep company" means not mixing or associating with that person. A "fornicator" is someone who lives in sexual immorality; a "covetous" person is one who is greedy; a "railer" is someone who insults or slanders. "No, not even to eat" means not sharing a meal with him.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a man living openly in immorality. He wants the church to guard its purity and correct its own members. God judges those outside. Many understand that the purpose of this discipline was that the person would be moved to change and be restored.

For today: if a brother lives in sin and refuses to change, love him enough to speak to him with humility and truth, praying for his restoration, and without treating with contempt those who do not believe.
exp.10:24:
It says that Jesus, after supper, took the cup and explained that this cup represents the new covenant, that is, a new agreement between God and his people, sealed with his blood. He asked that this act be repeated in his memory. Old words: "drink" is the word for what the verse calls "drink it."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the Lord's Supper was being celebrated with disorder and selfishness. He reminds them of what he himself received and taught: what Jesus did the night he was betrayed. Christians understand in different ways how Christ is present in the Supper, but all agree that it remembers his sacrifice.

For today: when you take part in the Supper, do so with calm and gratitude, remembering that Christ gave his life for you. Beforehand, examine your heart and seek to be reconciled with anyone you have an unresolved offense against.
exp.9:19:
Paul says that when pagans offer sacrifices to their idols, they are actually offering them to demons and not to God. For this reason he does not want believers to have fellowship, that is, to join together or share in common, with demons.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, surrounded by pagan temples and festivals. Some believers were attending banquets held in idol temples. Paul had already said that an idol is nothing in itself, but he warns that behind this worship stand spiritual realities opposed to God. He compares this with Israel, where eating from the sacrifice joined the person to the altar.

For today: examine which practices or environments lead you to divide your loyalty. If something pulls you away from Christ, even if it seems harmless, be honest and choose to remain faithful to Him.
exp.0:23:
He says that for those whom God has called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Pausing on the word "but" here is no obstacle; the verse reads "But unto them which are called." What others see as weakness or foolishness, those who are called recognize as the greatest work of God.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and took pride in human wisdom. The Jews asked for miracles and the Greeks sought philosophy, so a crucified Messiah seemed to them scandalous or absurd. Paul reminds them that God's calling changes the way we see the cross.

For today: you do not need to impress anyone with your intelligence or your strength. Trust that Christ is sufficient, and in your decisions and problems, seek first his wisdom and his power, even when the world sees him as small.
exp.8:23:
This verse says that in a race in the stadium all the runners take part, but only one wins the prize. So Paul urges us to run with such effort and discipline that the goal is reached. Some older words need a note: the phrase meaning "in truth" is the same as "in reality," the word for "know" is "know," and the word for "run" is the same as "run."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, a city where athletic games were well known. He had been explaining that he adapted himself to different people in order to bring them the gospel. He uses the image of the race to show that his life of service has a clear purpose and calls for total commitment.

For today: the Christian life is not meant to be improvised or lived halfway. Think of one area, such as prayer, Bible reading, or serving others, and decide on one concrete habit for this week. Practice it with steady consistency, trusting in the grace of God.
exp.0:21:
This verse says that the Jews asked for signs, that is, miracles or visible proofs from God, and that the Greeks looked for wisdom, meaning reasoning and philosophy that would convince them. Each group wanted God on its own terms.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and took pride in its human wisdom. He reminds them that the message of Christ crucified did not fit what either Jews or Greeks expected. To some it was a stumbling block, to others foolishness, but to those called by God it is power and wisdom. The exact details of each kind of seeking are understood in several ways, but the central idea is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we demand from God proofs or explanations made to our own measure. Let us instead trust in Christ, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.14:20:
This verse says that death came into the world through one man, and that the resurrection of the dead also comes through one man. The phrase "since" in the verse expresses the same reasoning as the original. The first man is Adam, and the second is Christ, as the following verses explain.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, where some were saying that there was no resurrection of the dead. Paul answers them that if Christ was not raised, faith is empty. Here he shows that Christ's resurrection is the beginning and the guarantee of the resurrection of those who believe in him.

For today: if you face the loss of a loved one or the fear of death, remember that death does not have the final word. You can rest in the hope that Christ, who overcame death, will also give life to his own.
exp.6:39:
Paul says that a widow will be "happier", that is, more blessed, if she decides not to marry again. He makes clear that this is his "advice", not a command. "Yet" in this place means "but". He adds that he believes he also has the Spirit of God, so that his opinion is taken seriously.

Paul is answering questions the Corinthians had asked him about marriage and singleness. He has just said that a widow is free to marry another believer. Now he gives his view: because of the difficulties of that time, and because a single person can serve the Lord with fewer distractions, he judges it better for her to remain alone. Some scholars debate how to understand the "distress" he mentions earlier in the chapter.

When you make decisions about your marital status, seek God's guidance and that of wise people, without pressure or comparisons. Both marrying and remaining single can be a good path, if it is lived for the Lord.
exp.14:46:
The first man is Adam, made from the dust, which is why he is "earthy", that is, of the earth. "The second man" is Christ, whom Paul calls "the Lord", and his origin is "from heaven". There is a difference between what we inherit from Adam and what we receive in Christ.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. He explains that the raised body will be different from the present one, because just as we have been like Adam, we will be like Christ. The contrast between the two was shown in the phrases "living being" and "life-giving spirit": Adam received life, but Christ gives life.

For today: although we live in fragile bodies, our hope does not end in the earth. You can face tiredness, sickness, or loss with confidence, because Christ will bring us into his heavenly likeness.
exp.14:6:
It says that the risen Jesus was seen by James, and then by all the apostles. The word "seen" here means he truly let himself be seen. Here "James" is probably the brother of the Lord, the leader of the church in Jerusalem, though the text does not make this clear. The phrase "all the apostles" seems to refer to a wider group than the twelve, but it is not known exactly who they were.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection of the dead. For that reason he presents a list of witnesses who saw Christ alive. Many of them were still living, so anyone could ask them. Paul places himself at the end of the list, as the last witness.

For today: our faith does not rest on a vague idea, but on the testimony of real people. We can believe with confidence and share what Christ has done in us, with humility and simplicity.
exp.11:25:
It says that in the church we are all as closely joined as the parts of a body. If one part suffers, all of them feel that pain together. If one part is honored, meaning recognized or praised, all of them rejoice together.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and rivalry over spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the body to show that every believer is necessary, and that God gave greater honor to those who seemed less important, so that there would be no division and everyone would care for one another.

Today we can practice this with a simple step: go to a brother or sister who is suffering and support them with prayer and your presence. And when someone in the church receives an achievement or a blessing, celebrate it wholeheartedly, without envy.
exp.9:8:
He says we should not put Christ to the test, that is, not abuse his patience or doubt his care, as some Israelites did in the desert. Here "test" means to try or to challenge, and the words "destroyed" means that they died. They died from the serpents.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who lived surrounded by many temptations and felt secure in themselves. He reminds them of what happened to Israel after leaving Egypt (Numbers 21), when the people spoke against God and against Moses. Paul sees in Christ the God who accompanied his people, and he uses that story as a warning.

For today: do not live putting God to the test with your disobedience, thinking that his forgiveness permits everything. Give thanks for his mercy and trust in him with humility.
exp.11:29:
Paul asks three rhetorical questions, and the expected answer to each is "no." Not everyone in the church has gifts of healing, not everyone speaks in tongues (other languages or spiritual speech), and not everyone interprets what is said in tongues. "Teachers" are those who instruct, and "works of power" probably refers to miracles.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over the most showy gifts. He reminds them that the church is a body with many members, and that God distributes gifts as he wishes. For that reason, no one should feel superior or inferior. Then he leads them to "the more excellent way": love, from chapter 13.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or envy their gifts. Discover how God has equipped you to serve, use it with humility, and always accompany it with love.
exp.5:7:
Paul says that instead of putting up with an offense, the Corinthians themselves are going around doing harm and taking what does not belong to them, and the worst part is that they do it to their own brothers and sisters in the faith.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided. Some believers were taking one another to court before judges who did not know God. Paul is saddened because this damages the church's witness. So he reminds them that they themselves are causing the very harm they should be willing to suffer.

For today: before you get into a fight with another believer, stop and pray. Seek first to speak with humility and to be reconciled, even if it costs you something. Caring for the unity and the witness of Christ is worth more than winning an argument.
exp.3:8:
He says that God has placed the apostles at the end of the line, like people condemned to death. "I think" means "as it seems to me." "Last" means the very last ones. "Spectacle" is something everyone looks at, as in a theater. The apostles are seen by the world, by the angels, and by people.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who felt proud, rich, and superior. With some irony, he shows them that his life as an apostle is very different: he suffers, he is despised, and he lives in humility. He probably alludes to Roman parades, where condemned prisoners walked at the end, although this is a common interpretation, not something the text states.

Today, let us not measure the value of a Christian life by success, applause, or comfort. Serving Christ can cost, and humility matters more than fame.
exp.12:0:
Here the verse says that even if someone speaks the languages of men and even those of angels, without love they only make noise. The word "charity" here means love; in the original it is the love that gives without expecting anything in return. The "sounding brass" is a bronze that rings loudly, and the "tinkling cymbal" is a cymbal that makes only an empty clink. "Am become" means "become."

The apostle Paul is speaking, writing to the church in Corinth. That community highly valued spiritual gifts, such as speaking in tongues, but there were divisions and pride. Paul reminds them that gifts without love lose their worth. Some think "tongues of angels" is an exaggerated way of speaking; others take it to refer to a spiritual language. This cannot be stated with certainty.

Before seeking to stand out for what you know or do in the church, ask yourself whether you are doing it with love. Today, treat someone with patience and kindness, even if no one notices.
exp.7:12:
It says that Paul is willing to stop eating meat forever if doing so would cause another believer to stumble. "Causing to fall" means something leads them to fail in their faith or in their conscience. To "offend" does not mean spreading gossip, but being a stumbling block. The "weak" person is the believer whose conscience is weak, who does not yet have clarity.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. There, people debated whether it was right to eat meat that had been offered to idols, which was then sold in the marketplace. Paul acknowledges that idols are nothing, but some newly converted brothers and sisters still felt that eating it was worshiping idols. He asks that knowledge be used with love, not with pride.

Today: before using your freedom in something doubtful, ask yourself whether it could cause someone close to you to stumble. Sometimes love means giving up a right for the good of another.
exp.14:22:
The verse says that the resurrection happens in an order, like a line. First comes Christ, whom Paul calls "the firstfruits," meaning the first part of the harvest, which shows that the rest will follow. Then those who belong to Christ rise, the ones who are his through faith, and this will happen "at his coming," when Jesus returns.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, where some denied that the dead would be raised. He reminds them that just as death came through Adam, life comes through Christ. His resurrection is the guarantee of ours. The verses that follow speak of the end, when Christ will hand over the kingdom to the Father; Christians explain the details of that time in different ways.

For today: if Christ has already risen, death does not have the final word. That hope can bring comfort in grief and strength to live faithfully today.
exp.14:54:
Here Paul asks a question as if mocking death. The "sting" is the venomous jab, like that of a scorpion or a wasp. The "grave" is the tomb, and the question is: where has its power and its triumph gone? "Swallowed up" means completely consumed.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who doubted the resurrection. After explaining that Christ rose and that believers will also be transformed, he uses words that echo the prophet Hosea (13:14) and Isaiah (25:8). The verses that follow say that the sting of death is sin, and that God gives us the victory through Jesus Christ.

For today: when the fear of death or the grief over a loved one weighs on you, remember that for the one who trusts in Christ, death does not have the last word. You can weep with hope.
exp.13:35:
Paul asks the Corinthians two pointed questions. He asks whether the word of God started with them, or whether it came only to them. The word "What?" here works like "Did it really...?" and expects the answer no.

Paul is writing to a church whose gatherings were very disorderly. With these questions he reminds them that they are not the center, nor the only authority, of Christian life. There are other churches, and all of them should follow the same order. The verses before this one about women are much debated: some read them as a general rule, others as instruction for a specific problem in Corinth. There is no single agreed view.

For today: before we assume that our own way of doing things is the only right way, let us be humble and listen to the Bible and to the church of every age.
exp.9:4:
It says that although all the Israelites received the same blessings from God in the wilderness, God was not pleased with most of them. The verse says they were overthrown in the wilderness, meaning they fell and died there.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, a city full of immorality and idolatry. He reminds them of what happened to Israel after leaving Egypt (Numbers 14). They had received the manna, the water from the rock, and God's guidance, yet they still rebelled. Paul uses this as a warning so the Corinthians would not become complacent simply because they had received blessings.

For today: having received God's blessings, or being part of a church life, does not replace sincere obedience. Today you can ask yourself with humility: "Am I trusting God, or just enjoying what He gives me?"
exp.3:18:
Paul says he will come to visit the Corinthians soon, if the Lord allows it. When he arrives, he will not be concerned with what those who are puffed up with pride say in words. He wants to find out whether they have real power, meaning the actual working of God in their lives.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided. Some, full of pride, criticized Paul and thought he would not come back. That is why he sent Timothy to remind them of how he taught. The verses that follow say that the kingdom of God is not a matter of words, but of power.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed only by someone who speaks beautifully. Look at whether a person's life, including your own, shows humility, love, and true fruit.
exp.4:7:
It says that the Christian life is like a continuous celebration, but not with "old leaven," which here represents sin, malice (ill intent), and wickedness. We should celebrate it with unleavened bread, that is, bread without yeast, which symbolizes sincerity (a heart without duplicity) and truth. The celebration refers to living thankful for what Christ has done.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which tolerated a serious case of immorality and even boasted about it. He uses the image of the Jewish Passover, when all yeast was removed from the house. Since Christ is our Passover, sacrificed for us, Paul calls them to clear out what harms the whole community.

Today, we can ask ourselves: is there some hidden sin or false attitude that I am letting grow? Ask God for help to live with honesty, to recognize it and to change, grateful for the forgiveness of Christ.
exp.14:32:
Paul says not to be deceived: the "bad company" he has in mind is harmful companionship or conversation, and "good manners" means upright conduct and a healthy character. In other words, bad influences can ruin a life that was going well.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and defending the resurrection. Some among them were saying there is no resurrection, and Paul sees that this belief leads people to live without restraint. The verse appears to be a familiar saying that Paul quotes, and he uses it as a warning. Then he calls them to wake up and stop sinning.

Today, think about whom you spend the most time with, what you listen to, and what you see every day. Seek out friendships and conversations that strengthen your faith, and set kind but firm limits on whatever pulls you away from God.
exp.15:5:
Paul tells the Corinthians that he may stay with them for a while, even spending the winter there. In this way they could help him continue his journey, bringing him on to his next destination. The word "winter" here means spending the winter season, and the word "bring" means to accompany him or help him with what he needs for the road.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus, and he is planning his trip. First he will pass through Macedonia, and then he will come to Corinth. He does not want to make just a quick visit, but to stay a good while, if the Lord permits. Even so, he leaves his plans in God's hands.

For today: make your plans with good sense, but with humility. Place your projects before the Lord and keep your heart open to Him adjusting them. We can also support generously those who serve God on their way.
exp.4:6:
It says that believers must remove from their lives and from their church whatever contaminates them, called here "the old leaven." Leaven makes the dough rise; here it represents sin that spreads. "New dough" is a renewed people. "You are unleavened" means that, in Christ, they are already declared clean. "Passover" is the lamb sacrificed at the Jewish feast; Paul says that Christ is that Lamb. "Was sacrificed" is the sacrifice itself.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whom he corrects because they were proudly tolerating a serious case of immorality in the church. He uses the image of the Passover, when the Israelites removed leaven from their homes. His point is that tolerated sin can affect the whole community.

For today: if Christ gave his life for us, we must not treat sin lightly. Ask God to show you some habit or attitude you should leave behind, and do so with humility and gratitude.
exp.15:14:
Paul makes a request of the brothers in Corinth. He reminds them that the household of Stephanas was among the first to believe in Christ in Achaia (the region of Greece where Corinth was located). The word "firstfruits" refers to the first part of the harvest. He also says that they have devoted themselves completely to serving the believers, whom he calls "saints," that is, the people of God.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus to correct and encourage a church with divisions. The appeal in this verse is completed in the next one: that the readers respect and follow the example of those who serve with diligence. Paul does not say that Stephanas held an official office; he emphasizes his voluntary devotion.

For today: notice the people in your church who serve quietly, and thank them. Better still, be willing to serve alongside them.
exp.13:13:
Paul says that if someone prays in a tongue that no one understands, their spirit prays, but their mind is left without benefit. "Unknown tongue" is a language that nobody understands without interpretation. "Unfruitful" means it produces no benefit, neither for the one who prays nor for those who listen.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued very highly speaking in tongues during the gatherings. He corrects them with affection: the gifts must serve to build up everyone. For this reason he asks that whoever speaks in a tongue also ask for the gift of interpreting it. Some understand that he is speaking of private prayer, others of public worship.

For today: when you pray or sing, try to keep your heart and your mind present. In church, look for what is said to help everyone understand and to say "Amen."
exp.13:33:
It says that women should keep silent in the church meetings, because they are not permitted to speak, but should be under obedience, as the law also says. "Congregations" are the gatherings of believers. "Under obedience" means that they place themselves under order or authority.

Paul writes to a church in Corinth that had a great deal of disorder in its worship. The whole chapter is about putting the gifts and prophecies in order so that there may be peace. It is not clear which "law" he means; some think of the Old Testament, others of custom. Christians understand it in different ways: as a general rule, or as an instruction for a specific problem, such as the questions that interrupted the meeting. Paul himself allows women to pray and prophesy in 1 Corinthians 11:5.
