For today: let us seek to make our meetings orderly and peaceful, and let us study this passage with humility, comparing it with the rest of the Bible.
exp.13:25:
Paul asks what a church meeting should be like. When the brothers and sisters come together, each one may bring something: a psalm (a song), a teaching, a message in a tongue, a revelation, or the interpretation of a tongue. "You" here refers to all of you. What matters is that everything be done for edification, that is, to strengthen and help grow the faith of everyone.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, whose meetings were disorderly. Many wanted to show off their spiritual gifts and did not think about the others. That is why, before and after this verse, Paul speaks about visitors being able to understand and about bringing order to the use of tongues.

For today: before you take part in your church, whether by singing, teaching, or praying, ask yourself: "Will this help others grow in faith?" Use your gifts to serve, not to stand out.
exp.2:5:
Paul says that he "planted" the seed of the gospel in Corinth, and that Apollos "watered" it, meaning he continued caring for and teaching the believers. But it is God who actually makes the plant grow. "Gave the increase" means that God is and continues to be the one who gives life and fruit.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided. Some said "I am of Paul" and others "I am of Apollos." Paul calls them "fleshly" because they fought over human leaders. He reminds them that he and Apollos are only "ministers," that is, servants, through whom they came to believe, each with the task the Lord gave him.

For today: serve faithfully in what God has entrusted to you, without comparing yourself or boasting. And if you see fruit in others, do not fight over who deserves the credit. Thank God, because it is He who makes things grow.
exp.14:7:
This verse says that the risen Christ appeared to Paul last of all, after the other witnesses. Paul describes himself as one born out of due time, meaning someone who came along unexpectedly and at an unusual moment. The phrase "he was seen of me" means that Jesus showed himself to Paul personally.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to argue that Christ truly rose from the dead. He lists the witnesses: Peter, the twelve, more than five hundred people, James, and all the apostles. He includes himself at the end. Scholars debate why he uses such a harsh description of himself. Perhaps his critics used it against him, or perhaps he is speaking of his unworthiness because he had persecuted the church. It is not certain.

God can reach and use anyone, regardless of their past. If you feel unworthy or late, remember that Paul credited everything to God's grace. Acknowledge your failings with humility, but rest in the knowledge that grace sustains you and enables you to serve.
exp.6:27:
Saying that marriage is not a sin, for either a man or an unmarried woman, is the point of this verse. Paul makes clear, however, that those who marry will face "trouble in the flesh," meaning the difficulties and pressures that come with everyday life. A "virgin" is an unmarried young woman, and "such" refers to those who marry. At the end, Paul says "but I spare you," meaning that he wishes to spare them those hardships.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage. He speaks of a "present distress," probably a time of pressure or suffering, and reminds them that "the time is short." He does not condemn marriage; he offers pastoral advice with real care. Some interpreters debate exactly which crisis he had in mind.

For today: if you are married or are thinking about marriage, do not see it as a sin or as the solution to everything. Prepare for its difficulties, and put God first.
exp.9:24:
It says that believers may eat any meat sold in the market, without asking questions out of scruples of conscience. The word "shambles" means the meat market. The idea is not to complicate matters by investigating where the meat came from.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where much of the meat sold in the market came from sacrifices made in pagan temples. The believers were debating whether eating it was a sin. Paul answers that the earth and everything in it belongs to the Lord (Psalm 24:1), so the food itself is not defiled. But in the nearby context he also asks them to care for the weaker brother and to seek the good of others.

For today: do not make a heavy burden out of what is secondary. Enjoy with gratitude what God gives, but exercise your freedom in love, thinking about how your decisions affect the faith and conscience of those around you.
exp.1:2:
Paul recalls how he arrived in Corinth: he felt weak, very afraid, and trembling. "Weakness" means lack of strength, and "fear and trembling" describes deep anxiety, not an attitude of confidence or pride.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some admired eloquent speakers and human wisdom. He reminds them that he did not come with brilliant speeches, but proclaiming Christ crucified. The texts do not say exactly why he felt that fear, so it is not wise to invent a cause. What is clear is that his weakness left room for God's power to work.

Today, you do not need to feel strong or speak perfectly to serve God. If you feel weak or afraid when sharing your faith, trust that God can work even through your frailty.
exp.10:13:
Paul asks whether nature itself does not teach you that it is a shame for a man to have long hair. The word "shame" here does not mean lying or deceit, but something unbecoming or disgraceful. Letting hair grow long is what the verse describes.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, whose gatherings had become disorderly. He is speaking about how men and women should present themselves when praying and prophesying. He appeals to what they considered proper in their culture. Scholars debate exactly what "nature" means here: some think of the created order, others of social custom. There is also discussion about what long hair meant in that period.

For today: take care that the way you present yourself at church reflects respect for God and love for others, without making customs a cause for quarrel. What matters most is reverence and peace.
exp.0:26:
It says that God chose what the world considers foolish and weak in order to put to shame those who think they are wise and strong. The word "foolish" is used here for something that lacks sense or understanding, and "weak" means without strength; "to put to shame" means to expose human pride.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a divided community that boasted of its wisdom and importance. He reminds them that, when they look at who they themselves were, few were powerful or noble. His message is that the cross seems like madness to the world, yet God uses it to save. In this way, no one can boast before Him.

Today we can remember that our worth does not depend on titles, money, or success. If God calls you, do not become discouraged because you feel insignificant; let Him work through your weakness, and give Him the credit.
exp.14:0:
Paul tells the brothers in Corinth that he wants to remind them of the gospel, that is, the good news about Jesus, which he had already proclaimed to them. The phrase "I declare" in the verse means here what Paul is making known to them, that is, what he is reminding them of. They had received this message, and they remained firm in it, meaning they held steadfastly to that faith.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in a letter to the church in Corinth. Earlier he has addressed several problems in the community, such as divisions and disorder. Now he begins to speak about the resurrection, a subject on which some had doubts. So he returns to the basics: the central message they themselves had believed.

For today: even when we have many debates and worries, it is good to return often to the center of our faith, which is Christ, his death, and his resurrection. Read this slowly this week and thank God for that message.
exp.0:8:
God is faithful, that is, he does what he promises. He himself called us into fellowship with his Son, which means sharing a life of union and friendship with Jesus Christ, our Lord. The word "ye were called" in the verse above refers to those who were called by God, and the phrase "our Lord" points to Jesus Christ as the one we belong to.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He thanks them for the gifts they have received and reminds them that God will keep them strong until the end. But he will soon call their attention to their divisions and quarrels. First, he reminds them that all of them were called to the same thing: to be united with Christ.

For today: when there are tensions in your church or family, remember that God called you together with others to live in Christ. Trust that he is faithful, and seek unity with humility and patience.
exp.5:17:
It says we should flee from fornication, that is, from any sexual relationship outside of marriage. It does not say "avoid it" but rather run far away from it. It states that other sins are committed "outside the body," but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body. Interpreters explain that phrase in several ways, but they all agree that this offense touches the person in a very intimate way.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who lived in a city with a great deal of immorality. He reminds them that their body belongs to the Lord and is united to Him. Therefore they must not join themselves to what dishonors Christ. The next verse says that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.

For today: when temptation comes, don't test your strength; get away quickly. End the conversation, turn off the screen, or change where you are, remembering that your body belongs to God.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that no one should deceive himself. If someone in the church thinks they are wise by the standards of this age (that is, this present time or this world), they should become humble and free of pride, so that they can truly become wise.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided by rivalries and by admiration for certain teachers. He has just told them that they are God's temple, and that dividing the community harms it. For this reason he warns them against intellectual pride. The verses that follow explain that human wisdom, apart from God, is foolishness before Him.

For today: before arguing or boasting about what I know, I can ask God for humility, listen patiently to others, and recognize that I need to learn from Him.
exp.0:27:
It says that God chose what the world considers base, that is, of little value or low standing, and what the world despises. He also chose what is not, meaning what the world regards as counting for nothing at all. With this, God brings to nothing what the world believes is important.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community divided and proud of its wisdom and its favorite leaders. He asks them to look at who they were when God called them: few wise, powerful, or of noble birth. In this way he shows them that salvation comes from God and not from human merit, so that no one may boast before him.

For today: if you feel like nobody special, remember that God does not look at you for your status or your achievements. Serve with humility and, if anything good comes out of your life, give God the glory.
exp.5:19:
You were bought with a price, so honor God with your body and with your spirit, because both belong to him. The wording "bought" means "were bought," and "glorify" means "honor" or "give glory to." The King James Version includes the phrase "and in your spirit," but that phrase appears in some manuscripts and not in all of them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city known for much sexual immorality. He reminds them that their body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and that they no longer belong to themselves. The "price" refers to what Christ gave for them; Paul does not spell out the payment here, but in other passages he connects it with Christ's blood and his cross.

For today: before you make a decision about what you see, say, eat, or do with your body, ask yourself whether it honors God, who loved you and made you his own.
exp.2:11:
Paul says that someone can build on the foundation, which is Jesus Christ, using very different materials. Some are valuable and durable: gold, silver, and precious stones. Others are fragile and burn easily: wood, hay (dry grass), and stubble (straw or dry remains).

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided by rivalries between its leaders. He had founded the community, and other teachers continued teaching afterward. He reminds them that everyone works for God and that each person will answer for how they build. Christians have understood the fire and the reward in various ways, but all agree that God will evaluate the work.

For today: before you serve, teach, or counsel others, ask yourself whether you are doing it with truth, love, and humility, or out of pride and appearance. Build with what lasts.
exp.15:17:
Paul says that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus "refreshed" his spirit and that of the Corinthians, meaning they encouraged him, revived him, and gave him rest. For this reason he asks that such people be acknowledged, that is, that people like them be publicly valued and honored.

Paul writes from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, at the close of his letter. These three men visited him and made up, by their presence, what the Corinthians could not give him while they were far away. They probably carried the church's questions to Paul, though the letter does not state this with complete clarity.

Today we can notice those who serve without drawing attention and thank them. This week, tell someone in your church, in specific words, how their service has encouraged you.
exp.9:28:
Paul makes clear that when he speaks of "conscience," he means the conscience of the other person, not of the one who is eating. If someone warns you that this meat was offered to an idol, you must take care of that person's conscience. Then Paul asks: "why is my liberty judged by another man's conscience?" This sentence is difficult: some believe it is an objection from Paul himself, and others think it is the words of an opponent. It can be understood in several ways.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city where meat was sold after pagan sacrifices. There was division over whether eating it was sin. Paul defends liberty, but limits it with love.

For today: before using your freedom in something debatable, think about who is watching you and how it will affect them. Yielding out of love for a brother also glorifies God.
exp.2:9:
Paul says that, by the grace God gave him, he acted as a "wise masterbuilder," that is, a skilled and expert builder. He laid the foundation, and another builds on top of it. "Sobreedificar," meaning to keep building upon that foundation, is what the others do. And he warns: each one must take heed how he builds.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, which was divided by following different leaders. He founded that church by preaching Christ, and others, such as Apollos, continued the work. Here he reminds them that the workers serve God and should not become a cause of rivalry. The following verse makes clear that the foundation is Jesus Christ.

For today: if you teach, serve, or help others in the faith, take care that your work rests on Christ and is done with honesty and diligence. Ask yourself humbly: "Am I building with what truly lasts?"
exp.5:10:
Paul reminds the believers in Corinth that some of them used to live in those sins. But something changed: they were washed (cleansed from their guilt), sanctified (set apart for God), and justified (declared righteous before Him). All of this happened through Jesus and through the Spirit of God.

Paul writes to a church with many problems of conduct and division. He has just said that those who practice wrongdoing will not inherit the kingdom of God. Now he reminds them that their past no longer defines them, and that their new life must show in how they live, especially in how they use their bodies.

For today: if your past shames you, remember that in Christ God has cleansed you and given you a new identity. Live from that grace, not from your old story, and ask the Spirit to help you walk in it.
exp.7:4:
Paul says that although many people call various things "gods," whether in heaven or on earth, and although there are many "gods" and "lords" according to people's beliefs, that does not change the truth. Food is what is eaten, and "knowledge" means understanding.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city full of temples. They were asking whether they could eat meat that had been offered to idols. Paul recognizes that idols are nothing compared to the one God, but then he asks for care toward brothers and sisters with a weak conscience. Some understand "gods" as false spiritual powers; the text does not fully explain this.

Today there are many things that people worship: money, fame, pleasure. We can live without fear of them because only God is God, but also with love and respect for those who are still struggling in their faith.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that the rulers of that time did not understand God's hidden wisdom. If they had understood it, they would not have crucified Jesus, whom it calls "the Lord of glory," that is, the glorious Lord. The word "world" in the verse refers to the present age, and "princes" means the rulers or authorities.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some took pride in human wisdom. He reminds them that God's plan, centered on the cross, seemed foolishness to the world. Interpreters debate whether "princes" refers only to human leaders such as Pilate and the Jewish leaders, or also to spiritual powers; the text allows both readings.

For today: do not measure what God does only by what seems logical or successful. Ask him for humility to receive his wisdom, even when it does not fit the ideas that are in fashion.
exp.7:5:
This verse says that, for Christians, there is one God, the Father. From Him come all things, and we live for Him. It also says that there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist, and through whom we too have life.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted whether they could eat meat that had been offered to idols. Paul reminds them that idols are nothing compared to the one true God. But he also asks them to be careful, because not everyone has that same knowledge, and a weak conscience can be harmed.

Today we can remember that only God deserves first place in our hearts. And at the same time, we can lovingly care for those who are growing in faith, avoiding anything that we see as freedom from causing them to stumble.
exp.13:24:
When someone who does not believe comes into the meeting and hears God's word clearly, his deepest secrets are laid bare. Then he humbles himself, bows down with his face to the ground, worships God, and acknowledges that God is truly among the believers. "Falling down" means bowing to the ground. "Unbeliever" here refers to the one who does not believe, and "the unlearned" are those who do not know these things.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly and many spoke in tongues with no one understanding them. He wants everything to serve to build others up. He compares tongues spoken without interpretation, which confuse visitors, with prophecy, which is understood and reaches the heart.

For today: when we gather, let us aim to speak and serve in a way that everyone can understand. Let our words be clear, sincere, and full of the truth of God, so that whoever visits us may encounter Him.
exp.3:19:
It says that the kingdom of God, that is, God's rule and work among his people, is not shown by fine speeches, but by power. In the verse, the word for this is simply power: the real strength of God that changes lives. It also speaks of people who are puffed up and swollen with pride.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some boasted about their eloquence and looked down on his authority, thinking he would not come back. Paul tells them that he will come, if the Lord wills, and that he will not be concerned with their impressive words, but with whether there is truly the power of God in their lives.

For today: it is not enough to talk about faith, to know Christian phrases, or to sound convinced. Ask yourself whether your life shows the power of God in your character, your love, your patience, and your obedience.
exp.5:16:
It says that whoever is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with Him. The word "but" introduces the contrast with what came before. "Joined" means being bound closely to someone. It is a real and deep union with Christ, through faith, that reaches the innermost part of the person.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, a city where sexual immorality was common. He has just said that joining oneself to a prostitute makes the two "one body." Now he contrasts this: the believer already belongs to Christ and is united with Him. For that reason he cannot take his body and give it over to something else as if it were his own.

For today: before deciding how to use your body, your time, or your relationships, remember that you are united with Christ. Ask yourself: "Does this honor the One with whom I am joined?"
exp.10:9:
Paul says that the woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, and he says this "because of the angels." Some understand this to mean wearing a covering on the head during worship.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its meetings. He is speaking about customs for how men and women prayed and prophesied in public. The phrase "because of the angels" is hard: some think the angels watch over the order of the church; others think there is a background we do not know well. Scholars do not agree.

For today: although customs change, we can make sure that the way we worship shows respect for God, and remember, as the next verse says, that man and woman need each other "in the Lord."
exp.2:1:
Paul says he gave the Corinthians "milk" and not "meat," meaning solid food. "Meat" in the verse above is an old word for food in general, and in this context it means solid food. Milk represents the most basic teachings of the faith. Paul explains that they were not ready for something deeper, and that they still were not ready when he wrote the letter.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, whom he himself had brought to the Gospel. He calls them "babes in Christ" because there was jealousy, quarrels, and factions among them: some said they belonged to Paul and others to Apollos. He speaks to them firmly, but as a father who wants to see them grow.

For today: growing in faith is not measured by how much we know, but by how we live and how we treat others. Ask yourself whether there is envy or rivalry in your heart, and ask God for humility so that you may mature.
exp.1:10:
It says that no one knows the innermost thoughts of a person except that person's own spirit. In the same way, no one can know the depths of God except the Spirit of God. "Knoweth" here means "has come to know" or "understands."

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who boasted of human wisdom. He reminds them that the message of the cross is not discovered through one's own intelligence. God himself makes it known through his Spirit, and believers have received it.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God to help you understand it through his Spirit. Do not rely only on your own intelligence or your opinions. Pray with humility before reading, and listen patiently to what God wants to show you.
exp.4:9:
What it says: Paul clarifies an earlier instruction. When he told them not to associate with the sexually immoral, he did not mean all the immoral, the greedy, the thieves, or the idolaters of this world. The "sexually immoral" are those who practice sexual sin; the "covetous" are those who crave what belongs to others. Avoiding all such people would be impossible without leaving the world altogether.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a man living in serious sexual sin. They had misunderstood an earlier letter. Paul clarifies that his concern is the conduct of those who call themselves brothers, not that of unbelievers.

For today: We can treat neighbors and coworkers who do not believe with kindness, without isolating ourselves, and at the same time humbly guard purity and integrity within the church.
exp.14:49:
Paul says that our present body, fragile and mortal ("flesh and blood"), is not made to live in God's eternal kingdom. "Neither doth" means "does not," and "corruption" refers to what wears out and dies. What perishes cannot inherit what lasts forever.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. Earlier he spoke of Adam, the earthly man, and of Christ, the heavenly one. Here he makes clear that we need to be changed. Right after, he explains this "mystery": believers will be transformed when the final trumpet sounds.

For today: do not live as if this fragile life were all there is. Rest in the fact that God will give you a new body, and so invest your time and strength in what endures: loving, serving, and trusting in Christ.
exp.2:16:
It says that if anyone defiles the temple of God, that is, if he damages it, corrupts it, or ruins it, God himself will destroy him. The reason is that this temple is holy, meaning set apart for God. And Paul makes clear that this temple is you: the community of believers.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, divided by rivalries between leaders and by pride in human wisdom. He reminds them that, as a community, they are the place where the Spirit of God dwells. For this reason he warns with seriousness those who, through divisions or twisted teachings, harm the church. Interpreters debate how to understand "destroy," but all see here a grave warning.

For today: take care of the unity of your church. Before criticizing, gossiping, or dividing, remember that this community is holy to God.
exp.15:18:
This verse says that the churches of the province of Asia send greetings to the believers in Corinth. Aquila and Priscilla, a Christian married couple, also greet them with great affection "in the Lord," that is, as brothers and sisters united to Christ. The church that meets in their house greets them along with them. "The churches of Asia salute you" means they are sending greetings to you.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus, in Asia, near the end of it. Aquila and Priscilla had lived for a time in Corinth and knew that church well. In those days believers often met in homes. These greetings remind the Corinthians that they are not alone, but united with other churches.

For today: the Christian faith is not lived in isolation. We can strengthen others with a message, a call, or a visit. And if we have a home, we can open it simply so that others may gather, pray, and encourage one another.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that when the church gathered for the meal, each person went ahead to eat his own food without waiting for the others. The result was unfair: some went hungry while others ate and drank so much that they became drunk. "Supper" here is the meal that accompanied the Lord's Supper.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to correct divisions among them. The poorer members, who had less, were humiliated in front of those who had more. That is why Paul says that in this way they are not really eating the Lord's Supper, since they were forgetting the love and unity that it represents.

For today: before taking part in communion or in any gathering of the church, let us consider whether we are waiting for, caring for, and looking after our brothers and sisters who are in greatest need, instead of seeking only our own.
exp.2:6:
It says that the one who plants and the one who waters are not what matters most. The essential one is God, because only He makes the seed grow. "Ministers" means servants, and "fellow workers" means co-workers.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the people were divided and boasted of following one leader or another, Paul or Apollos. He reminds them that both are only servants. Paul began the work in Corinth, Apollos continued it, and God gave the fruit. Each one will receive his reward according to his labor.

Today we can serve with enthusiasm, whether by teaching, praying, or helping, without competing or seeking applause. We do our part faithfully and trust that God is the one who transforms hearts. In this way we also avoid admiring a leader too much.
exp.14:23:
This verse says that after the resurrection the end will come. Then Christ will hand over the kingdom to God the Father, after he has put down every rule, authority, and power that opposes God.

The words "rule, authority, and power" refer to forces that hold power. Some believe they refer to spiritual powers, others to human powers, or to both.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection. He explains the order of events: Christ was raised first, then those who belong to him will be raised when he comes, and at the end Christ will present his complete victory to the Father. Paul wants to give them hope and assurance.

For today: even when you see injustice or powers that seem to be in charge, history is not outside God's control. You can live with peace and faithfulness, trusting that Christ reigns and will bring everything to its fulfillment.
exp.10:22:
Paul says that he received from the Lord what he had already taught the Corinthians: that Jesus, on the night he was handed over, took bread. The word "delivered" is an older form of "was delivered over." "Handed over" refers to the time when Jesus was betrayed and placed in the hands of his enemies.

Paul is writing to a divided church. Some were eating and drinking too much during the gathering, while others went hungry and felt humiliated. That is why he reminds them of where the Lord's Supper comes from. Scholars discuss how he "received" this from the Lord: it may have been through direct revelation or through tradition handed down, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: when we take part in the Lord's Supper, let us do so with gratitude and reverence, thinking of Christ and of our brothers and sisters. Before we eat together, let us ask ourselves whether we are caring for those in greatest need.
exp.13:22:
This verse says that if the whole church comes together in one place and everyone speaks in tongues at the same time, and people come in who do not know what is going on in the church, or who do not yet believe, they will think the believers are out of their minds. It is a question that expects the answer yes.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had a great deal of disorder in its meetings. He valued the spiritual gifts, but he wanted everything to help build up everyone. So he compares speaking in tongues, which without interpretation cannot be understood, with prophecy, which speaks clearly and reaches the heart. Scholars debate exactly what speaking in tongues was like in Corinth.

For today: when we gather, let us think of the person who comes for the first time. Let us make sure that what we do or say is clear, orderly, and useful, so that others can understand and find God.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that whoever takes part in the Lord's Supper in an unworthy manner, that is, without respect or seriousness, brings judgment on himself. Here "judgment" means correction or punishment, not necessarily eternal condemnation. Not recognizing what the bread means is the sense of the phrase about not discerning the Lord's body: the sacrifice of Christ and, according to many, the church as his body.

Paul writes to the Corinthians because in their communal meals some were getting drunk while others went hungry, looking down on the poorer members. The Supper had become selfish. Interpreters explain in various ways the sickness and death he mentions afterward, but he sees them as God's discipline.

Before taking part in the Supper, stop and examine your heart: confess whatever is wrong, ask forgiveness, and make peace with anyone you have offended. Then eat and drink with gratitude and respect toward Christ and toward your brothers and sisters.
exp.6:11:
Paul is speaking about a believer who is married to someone who does not believe. In this older version, "infidel" means "unbelieving," not "one who deceives a partner." To "put away" means to "send away" or "divorce." If the unbelieving wife is willing to keep living with him, the believer must not leave her.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage. Earlier he had cited a clear teaching of Jesus about not divorcing. Here he says "I say, not the Lord" because Jesus had not addressed this particular case: mixed marriages of faith. This does not mean his word lacks authority, but that he is giving apostolic guidance for this new situation.

If your spouse does not share your faith, do not take that as a reason to abandon the home. Serve with patience, love, and a good example, and trust that God can work in your family.
exp.8:22:
Paul says that everything he does, adapting himself to different people, he does for the sake of the gospel. "Partaker of it" means that he wants to share in its blessings too, not only to proclaim it to others. Old words: the "weak" are those who are weak in faith or in conscience; "by all means" means "by every possible means."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. In this chapter he explains that he gave up some of his rights so as not to hinder anyone. He adapted himself to Jews, to Gentiles, and to the weak, without changing the message or abandoning the law of Christ. Right after this, he moves on to the image of the race, which speaks of discipline.

For today: think of someone close to you who thinks differently from you. Ask yourself what you might give up, or how you could listen to them with more patience, so that they may see the love of Christ, without compromising the truth.
exp.15:2:
In this verse Paul tells the Corinthians that when he arrives, he will send to Jerusalem whomever they choose and approve through letters. These men will carry the church's gift.

The word "liberality" in the King James text refers to the gift itself, the generous help. The phrase "when I come" is the same idea as "when I arrive."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He has already explained how to set aside money each week. Now he clarifies who will carry the money: not he alone, but people approved by the church itself. In this way trust was protected and any suspicion was avoided. Some think the letters were letters of introduction; the text gives no further details.

For today: if we handle money for a church or for a relief work, let us do it with order, clarity and accountability. Generosity is best cared for when everything is done with transparency.
exp.4:11:
Paul asks: what have I to do with judging those outside the church? That is, it is not his place or the church's place to correct outsiders. Instead, he asks the Corinthians whether they themselves should not judge, that is, evaluate and correct, those who are inside the community of faith. "Judge" here means to discern and act with discipline, not to condemn with contempt.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a brother who was living in serious immorality (this has been the subject since verse 1). They were even proud of it. Paul makes clear that he is not asking them to isolate themselves from the world, but not to give shelter or close fellowship to someone who calls himself a Christian and lives in sin without repenting. His goal is to protect the church and, according to other passages, also to help the person return to God.

For today: instead of criticizing those who do not believe, care with humility and love for the life of your own community. If a brother is going astray, speak with him in private, with the aim of restoring him, and leave the final judgment of others to God.
exp.2:2:
It says that the Corinthians still live by their human impulses and not by the Spirit. The proof is the jealousy, the quarrels, and the divisions among them. "Carnal" means guided by human nature without the influence of God, and "walk as men" means they behave like any ordinary person in the world. "Strife" refers to arguments and lawsuits.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had split into groups: some said they belonged to Paul and others to Apollos. He calls them "babes in Christ" because their conduct showed little maturity. He had given them milk, basic teachings, and not solid food.

For today: if there is rivalry in your church or family, ask yourself whether you are defending a person or a faction instead of Christ. Seek peace and serve with humility.
exp.6:22:
God says that he paid a price for us, that is, he bought us for himself. For that reason we should not live as slaves to other people's opinions, fear, or demands. Here "servants" means slaves. "Ye are bought" refers to what Christ did on the cross to redeem us.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about how to live their faith in everyday life. Earlier he spoke about slaves: if they could become free, that was better, but their worth did not depend on their social standing. Some scholars believe he also warns against submitting to human pressures that pull people away from Christ.

For today: before deciding something, ask yourself whom you want to please. Seek to live for God with freedom, and not to be controlled by what others will say.
exp.15:3:
Paul says that if the offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem is important or significant enough to be worthwhile, he will also go, and the men the church chooses will travel with him. Here "business" means a matter or assignment, not a commercial deal. "Worthy" means that it is fitting for it to be done.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and gives them instructions for the collection for Jerusalem. He had already asked them to set money aside each week. Here he leaves open the possibility of accompanying the delivery, without requiring it. Some think the amount collected would influence his decision, but the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when we handle church money or help for others, let us do it with order, with several responsible people involved, and with complete transparency, so that no one doubts our integrity.
exp.6:26:
This verse says that a man who is married should not seek to be released from his wife, and a man who is not married should not go looking for a wife. "Bound" means joined in marriage, and "loosed" means having that bond undone. "Loosed" refers to someone who has no spouse.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage and staying single. He makes clear that here he is giving his own judgment, not a direct command from the Lord. He speaks of "the present distress," a difficult situation that some understand as persecution or crisis in that time. Scholars interpret it in different ways. He does not forbid marriage, as the next verse shows.

For today: trust in your present situation and serve God there. If you are married, take care of your marriage. If you are single, do not live anxiously about getting married; make the most of this season with peace and devotion.
exp.12:6:
This verse describes what love is like. In the Reina-Valera 1909 it is called "caridad," but your reader sees the word "love" in the verse, so we speak of love here. The idea of enduring means bearing up patiently under hard things, and the idea of holding firm means staying steady without giving up. Believing all things and hoping all things speak of trusting others and holding onto hope for them. Many understand this not to mean being naive, but to mean not being quick to suspect.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and boasted about its spiritual gifts. In this chapter he shows them that without love, the gifts are worth nothing. He describes how true love behaves, and then says that love remains, while the gifts are temporary.

For today: when someone lets you down, before reacting with anger or distrust, pray and choose to give them one more chance, with patience and hope, without giving up on telling the truth.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that the temptation we face is common to all human beings; no one experiences something completely unique. God is faithful: he will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear. Along with the temptation, he provides a way out, a way of escape, so that we can endure it. Enduring means bearing up without giving in.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of idolatry and immorality. He has just recalled how Israel fell in the desert, and he warns that whoever thinks they stand firm must be careful. This verse encourages: falling is not inevitable. Right after this, he asks them to flee from idolatry.

For today: when temptation comes, do not think there is no remedy. Ask God for help and look for the concrete way out: move away from the place, end a conversation, or tell a trusted friend.
exp.14:57:
Here is what the verse says: because of what Christ has already accomplished, believers should stand firm and not be moved from their faith. The word "abounding" here means giving more and more in service to the Lord. The word "in vain" means useless or without result. Nothing done for God is lost.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had doubts and divisions, and some denied the resurrection of the dead. After explaining that Christ rose and that believers will also rise, and after saying that God gives us victory over death, he closes with this call. Because the resurrection is real, Christian work has eternal value.

For today: when you grow tired of serving, of praying, or of doing good without seeing results, remember that God sees and does not forget. Stay faithful today in one concrete task, such as helping someone or serving in your church.
exp.7:10:
It says that a person with a lot of knowledge can cause a weaker brother in the faith to be lost. And it makes this more serious by reminding us that Christ died for that brother. "Knowledge" here means understanding. The weak one is someone whose faith or conscience is fragile. "Shall perish" speaks of falling into spiritual ruin; interpreters debate whether this is a final loss or a serious harm to his faith.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were arguing about whether it was right to eat meat offered to idols. Those who were more informed knew that idols are nothing and ate without guilt. But some believers, newly come out of paganism, were confused when they saw this. Paul asks them not to use their freedom without thinking of others.

For today: before doing something you consider permissible, ask yourself how it will affect someone whose faith is more fragile. Loving that brother is worth more than defending your right.
exp.14:19:
He says that Christ truly rose, and that His resurrection is the beginning of a greater one. The "firstfruits" are the first part of a harvest, and they announce that the rest will follow. "Have slept" is a gentle way of speaking of those who died, as one who expects to wake up.

The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom some denied the resurrection of the dead. Earlier he has said that if Christ has not risen, faith is empty. Here he answers firmly: "But now," that is, things are not that way, Christ has risen. Then he compares Him with Adam: by one man came death, and by another comes life.

Today, this truth gives us hope in the face of pain and death. If you have lost a loved one who trusted in Christ, you can rest in the knowledge that the grave does not have the last word. Live with that firm hope.
exp.13:7:
This verse says that if a trumpet does not sound clearly, no one knows what to do. "Uncertain sound" is a confused call, one that cannot be understood. The word "battle" in the verse refers to war, and in ancient times the trumpet gave signals to soldiers: to advance, to retreat, or to get ready. If the signal was not clear, no one knew how to respond.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were proud of speaking in tongues during the meetings, yet no one understood what they were saying. Paul uses the examples of musical instruments and the trumpet to show that a confusing message helps no one. His goal is for the church to be built up.

For today: when we teach, pray together, or share the Word, let us speak with clarity and simplicity. What matters is not sounding impressive, but helping others understand and obey God.
exp.8:18:
It says that Paul is free and does not depend on anyone, yet he still chose to put himself at the service of everyone. His aim was to gain more people, that is, to win more people to Christ. The word "servant" means slave or servant, and "gain" means to bring people to believe the gospel.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. In this chapter he explains that, as an apostle, he had the right to receive financial support for his work, but he did not demand it. He preferred to preach without charge so that nothing would hinder the gospel. With this decision to give up his rights, he gives them an example to follow.

Today we can ask ourselves what rights or comforts we are willing to set aside out of love for others. Perhaps it is listening patiently to someone different from us, or serving without expecting recognition, so that others may see the love of Christ in our lives.
exp.9:0:
Paul says he does not want the believers to be unaware of something important: the ancestors of Israel, "our fathers," were all under the cloud that guided them, and all of them passed through the Red Sea. The word "ignorant" in the verse above means not knowing or failing to understand, and the sea is simply the sea.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community marked by divisions and a great tolerance of sin. He reminds them of Israel's story in the Exodus. All of them received great blessings from God, but then many fell into idolatry and immorality, as he explains in the verses that follow. He says "our fathers" because he sees the church as part of God's people.

Having received God's blessings is not the same as living in obedience. Do not rely on your spiritual past, your church, or your experiences. Ask God to keep you faithful and attentive today.
exp.3:6:
Paul asks three questions to show that no one has reason to boast. The first question, "who maketh thee to differ?", means "who makes you better than others?" Then the second part, "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?", means that everything you have was given to you. If you received it as a gift, there is no sense in bragging as if you had obtained it on your own.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, who were divided and took pride in their favorite leaders, such as himself and Apollos. He asks them not to compare themselves with one another or think of themselves as superior. Then, with irony, he confronts them about their air of greatness, while the apostles were suffering.

For today: when you feel pride in your talents, your work, or your faith, remember that everything is a gift from God. That leads us to be thankful, to serve with humility, and to stop comparing ourselves with others.
exp.11:21:
Paul says that the members of the body that seem weaker ("feeble") are actually very necessary, even more than we realize. The word "feeble" here means fragile or having little appearance of strength. The word "necessary" in the earlier context means a need.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over spiritual gifts. Some believed they were more important than others. Paul uses the image of the human body to show that the church is one body with many members, and that all depend on one another.

For today: value those who go unnoticed in your church or family, such as the person who prays in silence, helps without being seen, or is going through a time of weakness. Today, seek out one of those people and thank them with specific words.
exp.9:11:
This verse says that a person who feels secure in their faith must be careful not to fall. The phrase "let him take heed" means "be careful" or "pay attention." To stand firm is to feel strong and steady on the path with God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. He reminds them how the people of Israel, although they had received great blessings from God, fell into idolatry, immorality, and complaining. Those stories were written as a warning for the church. Some Corinthians believed their knowledge made them immune to danger.

For today: do not trust in your past spiritual strength. Recognize your weak points, seek counsel from mature brothers and sisters, stay close to prayer and the Word, and flee quickly from whatever makes you stumble. Humility keeps us standing.
exp.3:16:
Paul says that for this reason he has sent Timothy to them, whom he calls his beloved son and faithful in the Lord. Timothy will remind them of Paul's ways in Christ, that is, his manner of living and teaching. To "admonish" means to advise and remind with affection, so Timothy will bring them back to Paul's way of life. Paul teaches the same thing in every church.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a divided and proud church. He founded it and regards himself as their spiritual father. Since he invited them to imitate him, he sends them Timothy, a living example of that life. Some had become puffed up, thinking Paul would not return.

Today we need humble and faithful examples who show us how to live out the gospel. Seek out someone like this to learn from, and try to be a simple and faithful example to others yourself.
exp.10:23:
That night Jesus was betrayed, he gave thanks to God for the bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples. He told them to take it and eat it, and explained that the bread stood for his body given up for them. He commanded them to keep doing this as a way of remembering him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had problems: at their shared meals some ate too much while others, the poor, were left embarrassed. Paul reminds them of what he received from the Lord about the supper, in order to correct their disorder. Christians understand in different ways how Christ is present in the supper, but all agree that it is an act of remembrance.

For today: when you take part in the Lord's Supper, do it with gratitude and attention, and treat the other believers with respect and care, especially those in greatest need.
exp.11:20:
It says that no member of the body can look down on another. The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you," nor can the head say to the feet, "I have no need of you." Some older words in the verse are explained as well, but those explanations do not carry over to the King James wording. Each part, even though it is different, is important for the body to work well.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride, especially over spiritual gifts. Some people felt superior to others. Paul uses the image of the body to explain that the church is one body with many members, and that all depend on one another.

Today we can ask ourselves: whom in my church or family have I looked down on? This week, thank someone whose service goes unnoticed, and tell them that you need them.
exp.4:12:
Paul says that God himself will judge the people who are outside the church. But the church is responsible for removing the wicked person, meaning the one who calls himself a brother and lives in serious sin without repenting. "Put away" means to take out or separate. The old spelling of the word "to" is written with an accent mark, which is why it looks unusual on the page.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, a church that tolerated a man living in serious sexual immorality (5:1). He does not ask them to judge the world, but to protect the purity and witness of the community. Many understand that the goal of this discipline is also that the person would react and be restored; the letter later mentions something similar (2 Corinthians 2:5-8), although not everyone agrees that it concerns the same case.

For today: instead of criticizing those who do not believe, examine your own life and that of your church. If you must correct a brother, do it with humility, prayer, and a desire to see him restored, not with pride or rejection.
exp.13:1:
This verse says that whoever speaks in an unknown tongue is not speaking to people but to God, because no one understands him. Although he speaks mysteries in the spirit (hidden things that God reveals), the listeners do not grasp their meaning.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some people highly valued speaking in tongues and used it in their gatherings even though no one understood. He does not forbid it, but he teaches them that, in the congregation, what matters most is what helps everyone, such as prophecy, which builds up, encourages, and comforts. Some scholars think the tongues are real human languages, and others think they are a prayer language; the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you serve in church, ask yourself whether what you do or say helps others understand and grow in faith, because love seeks the good of others.
exp.11:4:
This verse says that in the church there are different ways of serving, but they all come from the same Lord. The word "administrations" points to the different kinds of service or work done for the benefit of others. In other words, God does not hand out just one kind of service, but many.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who were divided and placed too much importance on certain spiritual gifts. Earlier he spoke of the Spirit, now he speaks of the Lord Jesus, and next he will speak of God the Father. Many see here a glimpse of the Trinity, although Paul does not explain the subject in detail. His point is that variety should not divide, because the source is one.

Today, do not compare your service with that of others. Whether it is teaching, visiting the sick, praying, or helping with practical needs, do your part as service to the Lord, and value what others do.
exp.11:5:
The verse says there are "diversities of operations," meaning different ways in which work is carried out or an effect is produced, but behind all of them stands the same God. And the phrase "worketh all in all" means that God is the one who gives power and makes everything come to pass in each believer.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was divided and placed too much importance on certain spiritual gifts. Here he mentions all three Persons: the Spirit, the Lord, and God. Many see in this a reflection of the Trinity. His purpose is to show that variety is no reason for rivalry, because the source is one.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or look down on your own contribution. Serve with what God has given you, recognizing that the power comes from him, and value the brothers and sisters who serve in ways different from yours.

sum.3: Paul asks that people see him as a servant of Christ, and that what matters most is being faithful, since only the Lord truly judges. He calls the Corinthians to set aside their pride, reminding them that they have received everything they have. He presents himself as a father who corrects them out of love. He announces that he will come to them soon, and that the Corinthians must decide whether they would prefer to see him come with a rod or in gentleness.
sum.1: Paul recalls that when he went to Corinth, he did not use fancy words or human wisdom. Instead, he proclaimed Jesus Christ crucified, relying on the power of the Spirit, so that the faith of his hearers would rest on the power of God. He explains that God reveals his hidden wisdom through the Spirit, and that a person who is not spiritual does not understand it, but believers have the mind of Christ.
sum.4: Paul rebukes the church in Corinth for tolerating, and even taking pride in, a serious sexual sin among them, and he tells them to remove the person who committed it from the community. He reminds them that a little yeast works through the whole batch of dough, and that Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed, so they should live with sincerity and truth. They are not to judge the outside world, but to guard purity within the church.
sum.5: Paul rebukes the believers in Corinth for taking their lawsuits before judges who do not believe, and he tells them it is better to endure injustice than to harm a fellow believer. He also warns that those who live in sin will not inherit the kingdom of God, even though they have already been washed and made right with God in Christ. He asks them to flee sexual immorality, because their body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and belongs to God.
sum.13: Paul teaches that when the church gathers, everything should be done in love and for the building up of the church. For this reason he values prophecy more highly than speaking in tongues without interpretation, since prophecy is something everyone can understand. He calls for order and peace in worship. He concludes by saying that people should seek to prophesy, not forbid speaking in tongues, and that everything should be done properly and decently.
sum.0: Paul greets the church in Corinth and thanks God for the gifts he has given them in Christ. He urges them to put an end to their divisions, since each of them was claiming to follow a different leader. He teaches them that the cross seems like foolishness to the world, but it is the power and wisdom of God, so no one should boast except in the Lord.
sum.15: Paul asks that each Sunday they set aside an offering to help the saints in Jerusalem, and he tells them about his plans to visit them. He encourages them to stay alert, stand firm in the faith, and do everything with love, and he asks them to show respect to Timothy and to those who serve, such as Stephanas. He ends with greetings and a blessing of grace.
sum.12: Paul teaches that without love, the greatest gifts, such as speaking in tongues, prophesying, having faith, or giving everything to the poor, are worth nothing. He describes what love is like: patient, kind, without envy or pride, and that it never fails. Gifts will come to an end, but faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love.
sum.10: Paul corrects two problems in the church at Corinth: how people pray and prophesy during their gatherings, with instructions about covering the head, and abuses at the Lord's Supper, where some ate without waiting for others. He reminds them that the Supper proclaims the death of Christ and calls for self-examination, waiting for one another, and treating each other with respect.
sum.2: Paul rebukes the Corinthians for following human leaders and quarreling with one another, since this shows they are still immature. The leaders are only servants of God, who gives the growth, and each person's work will be tested. The Corinthians are God's temple, and everything belongs to them because they belong to Christ.
sum.14: Paul recalls the gospel: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, and many saw him. He explains that if there is no resurrection, faith is empty, but Christ has been raised as the firstfruits. Believers will be transformed with imperishable bodies, death will be defeated, and for this reason we must stand firm in the Lord.
sum.6: Paul answers questions from the Corinthians about marriage and staying single. He advises faithfulness and mutual devotion within marriage, that spouses should not separate, and that each person should remain in the situation they were called to. He prefers singleness because the time is short and because it allows a person to serve the Lord without distractions, but he permits marriage without sin.
sum.7: Paul explains that although Christians know that idols are nothing and that there is only one God, knowledge without love only puffs a person up with pride. Some believers who are weak still feel confused about food that has been offered to idols. For that reason, love leads us not to use our freedom in a way that causes a brother or sister to fall.
sum.9: Paul recalls how Israel fell into idolatry, sexual immorality, and grumbling in the wilderness, and he warns us not to trust too much in our own strength. God is faithful and provides a way out when we are tempted. He calls us to flee from idolatry and to live in freedom, seeking the good of others and the glory of God.
sum.8: Paul defends his status as a true apostle and says he would have the right to be supported by his ministry, but he gave up that right so that he would not place any obstacle in the way of the gospel. He became all things to all people so that he might win some. He compares the Christian life to a race that requires discipline and self-control.
sum.11: Paul teaches that there are many different spiritual gifts, but all of them come from the same Spirit, Lord, and God, and they are given for the good of everyone. The church is like a body with many parts: all of them are different, all of them are necessary, and they should care for one another. At the end, he invites people to seek the best gifts and announces a more excellent way.
